units.title: الحروف: the Arabic script

lessons.title: 1. Reading Arabic
lessons.subtitle: Direction, joined letters and vowel marks

explanations.title: Right to left
explanations.body: Arabic is written and read from right to left, so the first letter of a word is on the right and a page starts at the right-hand edge. There are no capital letters. The alphabet has 28 letters, and all of them are consonants, though three also stand for long vowels.

examples.translation: kitāb — a book
bayt — a house
madrasa — a school

explanations.title: Letters join up
explanations.body: Arabic is always joined up, in print as well as by hand. Most letters change shape a little depending on whether they join to the letter before, to the one after, or both. The table shows how separate letters become a word. Read each row from right to left.

explanations.title: The vowels are usually left out
explanations.body: Arabic has three short vowels, and ordinary texts do not write them: a newspaper prints كتاب, not كِتَاب. Fluent readers fill them in from the word and the sentence. In this course every word is written with its vowel marks so you can learn how to say it, and a transliteration (the Latin-letter “Sound”) is shown beside it at first. Treat the transliteration as scaffolding and learn to read the Arabic itself.

examples.translation: kitāb — with vowel marks, as in this course
without them, as in a newspaper

exercises.prompt: Which way is Arabic written and read?
exercises.explanation: Arabic runs right to left: the first letter of a word is on the right.

exercises.prompt: How many letters are in the Arabic alphabet?
What can you say about capital letters in Arabic?
options: Only the first word of a title has one
exercises.explanation: Arabic has no capital letters at all.

exercises.prompt: In a newspaper, how are the short vowels usually shown?
exercises.explanation: Ordinary texts leave short vowels out; readers supply them from context.

exercises.prompt: Arabic is written from ___ to left.
exercises.explanation: The first letter of an Arabic word is on the right.

exercises.prompt: The word بَيْت has how many letters?
exercises.explanation: ب, ي and ت: three letters. The small marks above and below them are vowel signs (and a sukūn), not letters.

exercises.prompt: Why does this course print a transliteration beside Arabic words?
options: Because Arabic is normally written in Latin letters
To help you at first while you learn to read
Because the transliteration is what the voice reads
exercises.explanation: It is scaffolding; the aim is to read the Arabic itself.

exercises.prompt: When letters join, in which order do you read a joined word?
options: Last letter first, then the rest left to right
Right to left, letter by letter
exercises.explanation: Each letter is read in the order it is written, starting from the right.

lessons.title: 2. The first six letters
lessons.subtitle: ا ب ت ث ن ي

explanations.title: Five letters, one shape
explanations.body: Four of these letters share one boat-like body and are told apart by their dots (the final ن also has a deeper, rounder bowl): ب has one dot below, ت two dots above, ث three dots above and ن one dot above. ي is nearly the same shape, with two dots below. The dots are part of the letter, so never leave them out.

rows: y as in yes; also a long ee
tables.note: Tap a name to hear it. Each letter has a form for the start of a word, the middle and the end.

explanations.title: Alif stands alone
explanations.body: ا (alif) is a straight line with no dots. It is a long “aa” as in father, and it is one of six letters that never join to the letter after them, so the next letter starts a new shape.

rows: a long aa, as in father

exercises.prompt: Which letter has one dot below?
exercises.explanation: ب (bāʾ) has a single dot under its body.

exercises.prompt: Which letter has three dots above?
Which letter has two dots above?
Which letter has one dot above?
Which letter makes the sound “th” as in think?
exercises.explanation: ث is th, as in think.
ت is tāʾ, the letter for t.

exercises.prompt: Which letter does NOT join to the letter after it?
Which is the form of ب that starts a word?
exercises.explanation: The starting form has its tail cut off and joins to the left.

exercises.prompt: Which is the form of ن that ends a word?
exercises.explanation: The ending form joins to the letter on its right and keeps its full curve.

explanations.title: Three vowels and a zero
explanations.body: Short vowels are small marks written above or below a consonant. The fatḥa is a short stroke above (a), the kasra a short stroke below (i) and the ḍamma a little loop above (u). The sukūn, a small circle above, means the letter carries no vowel at all.

rows: a, like the u in cut
i, like the i in sit
u, like the u in put

explanations.title: Syllables
explanations.body: A consonant plus a short vowel makes a syllable, and a syllable can end in a consonant with a sukūn. Read the table across, then try the word below it.

examples.translation: bint — a girl; a daughter

exercises.explanation: The fatḥa is a short stroke above the letter.
The kasra is a short stroke below the letter.

exercises.prompt: Which mark is the sukūn (no vowel)?
exercises.explanation: The sukūn is a small circle above the letter.
بِ is read “bi”: sound out the letters from right to left.
تُ is read “tu”: sound out the letters from right to left.
ثَ is read “tha”: sound out the letters from right to left.
A kasra gives the vowel i.
ب has a kasra (bi), ن has a sukūn (n) and ت is bare at the end: bint.

exercises.prompt: In بِنْت, what sits on the letter ن?
exercises.explanation: The small circle over ن means it has no vowel, so it closes the syllable: bint is a single syllable.

lessons.title: 4. Long vowels and و
lessons.subtitle: ā ī ū, and the glides ay and aw

explanations.title: A vowel plus a letter makes it long
explanations.body: Three letters double as long vowels. Alif after a fatḥa gives ā, yāʾ after a kasra gives ī and wāw after a ḍamma gives ū. The new letter و (wāw) is also a consonant w, as in water, and like alif it never joins to the letter after it.

rows: w as in water; also a long oo

explanations.title: Glides: ay and aw
explanations.body: A fatḥa followed by ي with a sukūn gives the glide ay, as in the English word eye said as one sound. A fatḥa followed by و with a sukūn gives aw, as in cow.

examples.translation: bayt — a house
thawb — a garment; a dress
bāb — a door
tīn — figs

explanations.title: The word “and”
explanations.body: وَ means “and”. It is written as one letter, attached to the word after it with no space.

examples.translation: bāb wabayt — a door and a house

exercises.explanation: بَاب is read “bāb”: sound out the letters from right to left.
تِين is read “tīn”: sound out the letters from right to left.
ثَوْب is read “thawb”: sound out the letters from right to left.
بَيْت is read “bayt”: sound out the letters from right to left.

exercises.prompt: Which letter, after a kasra, makes a long ī?
exercises.explanation: Yāʾ after a kasra gives ī.

exercises.prompt: Which letter, after a ḍamma, makes a long ū?
exercises.explanation: Wāw after a ḍamma gives ū.
وَ is the word “and”, written attached to the next word.

explanations.title: One body, three sounds
explanations.body: These three share a hooked body and are told apart by one dot. ج has a dot inside, ح has none, and خ has a dot above.

rows: ḥ: a breathy h from deep in the throat, like fogging a mirror
kh: like ch in Scottish loch

explanations.title: Your first words
explanations.body: You can now read words that use all the letters so far. Sound each one out, then tap it.

exercises.prompt: Which letter has a dot inside its body?
exercises.explanation: ج has a dot inside (below the line); ح has none and خ has one above.

exercises.prompt: Which of these has NO dot?
exercises.explanation: ح is the plain hooked letter.

exercises.prompt: Which letter sounds like ch in Scottish loch?
Which letter is a breathy h from the throat?
exercises.explanation: ح (ḥ) is a strong, breathy h.
نَحْنُ is read “naḥnu”: sound out the letters from right to left.
جَيْب is read “jayb”: sound out the letters from right to left.

lessons.title: 6. د ذ ر ز
lessons.subtitle: Four letters that never join forward

explanations.title: Short letters
explanations.body: These four are small and, like alif and wāw, never join to the letter after them. A word simply leaves a small gap after them.

rows: r, tapped or rolled, as in Spanish pero
tables.note: ذ is د with a dot, and ز is ر with a dot.

explanations.title: Words you can read now
explanations.body: With these letters you can read some of the most useful words in Arabic.

exercises.prompt: Which letter is d as in dog?
Which letter is dh as in this?
exercises.explanation: ذ (dhāl) is د with a dot above.

exercises.prompt: Which letter has a dot above and is read z?
exercises.explanation: ز (zāy) is ر with a dot.

exercises.prompt: Which letter is the rolled r?
What is special about د ذ ر ز و ا?
options: They do not join to the letter after them
They only appear at the end of words
exercises.explanation: These six letters join only to the letter before them.
جَدِيد is read “jadīd”: sound out the letters from right to left.
بَحْر is read “baḥr”: sound out the letters from right to left.

lessons.title: 7. س ش ص ض
lessons.subtitle: The “teeth” letters and two heavy ones

explanations.title: Plain and heavy
explanations.body: س and ش have three small teeth; ص and ض have a closed loop. ص and ض are “emphatic” letters: you say them with the tongue pulled back and the mouth hollow, which gives the neighbouring vowels a darker, heavier sound. English has nothing like it, so listen and copy.

rows: ṣ: a heavy s, with the mouth hollow
ḍ: a heavy d, with the mouth hollow
tables.note: ش is س with three dots; ض is ص with one dot.

explanations.title: More words
explanations.body: Read these aloud. The first one is the first word of “good morning”, صَبَاح الْخَيْر.

exercises.prompt: Which letter is sh as in ship?
Which letter is a plain s?
Which letter is the heavy s?
Which letter is the heavy d, with a dot above?
exercises.explanation: ض (ḍād) is ص with a dot.

exercises.prompt: Which letter has three dots above its teeth?
exercises.explanation: ش has three dots above; س has none.
صَبَاح is read “ṣabāḥ”: sound out the letters from right to left.
شَخْص is read “shakhṣ”: sound out the letters from right to left.

lessons.title: 8. ط ظ ع غ
lessons.subtitle: Two heavy letters and two throat letters

explanations.title: Heavy ṭ and ẓ
explanations.body: ط and ظ are the emphatic partners of ت and ذ: the same sounds, said with the tongue pulled back and the mouth hollow. ظ is ط with a dot above.

rows: ẓ: a heavy dh, as in this

explanations.title: Two sounds with no English letter
explanations.body: ع (ʿayn) is made by squeezing the throat while voicing; it is the sound many learners find hardest, so listen to it often. غ (ghayn) is ع with a dot above and sounds like a gargled French r. Both have four shapes, and the middle shape of ع looks like a small triangle.

rows: ʿ: a voiced squeeze deep in the throat
gh: like a gargled French r

explanations.title: More words
explanations.body: Some useful words made of the letters you know.

exercises.prompt: Which letter is the heavy t?
Which letter is the heavy dh, with a dot above?
exercises.explanation: ظ (ẓāʾ) is ط with a dot.

exercises.prompt: Which letter is the throat squeeze ʿ?
exercises.explanation: ع (ʿayn) has no dot; غ (ghayn) has one.

exercises.prompt: Which letter sounds like a gargled French r?

exercises.explanation: طَبِيب is read “ṭabīb”: sound out the letters from right to left.
عَيْن is read “ʿayn”: sound out the letters from right to left.

explanations.title: Four more
explanations.body: ف has one dot above and ق two, both with a round head. ك, in its separate and final forms, has a small zigzag above a flat base and ل is a tall stroke with a hook. ق (qāf) is a k said far back in the throat.

rows: q: a deep k from the back of the throat

explanations.title: Lām plus alif
explanations.body: When ل is followed by ا the two letters fuse into one shape, لا, which is read lā. It is not a new letter, just how those two always look together. It is also the word لَا: no, not.

examples.translation: lā — no; not

explanations.title: Words with the new letters
explanations.body: Read these aloud, then tap them.

exercises.prompt: Which letter has two dots above and a round head?
exercises.explanation: ق (qāf) has two dots; ف has one.

exercises.prompt: Which letter is a k said far back in the throat?
Which letter is the plain k, with a zigzag?
What do ل and ا make when they meet?
exercises.explanation: Lām and alif always fuse into لا.
كِتَاب is read “kitāb”: sound out the letters from right to left.
قَرِيب is read “qarīb”: sound out the letters from right to left.

lessons.title: 10. م ه and the whole alphabet
lessons.subtitle: The last letters, and the alphabet in order

explanations.title: The last two
explanations.body: م is a small round head on a line and ه has four quite different shapes, so look at it carefully. ه is a light h as in hat, breathed out.

rows: h as in hat, but lighter

explanations.title: The alphabet in order
explanations.body: This is the traditional order. Dictionaries and word lists follow it. You now know every letter.

explanations.title: Small, useful words
explanations.body: These very common words are all built from letters you have met.

exercises.prompt: Which letter is a light h as in hat?
exercises.explanation: ه (hāʾ) is the light h; ح is the heavy throat h.

exercises.prompt: Which letter comes right after ا in the alphabet?
exercises.explanation: The order starts ا ب ت ث.

exercises.prompt: Which letter comes last in the alphabet?
exercises.explanation: The alphabet ends ... ن ه و ي.

exercises.prompt: Which letter comes right before م in the alphabet?

exercises.explanation: هُوَ is read “huwa”: sound out the letters from right to left.
مِنْ is read “min”: sound out the letters from right to left.

explanations.title: Shadda: say it twice
explanations.body: The shadda ـّ, a small w-shaped mark, doubles a consonant: the letter is held a little longer, as in the English “book-case” or the Italian “nonno”. The vowel goes on the shadda, above or below it.

examples.translation: mudarris — a teacher
ʿarabiyy — Arab; Arabic
jayyid — good

explanations.title: Tanwīn: the -an ending
explanations.body: Tanwīn is a doubled vowel mark at the end of a word that adds an n sound. The most common one, the double fatḥa ـً, is usually written with an extra alif (but not after ة or ـاء) and forms many adverbs and greetings.

exercises.explanation: The shadda holds the letter for twice as long.

exercises.prompt: What does a tanwīn on the end of a word add?
options: an n sound after the vowel
exercises.explanation: ـً is read -an, ـٌ is read -un and ـٍ is read -in.
مُدَرِّس is read “mudarris”: sound out the letters from right to left.
عَرَبِيّ is read “ʿarabiyy”: sound out the letters from right to left.
شُكْرًا is read “shukran”: sound out the letters from right to left.
The د in جِدًّا is doubled (jid-dan); the others have only a tanwīn.

lessons.title: 12. Hamza, tāʾ marbūṭa and alif maqṣūra
lessons.subtitle: Letters that look like other letters

explanations.title: Hamza ء
explanations.body: The hamza is the catch in the throat in the middle of “uh-oh”. It is not one of the 28 letters, but it appears all the time. It sits on a “chair” that depends on the neighbouring vowels: on an alif (أ above, إ below), on a و (ؤ), on a ي without dots (ئ), or alone (ء). At the start of a word the chair is always an alif.

explanations.title: Two endings
explanations.body: ة (tāʾ marbūṭa) is a ه with two dots and marks most feminine words. At the end of a word it is read simply a, not t. ى (alif maqṣūra) looks like ي without dots but is read as a long ā.

options: A catch in the throat, as in uh-oh

exercises.prompt: On which letter does a hamza always sit at the start of a word?
exercises.explanation: At the start of a word the chair is an alif.

exercises.prompt: How is ة read at the end of a word?
exercises.explanation: ة ends feminine words and is read a (it becomes t when more is added).

exercises.prompt: How is ى at the end of a word read?
exercises.explanation: Alif maqṣūra is a long ā written with the yāʾ shape and no dots.
أَنَا is read “ʾanā”: sound out the letters from right to left.
مَدْرَسَة is read “madrasa”: sound out the letters from right to left.
عَلَى is read “ʿalā”: sound out the letters from right to left.

explanations.title: One word for “the”
explanations.body: Arabic has one word for “the”: the prefix ال, written attached to the noun and the same for masculine, feminine, singular and plural. A noun without it is indefinite, so كِتَاب is “a book” and الْكِتَاب is “the book”.

examples.translation: al-kitāb — the book
al-bayt — the house
al-madrasa — the school

explanations.title: Moon letters and sun letters
explanations.body: The ل of ال is pronounced before 14 letters, called moon letters (الْقَمَر, al-qamar). Before the 14 sun letters it is not heard: it melts into the next letter, which is doubled and marked with a shadda (الشَّمْس, ash-shams, not al-shams). The spelling does not change; only the pronunciation and the marks do.

rows: ا ب ج ح خ ع غ ف ق ك م ه و ي
ت ث د ذ ر ز س ش ص ض ط ظ ل ن

explanations.title: Practice with both kinds
explanations.body: Sun letters: the shadda is your clue. Moon letters: the lām carries a sukūn.

exercises.prompt: How many words for “the” does Arabic have?
exercises.explanation: ال is used for every noun.
ال is attached to the front of the noun.

exercises.prompt: Which kind of letter is ك after ال?
options: a letter that cannot follow ال
exercises.explanation: ك is a moon letter: الْكِتَاب, with a sukūn on ل.

exercises.prompt: Which kind of letter is ش after ال?
options: a letter that cannot follow ال
exercises.explanation: ش is a sun letter: الشَّمْس.
الْقَمَر is read “al-qamar”: sound out the letters from right to left.
الشَّمْس is read “ash-shams”: sound out the letters from right to left.
الطَّبِيب is read “aṭ-ṭabīb”: sound out the letters from right to left.

exercises.prompt: What marks a sun letter after ال?
exercises.explanation: The lām is not pronounced; the sun letter is doubled instead.
د is a sun letter, so ال is assimilated and د is doubled.
ب is a moon letter, so the lām is pronounced.

explanations.title: Words you will see around town
explanations.body: These words are on signs in any Arab city. Sound them out first, then check the transliteration.

explanations.title: More signs
explanations.body: Entrances, exits and places to go.

exercises.explanation: جَامِعَة is read “jāmiʿa”: sound out the letters from right to left.
مَحَطَّة is read “maḥaṭṭa”: sound out the letters from right to left.

explanations.title: The digits
explanations.body: Most Arab countries write numbers with the Eastern Arabic digits, and the tables in this course use them. Although Arabic letters run right to left, a number is still read left to right: ١٢ is twelve, written with the one first. (Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia and Libya mostly use 0 1 2 3 like English.)

explanations.title: Six to ten
explanations.body: The words for three to ten have a second form without ة (ثَلَاث، أَرْبَع…), and the rule for choosing between them is one of the stranger ones in Arabic; it comes in a later unit. For now, learn these as a counting list.

exercises.prompt: Which direction is the number ١٢ read?
exercises.explanation: Numbers are read left to right even inside Arabic text.
٥ looks like a small circle, ٠ is a dot, ٤ and ٦ differ in shape.

units.title: التعارف: greetings and introductions

explanations.title: Saying hello
explanations.body: أَهْلًا and مَرْحَبًا are the everyday hellos, and either can be answered with the other. A warmer welcome is أَهْلًا وَسَهْلًا. Among Muslims, and widely across the Arab world, people also greet with “peace be upon you”, and the reply turns the words around.

examples.translation: ʾahlan — Hello; welcome
marḥaban — Hello; welcome
ʾahlan wasahlan — Welcome (a warm welcome)
as-salām ʿalaykum — Peace be upon you (hello)
waʿalaykumu as-salām — And upon you, peace (the reply)

explanations.title: Morning and evening
explanations.body: The greetings for the time of day are answered with a play on words: “morning of goodness” is returned as “morning of light”. The same pattern works in the evening.

examples.translation: ṣabāḥ al-khayr — Good morning
ṣabāḥ an-nūr — Good morning (the reply)
masāʾ al-khayr — Good evening
masāʾ an-nūr — Good evening (the reply)

explanations.title: Parting
explanations.body: To say goodbye, wish the other person safety. “See you” literally means “until the meeting”.

examples.translation: maʿa as-salāma — Goodbye (go with safety)
ʾilā al-liqāʾ — See you; until we meet again

exercises.prompt: Someone says صَبَاح الْخَيْر. What is the usual reply?
exercises.explanation: Morning of goodness is answered with morning of light.

exercises.prompt: Someone says مَسَاء الْخَيْر. What is the usual reply?
exercises.explanation: The evening greeting is answered the same way.

exercises.prompt: Someone says السَّلَام عَلَيْكُم. What is the natural reply?
exercises.explanation: The reply turns the words around: and upon you, peace.
أَهْلًا وَسَهْلًا is the warm welcome.
مَعَ السَّلَامَة wishes the other person safety.

options: See you; until we meet again

exercises.prompt: It is eight in the evening. Which greeting fits?
exercises.explanation: مَسَاء is evening; صَبَاح is morning.

exercises.promptTranslation: Good morning
Goodbye

explanations.title: Asking and answering
explanations.body: كَيْفَ الْحَال؟ asks “how are things?”. Drop ال and add the ending for your listener, and you get “how are you?”: the ending ـكَ is for a man and ـكِ for a woman. Arabic speech tells you who is addressed, so listen for the last vowel. A short, polite answer is بِخَيْر (well), often followed by thanks to God.

explanations.title: Please and thank you
explanations.body: Thanks are returned with عَفْوًا, which also means “pardon me”. For “please” when you ask for something, say مِنْ فَضْلِك (literally “from your favour”). When you offer something, or hold the door for someone, say تَفَضَّل to a man and تَفَضَّلِي to a woman.

rows: Please; go ahead; here you are

examples.translation: shukran jazīlan — Thank you very much
ʿafwan — You are welcome

explanations.title: A short exchange
explanations.body: Two friends meet in the corridor.

examples.translation: ʾahlan yā khālid, kayfa ḥāluk? — Hello, Khalid, how are you?
bikhayr, al-ḥamdu lillāh. waʾanta? — Fine, praise God. And you?
bikhayr, shukran. — Fine, thank you.

exercises.prompt: You ask a woman how she is. Which is right?
You ask a man how he is. Which is right?

exercises.explanation: بِخَيْر means well; الْحَمْدُ لِلَّه adds praise to God.

exercises.prompt: Which phrase means “Please” when you ask for something?
exercises.explanation: مِنْ فَضْلِك is the polite “please” of a request.

exercises.prompt: You hand a woman a cup of tea. What do you say?
exercises.explanation: تَفَضَّلِي is the feminine form of “here you are”.

exercises.prompt: You hand a man a cup of tea. What do you say?
Someone says شُكْرًا. What do you answer?

exercises.explanation: كَيْفَ الْحَال؟ asks how things are.
exercises.promptTranslation: How are things?

explanations.title: Giving your name
explanations.body: There are two easy ways to give your name: say اِسْمِي and the name (“my name, Khalid”), or say أَنَا and the name. Arabic has no word for “am”, so أَنَا خَالِد means “I am Khalid”. To ask someone else, say مَا اِسْمُك؟ with the man or woman ending.

examples.translation: ismī khālid. — My name is Khalid.
ʾanā māhir. — I am Maher.
mā ismuka? — What is your name? (to a man)
mā ismuki? — What is your name? (to a woman)

explanations.title: Names to know
explanations.body: Common Arabic names are easy to tell apart by gender. Many women’s names end in ة or ى or ا, but not all do.

explanations.title: Pleased to meet you
explanations.body: Once you know each other’s names, say تَشَرَّفْنَا, “we are honoured”. The usual answer repeats it or says that the honour is yours.

examples.translation: tasharrafnā. — Pleased to meet you.
ʾahlan wasahlan. tasharrafnā yā māhir. — Welcome. Pleased to meet you, Maher.

exercises.prompt: How do you say “My name is Khalid”?

exercises.explanation: أَنَا means I; Arabic needs no word for “am”.

exercises.prompt: You ask a woman her name. Which is right?
You ask a man his name. Which is right?
Which of these is a woman’s name?
exercises.explanation: هُدَى is a woman’s name; the others are men’s.
ـِي attached to a noun means “my”.

exercises.promptTranslation: I am Layla.

explanations.title: Mr, Mrs, Doctor, Professor
explanations.body: Arabic speakers like titles. Use a title and the first name, not the surname: أُسْتَاذ أَحْمَد. أُسْتَاذ (ustādh) means “Mr” for an educated man and also “teacher” or “professor”, دُكْتُور is used for medical doctors and anyone with a doctorate, and سَيِّد and سَيِّدَة mean “Mr” and “Mrs”. The feminine adds ة.

explanations.title: Calling someone: يَا
explanations.body: To get someone’s attention, put يَا before the name or title: يَا أَحْمَد, يَا أُسْتَاذ. It works like “hey” or “O” and is not rude.

examples.translation: ṣabāḥ al-khayr yā ʾustādh ʾaḥmad. — Good morning, Mr Ahmad.
ʾahlan yā duktūra sāra. — Hello, Dr Sara.
masāʾ al-khayr yā sayyida laylā. — Good evening, Mrs Layla.

explanations.title: Father of, mother of
explanations.body: Adults are often named after their eldest son: أَبُو أَحْمَد is “father of Ahmad” and أُمّ أَحْمَد “mother of Ahmad”. It is a mark of respect, and people may use it even for someone who has no child of that name.

examples.translation: ʾabū ʾaḥmad — father of Ahmad
ʾumm ʾaḥmad — mother of Ahmad

exercises.prompt: Which title would you use for a woman who is a doctor?

exercises.explanation: آنِسَة is used for an unmarried young woman.

exercises.prompt: How do you greet a male teacher called Ahmad respectfully?
exercises.explanation: Title + first name, with يَا to call him.

exercises.prompt: What does يَا do before a name?
options: It calls the person, like “hey” or “O”

exercises.prompt: Which is the title for a woman, “Mrs”?

exercises.explanation: Sara is a woman, so the title is feminine.
exercises.promptTranslation: Hello, Dr Sara.

exercises.explanation: Ahmad is a man, so the title is masculine.
exercises.promptTranslation: Good evening, Mr Ahmad.

explanations.title: Five little words
explanations.body: Personal pronouns are some of the most common words in any language. Arabic has a separate “you” for a man and a woman, and “he” and “she” are used for things too, because every Arabic noun is masculine or feminine (“it” does not exist).

explanations.title: Who is speaking?
explanations.body: In Arabic a pronoun can be left out of a sentence when the verb already shows who is meant, but when there is no verb you need it. Notice how it appears at the start of the sentence.

examples.translation: ʾanā ṭālib. — I am a student (a man speaking).
ʾanti ṭāliba. — You are a student (to a woman).
huwa mudarris. — He is a teacher.
hiya ṭabība. — She is a doctor.

exercises.prompt: Which pronoun do you use to a woman?
exercises.explanation: أَنْتِ is the feminine “you”; the final kasra marks it.

exercises.prompt: Which pronoun do you use to a man?
A book is on the table. Which pronoun stands for the masculine word كِتَاب?
A school (مَدْرَسَة, feminine) is big. Which pronoun stands for it?
exercises.explanation: مَدْرَسَة is feminine, so it is هِيَ.
طَبِيبَة is feminine: she is a doctor.
exercises.promptTranslation: She is a doctor.

exercises.explanation: مُدَرِّس is masculine: he is a teacher.
exercises.promptTranslation: He is a teacher.

lessons.title: 21. We, you (all), they
lessons.subtitle: نَحْنُ · أَنْتُم · هُم · and the dual

explanations.title: The plural pronouns
explanations.body: The plural pronouns copy the singular ones, with separate forms for men and women. For mixed groups, Arabic uses the masculine form. In practice the feminine plurals أَنْتُنَّ and هُنَّ are used only for groups of women.

explanations.title: The dual: exactly two
explanations.body: Arabic has a number between one and many: the dual, for exactly two. It has its own pronouns for “you two” and “they two”, the same for men and women.

examples.translation: naḥnu ṭullāb. — We are students.
hum mudarrisūn. — They are teachers.
humā ṭālibatān. — They (two women) are students.

exercises.explanation: هُم is masculine or mixed plural.

exercises.prompt: Which means “they” for a group of women?
Which means “you” to a group of men?

exercises.explanation: The dual pronouns end in ـمَا.

exercises.prompt: A man, a woman and a child are talking about themselves. Which pronoun?
exercises.explanation: The group includes the speaker: we.

exercises.prompt: You talk to three women. Which pronoun is most exact?

exercises.explanation: طُلَّاب is plural and the speaker is included: we.
exercises.promptTranslation: We are students.

explanations.title: No verb “to be”
explanations.body: In the present tense Arabic leaves “is, am, are” out. A sentence made of two nouns, or a pronoun and a noun, is already complete. This is called the nominal sentence and it has two parts: the subject (what you talk about) and the predicate (what you say about it).

explanations.title: This is…: هَذَا and هَذِهِ
explanations.body: To point at something, use هَذَا for a masculine noun and هَذِهِ for a feminine one. After them you can put a noun with no article: “this (is) a book”.

examples.translation: hādhā kitāb. — This is a book.
hādhā bayt. — This is a house.
hādhihi madrasa. — This is a school.
hādhihi sayyāra. — This is a car.

explanations.title: The, and a
explanations.body: With ال the noun becomes definite: “the book”. Arabic has no word for “a”: an indefinite noun is just the bare noun. A sentence in which the subject is definite and the predicate is not, as in الْوَلَد طَالِب, means “the boy is a student”.

examples.translation: al-walad ṭālib. — The boy is a student.
al-bint ṭāliba. — The girl is a student.
al-bayt kabīr. — The house is big.

exercises.prompt: How do you say “I am a student” (a man speaking)?
How do you say “She is a doctor”?
exercises.explanation: The pronoun is feminine and so is the noun.

exercises.prompt: What is the Arabic word for “a” in “a book”?
exercises.explanation: Indefiniteness is shown by leaving off ال.

exercises.promptTranslation: This is a school.
This is a book.

explanations.title: Masculine and feminine
explanations.body: Most job words add ة for a woman, as you saw with طَالِب and طَالِبَة. The word does not otherwise change, so the feminine is easy to learn.

explanations.title: More jobs
explanations.body: These nouns also change for gender with ة.

explanations.title: What do you do?
explanations.body: Ask مَاذَا تَعْمَل؟ to a man and مَاذَا تَعْمَلِين؟ to a woman, or ask what someone’s job is. The answer is a nominal sentence.

examples.translation: ʾanā muhandis. — I am an engineer.
hiya mudarrisa. — She is a teacher.
huwa sāʾiq. — He is a driver.

exercises.prompt: What is the feminine of مُهَنْدِس?
What is the feminine of مُدِير?
exercises.explanation: Add ة to make a woman manager.

exercises.prompt: What is the masculine of طَبِيبَة?

exercises.explanation: Pronoun and noun are both feminine.

exercises.prompt: Which means “I am a driver” (a man speaking)?
exercises.explanation: A man says the masculine noun.

exercises.prompt: A woman says she is a student. Which sentence?
exercises.explanation: A woman says the feminine noun.
مُوَظَّف is someone who has a job (a post).
The subject is feminine, so the predicate is too.
exercises.promptTranslation: She is a teacher.
He is a doctor.

explanations.title: From country to nationality
explanations.body: To say where a person is from, add the ending ـِيّ to the name of the country. The result is an adjective (called a nisba adjective) and it works like the job words: add ة for a woman. The article ال is dropped (الْعِرَاق → عِرَاقِيّ) and a few places lose a letter (سُورِيَا → سُورِيّ), but the pattern is very regular.

explanations.title: More nationalities
explanations.body: Some country names have a different shape, but the nationality adjective follows the same ending.

exercises.prompt: What is the feminine of مِصْرِيّ?
exercises.explanation: Add ة to the nisba adjective.

exercises.prompt: What is the masculine of عِرَاقِيَّة?

exercises.explanation: Add ـِيّ to the country name.

exercises.promptTranslation: He is Egyptian.
She is Lebanese.

exercises.explanation: A man says the masculine adjective.
exercises.promptTranslation: I am American.

explanations.title: Asking
explanations.body: مِنْ أَيْنَ is “from where”. Put the pronoun after it, using the form for a man or a woman, and the answer starts with أَنَا مِنْ and a place, or with أَنَا and your nationality.

examples.translation: min ʾayna ʾanta? — Where are you from? (to a man)
min ʾayna ʾanti? — Where are you from? (to a woman)
ʾanā min miṣr. — I am from Egypt.
ʾanā miṣriyy. — I am Egyptian.

explanations.title: A short conversation
explanations.body: Two people meet at a conference.

examples.translation: ʾahlan wasahlan. min ʾayna ʾanti? — Welcome. Where are you from?
ʾanā min lubnān. waʾanta? — I am from Lebanon. And you?

examples.text: أَنَا مِنَ الْمَغْرِب، لَكِنْ أَسْكُن فِي أَمْرِيكَا.
examples.translation: ʾanā mina al-maghrib, lākin ʾaskun fī ʾamrīkā. — I am from Morocco, but I live in America.

exercises.prompt: How do you ask a woman where she is from?
Which means “And you?” to a woman?

exercises.promptTranslation: Where are you from?

exercises.explanation: After مِنْ comes a place name.
exercises.promptTranslation: I am from Iraq.

explanations.title: Endings instead of words
explanations.body: Arabic does not have a separate word for “my” or “her”. It adds a short ending to the noun. You have already met two of them: اِسْمِي (my name) and اِسْمُكَ (your name).

explanations.title: Our, your, their
explanations.body: The plural endings are ـنَا (our), ـكُم (your, a group of men or mixed) and ـهُم (their). Add ـكُنَّ and ـهُنَّ for groups of women only. The noun itself does not change (except that ة becomes ت, see below), and an attached pronoun makes it definite, so it takes no ال.

explanations.title: A feminine noun changes its ة
explanations.body: A word that ends in ة changes it to ت when an ending is added. So مَدْرَسَة (a school) becomes مَدْرَسَتِي (my school) and مَدْرَسَتُهَا (her school).

examples.translation: madrasatī kabīra. — My school is big.
baytunā jadīd. — Our house is new.
ismuhā laylā. — Her name is Layla.

exercises.prompt: How do you say “your book” to a woman?
What happens to ة before an ending?
Does a noun with an attached pronoun take ال?

exercises.promptTranslation: Her name is Layla.

explanations.title: Verb–subject sentences
explanations.body: Arabic sentences often begin with the verb, followed by the subject: “studies Ahmad”. “Ahmad studies” (أَحْمَد يَدْرُس) is also correct. A verb that comes first agrees with its subject in gender, but stays singular even when the subject is plural. In the present tense, the “he” form of a verb starts with يَـ and the “she” form with تَـ.

examples.translation: yadrus ʾaḥmad fī al-madrasa. — Ahmad studies at school.
tadrus sāra fī al-jāmiʿa. — Sara studies at the university.
yadrus aṭ-ṭullāb al-ʿarabiyya. — The students study Arabic.

explanations.title: A few verbs
explanations.body: Four useful verbs, shown for “he” and “she”.

exercises.prompt: The students study (verb first). Which is right?
exercises.explanation: A verb before its subject stays singular.

exercises.promptTranslation: Ahmad studies at school.
Sara writes the lesson.

explanations.title: A prefix for the subject
explanations.body: In the present tense the person is shown by a prefix added to the same verb stem. The four prefixes are أَـ (I), نَـ (we), تَـ (you, and she) and يَـ (he). Because the verb itself shows who is meant, the pronoun is usually dropped: أَكْتُب is already “I write”.

explanations.title: You (woman)
explanations.body: When you speak to a woman, the verb adds the ending ـِين: تَكْتُبِين means “you (to a woman) write”.

examples.translation: ʾanta taktub. — You write. (to a man)
ʾanti taktubīn. — You write. (to a woman)

explanations.title: In a sentence
explanations.body: These sentences all use verbs you know. The object follows the verb.

examples.translation: ʾadrus al-ʿarabiyya. — I study Arabic.
naʿmal fī al-maktab. — We work in the office.
ʾaskun fī bayt kabīr. — I live in a big house.

exercises.prompt: Which means “We work in the office”?
Why is a pronoun usually not needed with a present-tense verb?
options: The prefix already shows the subject
The pronoun comes after the verb
exercises.explanation: The prefix and the ending tell you who is meant.

exercises.promptTranslation: I study at school.
We work in the office.

explanations.title: One small prefix
explanations.body: To talk about the future, put سَـ (or سَوْفَ as a separate word) in front of the present-tense verb. Nothing else changes, which makes this one of the easiest tenses in the language. سَـ is joined to the verb; سَوْفَ is written separately.

explanations.title: Time words for the future
explanations.body: غَدًا is “tomorrow”, and الْيَوْم is “today”. The next words fill out the future.

examples.translation: saʾadhhab ʾilā al-madrasa ghadan. — I will go to school tomorrow.
sawfa nadrus al-ʿarabiyya. — We will study Arabic.
hal sataktub? — Will you write?

exercises.prompt: How else can you say “will” in front of a verb?
exercises.explanation: سَوْفَ is the spaced-out form of سَـ.

exercises.prompt: Which means “I will go to school tomorrow”?
exercises.explanation: I = أَـ, with سَـ for the future.

exercises.promptTranslation: We will study tomorrow.

explanations.title: Words on a form
explanations.body: Forms in Arabic use a fixed set of nouns. Learn to read them and you can fill in almost any application.

explanations.title: A completed form
explanations.body: Each line gives the label, a colon and the answer.

examples.translation: al-ism: khālid — Name: Khalid
al-jinsiyya: suʿūdiyy — Nationality: Saudi
al-waẓīfa: muhandis — Job: engineer
al-ʿunwān: shāriʿ al-jāmiʿa — Address: University Street

explanations.title: Answering out loud
explanations.body: To answer the questions in speech, use the attached endings you learned.

examples.translation: mā jinsiyyatuk? — What is your nationality?
jinsiyyatī miṣriyya. — My nationality is Egyptian.
mā waẓīfatuk? — What is your job?
waẓīfatī mudarrisa. — My job is teacher. (a woman speaking)

exercises.prompt: Which word on a form means “name”?
What does رَقْم الْهَاتِف ask for?

exercises.explanation: ة becomes ت before an ending.

exercises.prompt: How do you say “What is your job?” to a man?

exercises.explanation: A phone number is رَقْم الْهَاتِف.
exercises.promptTranslation: phone number

exercises.explanation: In a full sentence the adjective agrees with جِنْسِيَّة, which is feminine.
exercises.promptTranslation: My nationality is Egyptian.

lessons.title: 31. Review: meeting someone
lessons.subtitle: Greetings, introductions and a first conversation

explanations.title: A first meeting
explanations.body: Read the conversation, then use it for the exercises. Sara is a student; Maher works at a bank.

examples.translation: as-salām ʿalaykum. ʾanā māhir. — Peace be upon you. I am Maher.
waʿalaykumu as-salām. ʾanā sāra. tasharrafnā. — And upon you, peace. I am Sara. Pleased to meet you.
min ʾayna ʾanti yā sāra? — Where are you from, Sara?

examples.text: أَنَا مِنَ الْأُرْدُنّ، لَكِنْ أَدْرُس فِي أَمْرِيكَا.
examples.translation: ʾanā mina al-ʾurdunn, lākin ʾadrus fī ʾamrīkā. — I am from Jordan, but I study in America.
wamādhā tadrusīn? — And what do you study?
ʾadrus aṭ-ṭibb. waʾanta, mādhā taʿmal? — I study medicine. And you, what do you do?
ʾanā muwaẓẓaf fī bank. — I am a bank employee.

exercises.prompt: Maher begins with السَّلَام عَلَيْكُم. What does Sara answer?
exercises.explanation: The reply to the Islamic greeting.

exercises.prompt: How does Sara say she is from Jordan?
Maher asks Sara where she is from. Which question is for a woman?
Which sentence means “She is a student”?
Which means “We work in the office”?
Which is the feminine of مُدَرِّس?

exercises.promptTranslation: Good evening

units.title: الطقس والأماكن: places, weather and the present tense

lessons.title: 32. Question words
lessons.subtitle: مَنْ · مَا · أَيْنَ · كَيْفَ · مَتَى · لِمَاذَا · كَمْ

explanations.title: The question words
explanations.body: Arabic questions begin with the question word. Eight of them cover most of what you will ask. Two of them mean “what”: مَا goes in front of a noun or a pronoun, and مَاذَا in front of a verb.

explanations.title: In a sentence
explanations.body: Say the question word, then the rest of the sentence. A noun sentence needs no verb: أَيْنَ الْمَدْرَسَة؟ is just “where the school?”.

examples.translation: man hādhā? — Who is this?
mā ismuka? — What is your name?
mādhā tadrus? — What do you study?
ʾayna taskun? — Where do you live?
kayfa aṭ-ṭaqs al-yawm? — How is the weather today?
matā tadhhab ʾilā al-jāmiʿa? — When do you go to the university?
limādhā tadrus al-ʿarabiyya? — Why do you study Arabic?
kam ʿumruka? — How old are you? (literally: how much your age)

explanations.title: مَنْ (who) or مِنْ (from)?
explanations.body: These two small words differ only in their vowel, so the vowel matters. مَنْ asks about a person; مِنْ means “from”.

examples.translation: man ʾanta? — Who are you?
min ʾayna ʾanta? — Where are you from?

exercises.prompt: Which word asks about a person?
Which question asks “How old are you?”
Which means “Why do you study Arabic?”

exercises.promptTranslation: What is your name?

exercises.explanation: The question is about a place.
exercises.promptTranslation: Where do you live?
What do you write?

explanations.title: Starting a yes–no question
explanations.body: To ask something that can be answered with yes or no, put هَلْ at the start. The rest of the sentence does not change. The answers are نَعَمْ (yes) and لَا (no).

examples.translation: hal ʾanta ṭālib? — Are you a student?
naʿam, ʾanā ṭālib. — Yes, I am a student.
hal hiya miṣriyya? — Is she Egyptian?
lā, hiya sūriyya. — No, she is Syrian.

explanations.title: Questions with a verb
explanations.body: A verb question works the same way. In your answer the verb changes to fit the speaker: if you are asked تَسْكُن (you live), you answer أَسْكُن (I live).

examples.translation: hal taskun fī al-qāhira? — Do you live in Cairo?
naʿam, ʾaskun fī al-qāhira. — Yes, I live in Cairo.
hal tadrus fī al-jāmiʿa? — Do you study at the university?
lā, ʾaʿmal fī al-maktab. — No, I work in the office.

exercises.prompt: Which word begins a yes–no question?
exercises.explanation: هَلْ turns a statement into a yes–no question.

exercises.prompt: Which means “Are you a student?” (to a man)
Someone asks هَلْ هِيَ مِصْرِيَّة؟ and she is Syrian. The answer is…
exercises.explanation: No, and then the correct fact.

exercises.prompt: You are asked هَلْ تَسْكُن فِي الْقَاهِرَة؟ and you live there. You say…
exercises.explanation: The question’s تَـ (you) becomes أَـ (I) in your answer.

exercises.prompt: In an answer, the verb prefix تَـ of the question becomes…
exercises.explanation: You answer in the first person: أَـ.

exercises.promptTranslation: Are you a teacher? (to a woman)
Do you study today? Yes, I study today.

explanations.title: The compass
explanations.body: The four directions are masculine nouns. Place names after them are joined directly, as in جَنُوب مِصْر: the first noun has no ال, and the second names the place. With فِي the meaning changes from “south of” to “in the south of”.

examples.translation: miṣr fī shamāl ʾafrīqiyā. — Egypt is in the north of Africa.
as-sūdān janūb miṣr. — Sudan is south of Egypt.
lubnān gharb sūriyā. — Lebanon is west of Syria.
al-ʿirāq sharq sūriyā. — Iraq is east of Syria.

explanations.title: Left and right
explanations.body: عَلَى الْيَمِين is “on the right” and عَلَى الْيَسَار is “on the left”. Read the building names aloud; you will meet them again soon.

examples.translation: al-madrasa ʿalā al-yamīn. — The school is on the right.
al-bank ʿalā al-yasār. — The bank is on the left.

exercises.promptTranslation: Sudan is south of Egypt.
Lebanon is west of Syria.

explanations.title: Landscape words
explanations.body: These are the nouns for the shape of the land. Several are feminine, which you can usually see from the ending ة.

explanations.title: Names of places
explanations.body: A name such as “the Red Sea” is a noun followed by an adjective, and both take ال. Plain sentences about the land use the nouns you have just learned.

examples.translation: an-nīl nahr ṭawīl. — The Nile is a long river.
al-baḥr al-ʾaḥmar bayna miṣr was-suʿūdiyya. — The Red Sea is between Egypt and Saudi Arabia.
al-baḥrayn jazīra fī al-khalīj. — Bahrain is an island (really a group of islands) in the Gulf.
fī miṣr ṣaḥrāʾ kabīra. — There is a big desert in Egypt.
fī lubnān jibāl wabaḥr. — In Lebanon there are mountains and a sea.

exercises.prompt: Which means “The Nile is a long river”?
exercises.explanation: النِّيل is the Nile; نَهْر is river.
Bahrain lies in the Gulf, surrounded by water.
exercises.promptTranslation: Bahrain is an island in the Gulf.

lessons.title: 36. In, on, to, from, with
lessons.subtitle: فِي · عَلَى · إِلَى · مِنْ · عَنْ · مَعَ

explanations.title: Six small words
explanations.body: Prepositions come before their noun. Some of them change their last vowel when ال follows: مِنْ becomes مِنَ الْـ and عَنْ becomes عَنِ الْـ.

explanations.title: “There is…” without a verb
explanations.body: Arabic does not need a word for “there is”. Put the place first and an indefinite noun after it: “in the house a book” means “there is a book in the house”. Turn it around, with a definite noun first, and you get an ordinary sentence: “the book is in the house”.

examples.translation: fī al-bayt kitāb. — There is a book in the house.
al-kitāb fī al-bayt. — The book is in the house.
fī al-madīna masjid kabīr. — There is a big mosque in the city.
ʿalā al-maktab hātif. — There is a phone on the desk.
fī al-funduq maṭʿam. — There is a restaurant in the hotel.

explanations.title: Verbs and their prepositions
explanations.body: Some verbs usually take a particular preposition, like English “talk about”.

examples.translation: ʾadhhab ʾilā al-madrasa maʿa ṣadīqī. — I go to school with my friend.
ʾatakallam ʿani aṭ-ṭaqs. — I talk about the weather.
ʾanā mina al-maghrib. — I am from Morocco.

exercises.prompt: Which means “There is a book in the house”?
Which means “The book is in the house”?
exercises.explanation: A definite noun first makes an ordinary sentence.

exercises.promptTranslation: I go to school.
I study with my friend.
I am from Egypt.

explanations.title: Capital of…
explanations.body: To say “the capital of Egypt”, put the two nouns side by side: عَاصِمَة مِصْر. The first noun never takes ال and the second is the owner. This two-noun link is called an iḍāfa, and you will use it all the time.

examples.translation: ʿāṣima miṣr al-qāhira. — The capital of Egypt is Cairo.
mā ʿāṣima al-ʿirāq? — What is the capital of Iraq?
bayrūt ʿāṣima lubnān. — Beirut is the capital of Lebanon.

explanations.title: Countries and capitals (1)
explanations.body: Say each pair aloud, then cover one column and test yourself.

explanations.title: Countries and capitals (2)
explanations.body: Tunisia, Algeria and Kuwait share their name with their capital city.

exercises.prompt: What is the capital of Egypt?
What is the capital of Syria?
What is the capital of Iraq?
What is the capital of Saudi Arabia?
What is the capital of Morocco?
What is the capital of Qatar?

exercises.explanation: In an iḍāfa the first noun has no ال.

exercises.prompt: Which capital shares its name with its country?
exercises.explanation: تُونُس is both the country and its capital.
The first noun of an iḍāfa has no ال.
exercises.promptTranslation: Beirut is the capital of Lebanon.

explanations.title: Naming a language
explanations.body: A language is the feminine nisba adjective (the same ending as مِصْرِيَّة) with ال. The full phrase is اللُّغَة الْعَرَبِيَّة, “the Arabic language”, and in daily use the first word is simply dropped.

explanations.title: Speaking, writing, knowing
explanations.body: أَتَكَلَّم means “I speak”. To say “in Arabic”, join بِـ to the language: بِالْعَرَبِيَّة. Add قَلِيلًا (a little) or جَيِّدًا (well) at the end.

examples.translation: ʾatakallam al-ʿarabiyya wal-ʾinjilīziyya. — I speak Arabic and English.
hal tatakallam al-faransiyya? — Do you speak French?
naʿam, ʾatakallam al-faransiyya qalīlan. — Yes, I speak French a little.
ʾaktub bil-ʿarabiyya. — I write in Arabic.
natakallam ar-rūsiyya jayyidan. — We speak Russian well.

exercises.prompt: What does قَلِيلًا mean in أَتَكَلَّم الْعَرَبِيَّة قَلِيلًا?

exercises.explanation: You are asking the listener, تَـ.
exercises.promptTranslation: Do you speak French?
I write in Arabic.

explanations.title: One verb, thirteen persons
explanations.body: You already know the prefixes أَـ نَـ تَـ يَـ. Many persons also take an ending, shown in the highlight below. A masculine and a feminine “you” differ, and so do “you” and “they” in the plural. Here is the verb كَتَبَ, “to write”, in every person.

explanations.title: Two people: the dual
explanations.body: Arabic has a special form for exactly two. You will study it in unit 5. For now, notice that it ends in ـَان and that “you two” and “they two (women)” share the same verb, تَكْتُبَان.

explanations.title: A pronoun is optional
explanations.body: Because the prefix and ending already show who is meant, a pronoun is mostly used for emphasis or contrast.

examples.translation: hum yaktubūn wanaḥnu nadrus. — They write and we study.
ʾantum taktubūn bil-ʿarabiyya. — You (all) write in Arabic.
hunna yaktubna ad-dars. — They (women) write the lesson.

exercises.explanation: A woman is addressed with ـِين.
ـُون for a group of men.
ـْنَ for a group of women.

exercises.prompt: Which ending shows a woman being addressed?
What is the difference between تَكْتُب and يَكْتُب?
exercises.explanation: تَـ shows you or she; يَـ shows he.

exercises.promptTranslation: They write in Arabic.
You write the lesson. (to a woman)

explanations.title: A verb has three letters and a vowel
explanations.body: Most Arabic verbs are built on three root letters. For these verbs the prefix and endings you just learned stay the same, but the vowel on the middle letter of the present tense depends on the verb, and you have to learn it with the word. Textbooks and many dictionaries give the “he” form of the past together with the present-tense vowel, so they show the vowel for you.

explanations.title: The other two vowels
explanations.body: The same rule holds for verbs with ـَ and ـِ in the present tense. Say each pair aloud.

explanations.title: Using them
explanations.body: Once you know the vowel, every person follows the pattern from the last lesson.

examples.translation: ʾajlis fī al-maktab. — I sit in the office.
yaftaḥ ʾaḥmad al-bāb. — Ahmad opens the door.
nashrab al-māʾ. — We drink water.
hal taʿrifīn sāra? — Do you know Sara? (to a woman)
yakhrujūn mina al-bayt. — They go out of the house.

exercises.explanation: جَلَسَ takes ـِ in the present.
فَتَحَ takes ـَ in the present.
خَرَجَ takes ـُ in the present.
فَهِمَ takes ـَ in the present.

exercises.prompt: Why must you learn the present vowel with each verb?
options: It differs from verb to verb
exercises.explanation: The prefix shows the person; the middle vowel belongs to the verb.

exercises.promptTranslation: Ahmad opens the door.

exercises.explanation: First person singular, verb with ـِ.
exercises.promptTranslation: I sit in the house.

explanations.title: Negating a present-tense verb
explanations.body: To say that something is not happening, put لَا in front of the present-tense verb. The verb itself does not change at all: the prefix and endings stay exactly as they were.

explanations.title: In sentences
explanations.body: Keep the usual verb-first order. With تَـ, a similar form gives an order, “don’t…!” (some endings change); you will meet that in unit 6.

examples.translation: lā ʾaʿrif. — I don’t know.
lā ʾafham. — I don’t understand.
lā yaskun ʾaḥmad fī al-qāhira. — Ahmad doesn’t live in Cairo.
lā nadrus al-yawm. — We don’t study today.
lā tadhhab sāra ʾilā al-maktab. — Sara doesn’t go to the office.
lā, shukran. — No, thank you.

exercises.prompt: Which means “Ahmad doesn’t live in Cairo”?
Which word negates a present-tense verb?
exercises.explanation: لَا goes in front of the verb.

exercises.prompt: What happens to the verb after لَا?

exercises.promptTranslation: I don’t study today.
Sara doesn’t go to the office.
Do you understand? No, I don’t understand.

explanations.title: To be not
explanations.body: Arabic has no word for “is” in the present, so “he is a student” is just هُوَ طَالِب. To negate a sentence like that, use لَيْسَ. It is a verb that changes for the person, like a past-tense verb.

explanations.title: The word after لَيْسَ
explanations.body: The noun or adjective that follows لَيْسَ takes a new ending: ـًا, or ـً on a word that ends in ة. You can see it in the examples. Write it with the ending, even though it is not essential for understanding.

examples.translation: lastu ṭāliban. — I am not a student. (a man speaking)
lasti mudarrisatan. — You are not a teacher. (to a woman)
huwa laysa muhandisan. — He is not an engineer.
hiya laysat miṣriyyatan. — She is not Egyptian.
aṭ-ṭaqs laysa bāridan al-yawm. — The weather is not cold today.
lasnā ṭullāban. — We are not students.

explanations.title: لَا or لَيْسَ
explanations.body: Ask what comes next. A verb is negated with لَا; a noun or an adjective is negated with لَيْسَ.

exercises.prompt: Which means “I am not a student” (a man speaking)?
Which word negates a noun sentence?
Which negative goes with a verb like يَعْمَل?
Which ending appears on a word after لَيْسَ?
exercises.explanation: The word after لَيْسَ takes ـًا.

exercises.promptTranslation: I am not an engineer.
The weather is not cold.
She is not a student.

explanations.title: Describing the weather
explanations.body: These adjectives describe the weather. Use them after الطَّقْس or الْجَوّ, both of which mean “the weather” and are masculine, so the adjectives stay in the masculine form.

explanations.title: Weather nouns
explanations.body: Nouns for the things in the sky.

explanations.title: Talking about it
explanations.body: الْجَوّ is masculine, but السَّمَاء (the sky) is feminine, so its adjective ends in ة: السَّمَاء غَائِمَة.

examples.translation: aṭ-ṭaqs ḥārr al-yawm. — The weather is hot today.
al-jaww bārid was-samāʾ ghāʾima. — The weather is cold and the sky is cloudy.
kayfa aṭ-ṭaqs fī miṣr? — How is the weather in Egypt?
ḥārr wajāff. — Hot and dry.
hali al-jaww mumṭir? — Is it rainy?
lā, al-jaww mushmis. — No, it is sunny.
fī al-jibāl thalj. — There is snow in the mountains.

exercises.explanation: السَّمَاء is feminine, الْجَوّ is masculine.

exercises.promptTranslation: The weather is hot today.
There is snow in the mountains.

explanations.title: Four seasons
explanations.body: الْفَصْل is “the season”. Use فِي to say “in summer”.

examples.translation: fī aṣ-ṣayf aṭ-ṭaqs ḥārr. — In summer the weather is hot.
fī ash-shitāʾ al-jaww bārid. — In winter it is cold.

explanations.title: To like: أُحِبّ
explanations.body: The verb “to like, to love” has prefixes with ḍamma (أُـ تُـ يُـ نُـ) and ends in a doubled letter. It is different from كَتَبَ in how it looks, but the idea is the same: the prefix tells you who.

explanations.title: Saying what you like
explanations.body: لِأَنَّ means “because”. It is followed by a full sentence.

examples.translation: ʾuḥibb ash-shitāʾ. — I like winter.
hal tuḥibb aṣ-ṣayf? — Do you like summer?

examples.text: لَا أُحِبّ الصَّيْف لِأَنَّ الْجَوّ حَارّ جِدًّا.
examples.translation: lā ʾuḥibb aṣ-ṣayf liʾanna al-jaww ḥārr jiddan. — I don’t like summer because it is very hot.
tuḥibb sāra ar-rabīʿ. — Sara likes spring.
nuḥibb ash-shāṭiʾ fī aṣ-ṣayf. — We like the beach in summer.

exercises.promptTranslation: Sara likes spring.
In winter the weather is cold.

explanations.title: The comparative shape
explanations.body: To say “bigger”, “colder” and so on, fit the three root letters of the adjective into the pattern أَ _ْ _َ _. So كَبِير (big, root ك-ب-ر) becomes أَكْبَر (bigger). When it is used with مِنْ (“than”), the word does not change for gender or number.

explanations.title: Comparing with مِنْ
explanations.body: Use مِنْ for “than”: “Cairo bigger than Damascus”. The comparative stays the same for a feminine subject such as الْقَاهِرَة.

examples.translation: al-qāhira ʾakbar min dimashq. — Cairo is bigger than Damascus.
an-nīl ʾaṭwal mina al-furāt. — The Nile is longer than the Euphrates.
al-ʿirāq ʾaṣghar mina as-suʿūdiyya. — Iraq is smaller than Saudi Arabia.
ash-shitāʾ ʾabrad mina al-kharīf. — Winter is colder than autumn.

explanations.title: The biggest
explanations.body: To say “the biggest”, put the comparative before a singular noun without ال.

examples.text: الْقَاهِرَة أَكْبَر مَدِينَة فِي الْوَطَن الْعَرَبِيّ.
examples.translation: al-qāhira ʾakbar madīna fī al-waṭan al-ʿarabiyy. — Cairo is the biggest city in the Arab world.
an-nīl ʾaṭwal nahr fī ʾafrīqiyā. — The Nile is the longest river in Africa.

exercises.prompt: Which means “Cairo is bigger than Damascus”?
Which word means “than” in a comparison?
Does أَكْبَر change for a feminine noun when it is used with مِنْ?
exercises.explanation: With مِنْ, the comparative does not change.

exercises.prompt: Which means “The Nile is the longest river in Africa”?
exercises.explanation: The comparative before a singular noun without ال.

exercises.promptTranslation: Iraq is smaller than Saudi Arabia.
Winter is colder than autumn.

lessons.title: 46. Near, far, and how long
lessons.subtitle: قَرِيب مِنْ · بَعِيد عَنْ · نِصْف سَاعَة

explanations.title: Near and far
explanations.body: Say قَرِيب مِنْ for “near to” and بَعِيد عَنْ for “far from”. The adjective agrees with its noun: قَرِيبَة and بَعِيدَة for a feminine one.

examples.translation: al-maṭār baʿīd ʿani al-madīna. — The airport is far from the city.
al-funduq qarīb mina al-maṭār. — The hotel is near the airport.
madrasatī qarība min baytī. — My school is near my house.
al-jāmiʿa baʿīda ʿan baytī. — The university is far from my house.

explanations.title: Units of time
explanations.body: To say how long something takes, name the amount of time. “Half” is نِصْف and “a quarter” is رُبْع, both followed by the unit.

examples.translation: ar-riḥla niṣf sāʿa. — The trip is half an hour.

examples.text: كَمْ سَاعَة مِنَ الْقَاهِرَة إِلَى الْإِسْكَنْدَرِيَّة؟
examples.translation: kam sāʿa mina al-qāhira ʾilā al-ʾiskandariyya? — How many hours is it from Cairo to Alexandria?

exercises.prompt: Which means “a quarter of an hour”?
Which means “an hour and a half”?
Which means “The hotel is near the airport”?

exercises.explanation: الْجَامِعَة is feminine and the meaning is “far”.
exercises.promptTranslation: The university is far from my house.

exercises.explanation: مَدْرَسَة is feminine and the meaning is “near”.
exercises.promptTranslation: My school is near my house.
The trip is half an hour.

explanations.title: A forecast table
explanations.body: A winter forecast for six cities. The temperatures are in degrees Celsius, and the numbers are written with the Arabic digits from unit 1. The figures are made up for practice.

explanations.title: The same report in sentences
explanations.body: Reports use ordinary sentences. أَعْلَى means “higher” and أَقَلّ means “less, lower”.

examples.translation: aṭ-ṭaqs fī al-qāhira mushmis. — The weather in Cairo is sunny.
al-jaww fī ʿammān bārid wamumṭir. — In Amman it is cold and rainy.
as-samāʾ ghāʾima fī baghdād. — The sky in Baghdad is cloudy.

examples.text: دَرَجَة الْحَرَارَة فِي الرِّيَاض أَعْلَى مِنْ عَمَّان.
examples.translation: daraja al-ḥarāra fī ar-riyāḍ ʾaʿlā min ʿammān. — The temperature in Riyadh is higher than in Amman.

examples.text: دَرَجَة الْحَرَارَة فِي بَغْدَاد أَقَلّ مِنَ الْقَاهِرَة.
examples.translation: daraja al-ḥarāra fī baghdād ʾaqall mina al-qāhira. — The temperature in Baghdad is lower than in Cairo.

exercises.prompt: «الْجَوّ فِي عَمَّان بَارِد وَمُمْطِر.» What is the weather in Amman?
«الطَّقْس فِي الْقَاهِرَة مُشْمِس.» What is the weather in Cairo?
«السَّمَاء غَائِمَة فِي بَغْدَاد.» What is the sky like?
الْقَاهِرَة ١٩ · عَمَّان ٨ · الرِّيَاض ٢٤. Which city is the warmest?
الْقَاهِرَة ١٩ · عَمَّان ٨ · الرِّيَاض ٢٤. Which city is the coldest?

exercises.promptTranslation: The weather in Rabat is windy.

exercises.prompt: دَرَجَة الْحَرَارَة فِي الرِّيَاض ___ مِنْ عَمَّان.
exercises.promptTranslation: The temperature in Riyadh is higher than in Amman.

exercises.prompt: دَرَجَة الْحَرَارَة فِي عَمَّان ___ مِنَ الْقَاهِرَة.
exercises.promptTranslation: The temperature in Amman is lower than in Cairo.

explanations.title: Layla in Rabat, Omar in Cairo
explanations.body: Two friends talk on the phone. Read the conversation, then answer the questions.

examples.text: هَلْ أَنْتَ فِي الْقَاهِرَة يَا عُمَر؟
examples.translation: hal ʾanta fī al-qāhira yā ʿumar? — Layla: Are you in Cairo, Omar?

examples.text: نَعَمْ، أَنَا فِي الْقَاهِرَة. وَأَنْتِ، أَيْنَ أَنْتِ؟
examples.translation: naʿam, ʾanā fī al-qāhira. waʾanti, ʾayna ʾanti? — Omar: Yes, I am in Cairo. And you, where are you?
ʾanā fī ar-rabāṭ, ʿāṣima al-maghrib. — Layla: I am in Rabat, the capital of Morocco.
kayfa aṭ-ṭaqs hunāk? — Omar: How is the weather there?

examples.text: الْجَوّ بَارِد وَعَاصِف، لَكِنَّ الْمَدِينَة جَمِيلَة.
examples.translation: al-jaww bārid waʿāṣif, lākinna al-madīna jamīla. — Layla: Cold and windy, but the city is beautiful.

examples.text: هُنَا الْجَوّ دَافِئ وَمُشْمِس. الْقَاهِرَة أَكْبَر مِنَ الرَّبَاط.
examples.translation: hunā al-jaww dāfiʾ wamushmis. al-qāhira ʾakbar mina ar-rabāṭ. — Omar: Here it is warm and sunny. Cairo is bigger than Rabat.
ʾatakallam al-ʿarabiyya wal-faransiyya hunā. — Layla: I speak Arabic and French here.

exercises.prompt: Omar answers Layla’s first question with…
exercises.explanation: Yes, and the verb-less sentence أَنَا فِي الْقَاهِرَة.

exercises.prompt: Which word begins a yes–no question?
exercises.explanation: هَلْ turns a statement into a question.

exercises.prompt: How is the weather in Rabat?
What is the capital of Morocco?
Which means “Lebanon is west of Syria”?
Which means “I speak French a little”?
Which means “Cairo is bigger than Rabat”?

exercises.explanation: A question about how things are.
exercises.promptTranslation: How is the weather in Cairo?
I am not a student.

units.title: المدينة والأسرة: the city, plurals and the family

explanations.title: Public places
explanations.body: These are the words you need to find your way around a city. Nouns that end in ة are feminine; the others here are masculine.

explanations.title: More places
explanations.body: Some of these you saw in the last unit. Together they cover most of a city centre.

examples.translation: ʾayna al-mustashfā? — Where is the hospital?
al-mustashfā qarīb mina al-maḥaṭṭa. — The hospital is near the station.
fī al-madīna matḥaf wamaktaba waḥadīqa. — In the city there is a museum, a library and a park.
maktab al-barīd qarīb mina al-bank. — The post office is near the bank.

exercises.explanation: مَكْتَب الْبَرِيد = office of the mail.

exercises.prompt: Which means “The hospital is near the station”?

exercises.promptTranslation: Where is the hospital?
In the city there is a museum and a library.

explanations.title: Position words
explanations.body: These words say where something is in relation to something else. The first word never takes ال, and the noun after it completes the phrase, just as in عَاصِمَة مِصْر.

explanations.title: Asking and answering
explanations.body: Questions about places start with أَيْنَ. The answer is a noun sentence with one of these words.

examples.translation: ʾayna al-bank? — Where is the bank?
al-bank bayna al-maktaba wal-maṭʿam. — The bank is between the library and the restaurant.
hali al-matḥaf khalf al-ḥadīqa? — Is the museum behind the park?
lā, huwa ʾamām al-ḥadīqa. — No, it is in front of the park.
al-maḥaṭṭa bijānib as-sūq. — The station is next to the market.

exercises.prompt: Which word means “above, on top of”?
Which means “The school is in front of the mosque”?
The bank is between the library and the restaurant. What is between them?

exercises.explanation: The pen is below the book.
exercises.promptTranslation: The pen is under the book.
The café is next to the hotel.
I am at my friend’s.

lessons.title: 51. Plural of men and masculine nisbas: ـُون
lessons.subtitle: مُدَرِّسُون · مُهَنْدِسُون · مِصْرِيُّون

explanations.title: A group of men: ـُون
explanations.body: The regular plural for a group of men, or a mixed group, adds ـُون to the singular. It is called the sound masculine plural, and it works for many jobs and nationalities. Words ending in ـِيّ keep the doubled ي: مِصْرِيّ becomes مِصْرِيُّون.

explanations.title: A second ending: ـِين
explanations.body: After a preposition, or when the plural is the object of a verb, ـُون changes to ـِين. In a plain sentence where the plural is the subject, it stays ـُون. After لَيْسَ, the predicate takes ـِين too: لَيْسُوا مُدَرِّسِين.

rows: The engineers are in the office.

exercises.prompt: Which is the plural of مُدَرِّس (teacher)?
Which is the plural of مُهَنْدِس (engineer)?
Which is the plural of مِصْرِيّ?
exercises.explanation: Keep the doubled ي and add ـُون.

exercises.prompt: Which masculine plural ending is used after a preposition?

exercises.explanation: A preposition is followed by ـِين.

exercises.prompt: Which means “The (male) engineers are in the office”?
exercises.explanation: The plural is the subject: ـُون.

exercises.promptTranslation: They are engineers.

exercises.explanation: After مَعَ the plural ends in ـِين.
exercises.promptTranslation: I talk with the (male) teachers.

lessons.title: 52. Plural of women and many things: ـَات
lessons.subtitle: طَالِبَات · مُدَرِّسَات · سَيَّارَات

explanations.title: Drop ة, add ـَات
explanations.body: The sound feminine plural is made by removing the ة and adding ـَات. It is the usual plural of feminine jobs and nationalities, and it also serves many feminine nouns that name things.

explanations.title: In sentences
explanations.body: Not every feminine noun uses this plural: مَدْرَسَة (school) has a different one, which you will meet in the next lesson. Where this plural is available, it is the same in every position in the sentence.

examples.translation: hunna ṭālibāt fī al-jāmiʿa. — They (women) are students at the university.
al-muhandisāt fī al-maktab. — The (women) engineers are in the office.
fī al-madīna jāmiʿāt kathīra. — There are many universities in the city.
ʾadrus sāʿāt kathīra. — I study for many hours.

exercises.prompt: Which is the plural of طَالِبَة?
Which is the plural of مُدَرِّسَة?
Which is the plural of سَيَّارَة (car)?
Which is the plural of جَامِعَة?
What is removed from a feminine noun before ـَات is added?

exercises.promptTranslation: They (women) are students at the university.
There are many universities in the city.

explanations.title: Plurals made by rearranging the word
explanations.body: Most other nouns form the plural by changing the vowels and sometimes adding letters inside the word, as in English man and men. These are called broken plurals. There are patterns, but no reliable rule, so learn each plural together with its singular.

explanations.title: More common plurals
explanations.body: Say each pair aloud until the plural feels natural.

examples.text: فِي الْمَدِينَة مَسَاجِد وَمَدَارِس وَشَوَارِع كَثِيرَة.
examples.translation: fī al-madīna masājid wamadāris washawāriʿ kathīra. — In the city there are many mosques, schools and streets.
hādhihi kutub. — These are books.
aṭ-ṭullāb fī al-maktaba. — The students are in the library.

exercises.prompt: Which is the plural of كِتَاب (book)?
Which is the plural of بَيْت (house)?
Which is the plural of مَدِينَة (city)?
Which is the plural of مَدْرَسَة (school)?
Which is the plural of شَارِع (street)?
Which is the plural of رَجُل (man)?
Which is the plural of طَالِب?
exercises.explanation: طَالِب → طُلَّاب (the broken plural; women are طَالِبَات).

exercises.prompt: How should you learn a broken plural?

exercises.promptTranslation: These are books.
The students are in the library.

explanations.title: The adjective follows the noun
explanations.body: In Arabic the adjective comes after its noun and matches it in gender. For a feminine noun, add ة to the masculine adjective. Nouns that end in ة are nearly always feminine.

explanations.title: Noun and adjective together
explanations.body: A few feminine nouns do not end in ة, such as شَمْس (sun). You have to learn them one by one. Compare the pairs below.

examples.translation: bayt kabīr — a big house
madrasa kabīra — a big school
kitāb jadīd — a new book
madīna jamīla — a beautiful city
shāriʿ ṭawīl — a long street
ḥadīqa ṣaghīra — a small park
ash-shams ḥārra. — The sun is hot.

exercises.prompt: Which is “a big house” (بَيْت is masculine)?
Which is “a big school” (مَدْرَسَة is feminine)?

options: At the end of the sentence

exercises.prompt: What do you add to make a masculine adjective feminine?

exercises.promptTranslation: a small park
a new book

lessons.title: 55. The big house or the house is big?
lessons.subtitle: بَيْت كَبِير · الْبَيْت الْكَبِير · الْبَيْت كَبِير

explanations.title: Three patterns, three meanings
explanations.body: An adjective also agrees with its noun in definiteness. If the noun has ال, a describing adjective must have ال too, and together they are a phrase: “the big house”. If only the noun has ال, there is no ال on the adjective and you get a sentence: “the house is big”.

explanations.title: With هَذَا and with two adjectives
explanations.body: هَذَا + a noun with ال means “this …”. Compare هَذَا بَيْت كَبِير (this is a big house) with هَذَا الْبَيْت كَبِير (this house is big). Two adjectives can follow one another, and each takes ال if the noun does; joining them with و is also possible.

examples.translation: hādhā bayt kabīr. — This is a big house.
hādhā al-bayt kabīr. — This house is big.
ʾaskun fī al-bayt al-jadīd. — I live in the new house.
al-madīna al-qadīma jamīla. — The old city is beautiful.

examples.text: الْفُنْدُق الْكَبِير الْجَدِيد قَرِيب مِنَ الْمَحَطَّة.
examples.translation: al-funduq al-kabīr al-jadīd qarīb mina al-maḥaṭṭa. — The big, new hotel is near the station.

exercises.explanation: Both words take ال: a phrase.
Only the noun takes ال: a sentence.
ال on the noun only, feminine adjective.
هَذَا + noun with ال + adjective without ال.

exercises.prompt: Which means “This is a big house”?

exercises.explanation: The old city: ال on both words.
exercises.promptTranslation: The old city is beautiful.

exercises.explanation: The new house: ال on both words.
exercises.promptTranslation: I live in the new house.

explanations.title: Pairs of opposites
explanations.body: Learning adjectives in pairs makes them easy to remember. Each is shown in the masculine form.

explanations.title: Describing things
explanations.body: Remember to match the gender, and to use و between two adjectives in a predicate.

examples.translation: al-funduq jadīd wanaẓīf. — The hotel is new and clean.
ad-dars sahl wal-kitāb jayyid. — The lesson is easy and the book is good.
al-qiṭār sarīʿ. — The train is fast.
as-sayyāra sarīʿa waghāliya. — The car is fast and expensive.
al-maṭʿam qadīm warakhīṣ. — The restaurant is old and cheap.

examples.text: هَلِ الْمَطْعَم غَالِي؟ لَا، هُوَ رَخِيص.
examples.translation: hali al-maṭʿam ghālī? lā, huwa rakhīṣ. — Is the restaurant expensive? No, it is cheap.

exercises.prompt: Which word is the opposite of جَدِيد?
Which word is the opposite of سَهْل?
Which word is the opposite of سَرِيع?
Which word is the opposite of رَخِيص?
Which word is the opposite of جَمِيل?
Which means “The car is fast and expensive”?

exercises.explanation: The lesson is easy; الدَّرْس is masculine.
exercises.promptTranslation: The lesson is easy.
Is the restaurant expensive? No, it is cheap.

explanations.title: People: a plural adjective
explanations.body: When the noun is a group of people, the adjective is plural too: ـُون for men and ـَات for women (طُلَّاب مِصْرِيُّون, طَالِبَات مِصْرِيَّات).

explanations.title: Things: a feminine singular adjective
explanations.body: When the plural names things or animals, the adjective is feminine singular, whatever the gender of the noun in the singular. A plural of things is treated as one feminine group.

examples.translation: hādhihi kutub jadīda. — These are new books.
al-buyūt al-qadīma jamīla. — The old houses are beautiful.
al-mudun al-kabīra baʿīda. — The big cities are far.
al-muhandisūn al-miṣriyyūn fī al-maktab. — The Egyptian engineers are in the office.

exercises.explanation: People: the adjective is plural too.

exercises.prompt: An adjective for a plural of things is…
exercises.explanation: A plural of things is treated as feminine singular.

exercises.prompt: An adjective for a plural group of people is…

exercises.promptTranslation: These are new books.

exercises.explanation: A plural of things takes the feminine singular, with ال.
exercises.promptTranslation: The old houses are beautiful.

lessons.title: 58. The family
lessons.subtitle: أَب · أُمّ · أَخ · أُخْت · اِبْن · اِبْنَة

explanations.title: Close family
explanations.body: Pairs of masculine and feminine words. Most follow the usual rule of adding ة; أَخ and أُخْت, أَب and أُمّ are separate words.

explanations.title: Uncles, aunts and the family as a whole
explanations.body: Arabic names relatives on the father’s side and on the mother’s side separately.

explanations.title: Plurals for the family
explanations.body: These plurals are broken plurals, so learn them as they are. إِخْوَة can mean brothers, or brothers and sisters together.

examples.translation: hādhihi ʾusra kabīra. — This is a big family.
al-ʾab wal-ʾumm wal-ʾawlād fī al-bayt. — The father, the mother and the children are in the house.
al-jadd saʿīd wal-jadda saʿīda. — The grandfather is happy and the grandmother is happy.

exercises.explanation: خَال = mother’s brother; عَمّ = father’s brother.

exercises.prompt: Which is the plural of أَخ?
Which is the plural of أُخْت?

exercises.promptTranslation: The grandfather is happy and the grandmother is happy.

explanations.title: Endings on family words
explanations.body: The endings you learned in unit 2 attach to family nouns exactly as they do to كِتَاب. Two small points: a doubled letter keeps its shadda (أُمّ → أُمِّي), and ة turns into ت (جَدَّة → جَدَّتِي).

explanations.title: Father and brother are different
explanations.body: أَب and أَخ add a long vowel ـُو before ـكَ ـهُ ـهَا. With ـِي they are regular. Use the long-vowel forms below when the word is the subject of a sentence; in other positions the form changes.

examples.translation: ʾabī ṭabīb waʾummī mudarrisa. — My father is a doctor and my mother is a teacher.
ʾakhī kabīr waʾukhtī ṣaghīra. — My brother is grown-up and my sister is little.
hal ʾabūka muhandis? — Is your father an engineer?
ʾabūhā mudarris waʾummuhā ṭabība. — Her father is a teacher and her mother is a doctor.
jaddī kabīr wajaddatī saʿīda. — My grandfather is old and my grandmother is happy.

exercises.explanation: أَب lengthens to أَبُو before ـهَا.
أَخ lengthens to أَخُو before ـهُ.
A feminine word for the little one.
exercises.promptTranslation: My brother is grown-up and my sister is little.

exercises.explanation: Asking a man about his father.
exercises.promptTranslation: Is your father an engineer?

explanations.title: Adjectives for people
explanations.body: The same adjective-agreement rules apply: add ة for a woman. Remember that a man says أَنَا مَشْغُول and a woman says أَنَا مَشْغُولَة.

explanations.title: With family words
explanations.body: A noun with an attached pronoun is definite. So if you add an adjective to it as a description, that adjective takes ال: أَخِي الْكَبِير means “my older brother”.

examples.translation: ʾakhī ṭawīl waʾukhtī qaṣīra. — My brother is tall and my sister is short.
ʾummī saʿīda. — My mother is happy.
ʾakhī al-kabīr muhandis. — My older brother is an engineer.
ʾukhtī aṣ-ṣaghīra ṭāliba. — My younger sister is a student.
hal ʾanti saʿīda? — Are you happy? (to a woman)
ʾanā mashghūl al-yawm. — I am busy today. (a man speaking)

exercises.prompt: A woman says she is busy. She says…
exercises.explanation: A woman uses the feminine adjective.
Possessed noun is definite, so the adjective takes ال.
A sentence: no ال on the adjective.

exercises.promptTranslation: My sister is short.

exercises.explanation: “My older brother”: ال on the adjective.
exercises.promptTranslation: My older brother is an engineer.

explanations.title: Jobs, masculine and feminine
explanations.body: Jobs have a masculine and a feminine form. Use the one that matches the person you are describing.

explanations.title: Talking about the family’s work
explanations.body: To ask about work, use مَاذَا يَعْمَل …؟ (for a man) or مَاذَا تَعْمَل …؟ (for a woman); أَيْنَ يَعْمَل and أَيْنَ تَعْمَل ask where. With plural family words like إِخْوَتِي (my brothers and sisters), use the plural job words from the lessons on plurals.

examples.translation: mādhā yaʿmal ʾabūka? — What does your father do?
ʾabī ṭabīb. — My father is a doctor.
ʾayna taʿmal ʾummuka? — Where does your mother work?
taʿmal ʾummī fī mustashfā. — My mother works in a hospital.
ʾikhwatī muhandisūn waʾakhawātī mudarrisāt. — My brothers are engineers and my sisters are teachers.
zawjī muwaẓẓaf fī bank. — My husband is a bank employee.

exercises.prompt: Which means “My father is a doctor”?
Which means “My mother is a doctor”?
Which question asks “What does your father do?”
Which means “Where does your mother work?”

exercises.promptTranslation: My mother works in a hospital.
My husband is a bank employee.

explanations.title: Asking
explanations.body: رَقْم is “number”. Add the ending to ask for someone’s phone number, with ـكَ for a man and ـكِ for a woman.

examples.translation: mā raqm hātifika? — What is your phone number? (to a man)
mā raqm hātifiki? — What is your phone number? (to a woman)
mā ʿunwānuka? — What is your address? (to a man)
ʾaskun fī shāriʿ al-jāmiʿa. — I live on University Street.
mā raqm ash-shaqqa? — What is the apartment number?

explanations.title: Saying a phone number
explanations.body: A phone number is usually read one digit at a time, in the order you see it from left to right, using the counting words from unit 1. The numbers below are made up.

rows: صِفْر · وَاحِد · اِثْنَان · ثَلَاثَة · أَرْبَعَة · خَمْسَة
خَمْسَة · خَمْسَة · خَمْسَة · صِفْر · وَاحِد · صِفْر · صِفْر
تِسْعَة · ثَمَانِيَة · سَبْعَة · سِتَّة · خَمْسَة · أَرْبَعَة

exercises.prompt: How do you ask a man for his phone number?
How do you ask a woman for her phone number?
What does مَا عُنْوَانُكَ؟ ask for?
What does مَا رَقْم الشَّقَّة؟ ask for?
