In which order is a phone number read?
options: digit by digit, left to right
exercises.explanation: Phone numbers are spelled out digit by digit.

exercises.promptTranslation: What is your phone number?
I live on University Street.

explanations.title: A short text
explanations.body: Read this description line by line. Everything in it uses the grammar of unit 4: plurals, adjectives that agree, and position words.

examples.translation: madīnatī kabīra wajamīla. — My city is big and beautiful.

examples.text: فِي الْمَدِينَة شَوَارِع طَوِيلَة وَحَدَائِق كَثِيرَة.
examples.translation: fī al-madīna shawāriʿ ṭawīla waḥadāʾiq kathīra. — In the city there are long streets and many parks.

examples.text: الْمَدِينَة الْقَدِيمَة فِي الشَّمَال وَالْجَامِعَة فِي الْجَنُوب.
examples.translation: al-madīna al-qadīma fī ash-shamāl wal-jāmiʿa fī al-janūb. — The old city is in the north and the university is in the south.

examples.text: بِجَانِب الْجَامِعَة مَكْتَبَة كَبِيرَة وَمَقْهَى صَغِير.
examples.translation: bijānib al-jāmiʿa maktaba kabīra wamaqhā ṣaghīr. — Next to the university there is a big library and a small café.
as-sūq al-qadīm rakhīṣ wal-maṭāʿim jayyida. — The old market is cheap and the restaurants are good.
ʾuḥibb madīnatī liʾanna an-nās laṭīfūn. — I like my city because the people are kind.

exercises.prompt: «الْمَدِينَة الْقَدِيمَة فِي الشَّمَال وَالْجَامِعَة فِي الْجَنُوب.» Where is the university?
«بِجَانِب الْجَامِعَة مَكْتَبَة كَبِيرَة وَمَقْهَى صَغِير.» What is next to the university?
options: A big library and a small café
A small library and a big café
exercises.explanation: كَبِيرَة goes with مَكْتَبَة; صَغِير goes with مَقْهَى.

exercises.prompt: «السُّوق الْقَدِيم رَخِيص.» What is the old market like?
«فِي الْمَدِينَة شَوَارِع طَوِيلَة.» What are the streets like?
«أُحِبّ مَدِينَتِي لِأَنَّ النَّاس لَطِيفُون.» Why does the writer like the city?

exercises.explanation: A plural of things takes the feminine singular.
exercises.promptTranslation: In the city there are long streets.
The people are kind.

lessons.title: 64. Review: my family and my home town
lessons.subtitle: A student introduces her family

explanations.title: Sara introduces her family
explanations.body: Read what Sara says, then answer the questions.

examples.text: اِسْمِي سَارَة وَأَنَا طَالِبَة فِي الْجَامِعَة.
examples.translation: ismī sāra waʾanā ṭāliba fī al-jāmiʿa. — My name is Sara and I am a student at the university.

examples.text: أَسْكُن فِي بَيْت كَبِير فِي مَدِينَة جَمِيلَة.
examples.translation: ʾaskun fī bayt kabīr fī madīna jamīla. — I live in a big house in a beautiful city.
ʾabī muhandis waʾummī ṭabība. — My father is an engineer and my mother is a doctor.

examples.text: أَخِي الْكَبِير مُوَظَّف فِي بَنْك وَأُخْتِي الصَّغِيرَة طَالِبَة.
examples.translation: ʾakhī al-kabīr muwaẓẓaf fī bank waʾukhtī aṣ-ṣaghīra ṭāliba. — My older brother is a bank employee and my younger sister is a student.
jaddatī laṭīfa watuḥibb ash-shitāʾ. — My grandmother is kind and likes winter.
ʾuḥibb ʿāʾilatī liʾannahum saʿīdūn. — I love my family because they are happy.

exercises.prompt: Which is the plural of كِتَاب?
Which means “the old houses are beautiful”?
exercises.explanation: A plural of things: feminine singular adjective.

exercises.prompt: The bank is between the library and the restaurant. Which word means “between”?

exercises.promptTranslation: My grandmother is kind and likes winter.

units.title: البيت والأرقام: the home, the dual and numbers

lessons.title: 65. Invitations
lessons.subtitle: تَفَضَّل · أَهْلًا بِكَ · أَدْعُوكَ إِلَى الْعَشَاء

explanations.title: Welcoming a guest
explanations.body: تَفَضَّل is what you say to invite someone in, to offer something, or to say “after you”. It changes for a woman and for a group. أَهْلًا بِـ plus an ending means “welcome to you”; you will see how these endings work after a preposition in the next unit.

explanations.title: Inviting, accepting, declining
explanations.body: أَدْعُو means “I invite”. The ending ـكَ or ـكِ, the same as in كِتَابُكَ, means “you” when it is added to a verb. To decline politely, thank the person and give a reason.

examples.translation: ʾadʿūka ʾilā al-ʿashāʾ. — I invite you (man) to dinner.
ʾadʿūki ʾilā al-ghadāʾ. — I invite you (woman) to lunch.
shukran ʿalā ad-daʿwa. — Thank you for the invitation.
bikulli surūr! — With pleasure!
shukran, walakin ʾanā mashghūl al-yawm. — Thank you, but I am busy today. (a man speaking)
lil-ʾasaf, ʾanā mashghūla ghadan. — Unfortunately I am busy tomorrow. (a woman speaking)
ʾahlan biki fī baytī. — Welcome to my home. (to a woman)

exercises.prompt: Someone says تَفَضَّلِي. Who are they speaking to?
Which welcomes a man to your home?
Which means “Thank you for the invitation”?
Which means “I invite you (man) to dinner”?
You cannot come. Which is a polite reply (man speaking)?

exercises.promptTranslation: Welcome to my home. (to a woman)
Thank you for the invitation.

explanations.title: Rooms
explanations.body: غُرْفَة النَّوْم is “the room of sleeping”, the bedroom: another two-noun phrase like عَاصِمَة مِصْر.

explanations.title: Parts of the house
explanations.body: Notice which are masculine and which are feminine: the adjective will have to match.

examples.text: فِي الشَّقَّة غُرْفَة نَوْم وَمَطْبَخ وَحَمَّام.
examples.translation: fī ash-shaqqa ghurfa nawm wamaṭbakh waḥammām. — In the apartment there is a bedroom, a kitchen and a bathroom.
al-maṭbakh bijānib aṣ-ṣālūn. — The kitchen is next to the living room.
al-bāb kabīr wan-nāfidha ṣaghīra. — The door is big and the window is small.
baytī qadīm, lākinna al-ḥadīqa jamīla. — My house is old, but the garden is beautiful.

exercises.prompt: Which means “The kitchen is next to the living room”?

exercises.promptTranslation: The door is big and the window is small.

exercises.explanation: A bedroom is a room of sleeping.
exercises.promptTranslation: In the apartment there is a bedroom and a kitchen.

explanations.title: Things in a room
explanations.body: Most of these end in ة and are feminine, but not all. Check the gender before you describe them.

examples.translation: aṭ-ṭāwila kabīra wal-kursiyy ṣaghīr. — The table is big and the chair is small.
as-sarīr jadīd wal-khizāna qadīma. — The bed is new and the wardrobe is old.
fī aṣ-ṣālūn ʾarīka waṭāwila watilfāz. — In the living room there is a sofa, a table and a television.
ath-thallāja fī al-maṭbakh. — The refrigerator is in the kitchen.

exercises.promptTranslation: The wardrobe is old.
In the living room there is a sofa and a table.

explanations.title: Describing a room
explanations.body: Combine what you know: the position words, the furniture, and the pattern “in the room there is…”. When the thing you name is new in the sentence, it has no ال.

examples.translation: fī ghurfatī sarīr wamaktab wakhizāna. — In my room there is a bed, a desk and a wardrobe.
as-sarīr bijānib an-nāfidha. — The bed is next to the window.
al-miṣbāḥ fawq al-maktab. — The lamp is above the desk.

examples.text: الْكِتَاب عَلَى الْمَكْتَب وَالْقَلَم تَحْت الْكُرْسِيّ.
examples.translation: al-kitāb ʿalā al-maktab wal-qalam taḥt al-kursiyy. — The book is on the desk and the pen is under the chair.
al-mirʾāh ʿalā al-jidār. — The mirror is on the wall.
ʾayna al-miftāḥ? huwa ʿalā aṭ-ṭāwila. — Where is the key? It is on the table.

exercises.prompt: «فِي غُرْفَتِي سَرِير وَمَكْتَب وَخِزَانَة.» What is in the room?
options: A bed, a desk and a wardrobe

exercises.prompt: «السَّرِير بِجَانِب النَّافِذَة.» Where is the bed?
«الْمِصْبَاح فَوْق الْمَكْتَب.» Where is the lamp?
«الْقَلَم تَحْت الْكُرْسِيّ.» Where is the pen?
Which means “The mirror is on the wall”?
Which means “In my room there is a bed”?
exercises.explanation: Place first, then a noun without ال.

exercises.promptTranslation: The book is on the desk.
The bed is next to the window.

explanations.title: A special form for two
explanations.body: Arabic has three numbers: singular, dual (exactly two) and plural. The dual is formed by adding ـَان to the singular. You do not need the word for “two”; the ending already says it. After a preposition, or when the dual is an object, ـَان changes to ـَيْن.

explanations.title: Feminine nouns change ة to ت
explanations.body: A noun that ends in ة changes it to ت before the dual ending. That is the same change you saw before an attached pronoun (مَدْرَسَتِي).

examples.translation: fī al-bayt ḥammāmān. — There are two bathrooms in the house.
fī ash-shaqqa ghurfatān. — There are two rooms in the apartment.
ʾanẓur ʾilā baytayn. — I am looking at two houses.
huwa maʿa waladayn. — He is with two boys.

exercises.prompt: Which means “I am looking at two houses”?
Do you need to say اِثْنَان (two) with a dual noun?
options: No: the ending already means two

exercises.promptTranslation: There are two bathrooms in the house.
There are two rooms in the apartment.

lessons.title: 70. The dual with adjectives and verbs
lessons.subtitle: الْكِتَابَان جَدِيدَان · هُمَا يَكْتُبَان

explanations.title: Adjectives agree in the dual
explanations.body: An adjective that describes a dual noun is also dual. Masculine adjectives add ـَان, feminine adjectives change ة to ت and add ـَان.

examples.translation: al-kitābān jadīdān. — The two books are new.
al-ghurfatān kabīratān. — The two rooms are big.

explanations.title: They two, you two
explanations.body: The pronouns for two people are أَنْتُمَا (you two) and هُمَا (they two, for men or women). A verb that follows its subject takes the dual ending ـَان, with يَـ for two males and تَـ for two females.

examples.translation: humā ṭālibān. — They (two men) are students.
humā ṭālibatān. — They (two women) are students.
aṭ-ṭālibān yadrusān fī al-maktaba. — The two students study in the library.
al-bintān talʿabān fī al-ḥadīqa. — The two girls play in the garden.
yalʿab al-waladān fī ash-shāriʿ. — The two boys play in the street. (verb first stays singular)

exercises.prompt: Which means “the two students study” (a verb after the subject)?
exercises.explanation: A masculine dual verb: يَـ + ـَان.

exercises.prompt: Which means “The two girls play” (verb after the subject)?
exercises.explanation: A feminine dual verb: تَـ + ـَان.

exercises.prompt: When the verb comes first, the verb is…
exercises.explanation: A verb before its subject stays singular.

exercises.promptTranslation: The two rooms are big.
The two books are new.

explanations.title: One: it follows the noun
explanations.body: “One” is an adjective: it follows the noun and agrees with its gender. A masculine noun takes وَاحِد and a feminine noun takes وَاحِدَة.

explanations.title: Two: the dual, plus an optional اِثْنَان
explanations.body: For two, you normally use the dual alone. If you want to stress “two”, add اِثْنَان (for a masculine noun) or اِثْنَتَان (for a feminine noun) after it. When you count out loud without a noun, you say وَاحِد, اِثْنَان.

examples.translation: fī al-bayt ḥammām wāḥid. — There is one bathroom in the house.
fī al-bayt ghurfatān wamaṭbakh wāḥid. — There are two rooms and one kitchen in the house.
ʾaskun fī shaqqa wāḥida. — I live in one apartment.

options: At the start of the sentence
exercises.explanation: “One” is an adjective, so it follows.

exercises.promptTranslation: There is one bathroom in the house.
I live in one apartment.

lessons.title: 72. Three to ten: with masculine nouns
lessons.subtitle: ثَلَاثَة كُتُب · خَمْسَة طُلَّاب

explanations.title: The number looks feminine
explanations.body: From three to ten, the number has the opposite gender to the singular of the thing counted. With a masculine noun, the number ends in ـَة, which looks feminine. The noun comes after the number, and it is plural. Digits are shown for reference; they are not read aloud here.

explanations.title: In sentences
explanations.body: A plural of things that follows the number is described with a feminine singular adjective, as before. A sound masculine plural after a number takes the ـِين ending.

examples.translation: ʿalā aṭ-ṭāwila thalātha kutub. — There are three books on the table.
sabʿa ʾayyām fī al-ʾusbūʿ. — There are seven days in a week.
ʾaʿmal khamsa ʾayyām fī al-ʾusbūʿ. — I work five days a week.
fī al-madrasa khamsa mudarrisīn. — There are five teachers in the school.
thalātha kutub jadīda — three new books

exercises.explanation: Masculine noun: the number ends in ـَة.

exercises.prompt: After the numbers three to ten, the noun is…
Which gender does the number 3–10 have, compared with the noun?

exercises.explanation: The adjective after a plural of things: feminine singular.

exercises.promptTranslation: There are three books on the table.
I work five days a week.

lessons.title: 73. Three to ten: with feminine nouns
lessons.subtitle: ثَلَاث غُرَف · عَشْر سَنَوَات

explanations.title: The number loses its ة
explanations.body: With a feminine noun, the number is in its short form with no ـَة. The noun is again plural and comes after the number.

explanations.title: In sentences
explanations.body: Compare these with the last lesson: the noun decides which form of the number you need.

examples.translation: fī ash-shaqqa thalāth ghuraf. — There are three rooms in the apartment.
ʾadrus ʾarbaʿ sāʿāt. — I study for four hours.
fī al-madīna tisʿ madāris. — There are nine schools in the city.
ʾaskun hunā mundhu ʿashr sanawāt. — I have lived here for ten years.
thalāth ghuraf kabīra — three big rooms

exercises.explanation: Feminine noun: the short number, plural noun.

exercises.prompt: Which means “three books” (masculine) and which “three rooms” (feminine)?

exercises.promptTranslation: There are three rooms in the apartment.
I study for four hours.

explanations.title: كَمْ + a singular noun
explanations.body: To ask “how many”, use كَمْ followed by a singular noun without ال. For three to ten, the answer is a number and then a plural noun, with the number in the form that fits the gender of the noun.

explanations.title: Questions and answers
explanations.body: In an answer, the place usually comes first, then the number and the thing counted.

examples.translation: kam ghurfa fī al-bayt? — How many rooms are in the house?
fī al-bayt khams ghuraf. — There are five rooms in the house.
kam kitāb ʿalā aṭ-ṭāwila? — How many books are on the table?
ʿalā aṭ-ṭāwila thalātha kutub. — There are three books on the table.
kam yawm fī al-ʾusbūʿ? — How many days are in a week?
sabʿa ʾayyām. — Seven days.

exercises.prompt: Which answers “How many books?” with three?
Which answers “How many rooms?” with three?
Which answers “How many days?” with five?
Which answers “How many hours?” with four?
Which answers “How many students (women)?” with six?
Which means “There are seven days in a week”?
exercises.explanation: يَوْم is masculine; the noun after the number is plural.

exercises.promptTranslation: How many rooms are in the house?
There are five rooms in the house.

explanations.title: Noun + noun
explanations.body: Arabic says “the house of the teacher”, “the key of the house”, by putting two nouns side by side. This is the iḍāfa. The first noun never takes ال or a possessive ending. The second noun decides whether the whole phrase is definite.

explanations.title: A chain, and an adjective
explanations.body: A third noun can be added, as in بَاب غُرْفَة النَّوْم. An adjective that comes at the end agrees with the noun it describes, and it takes ال, because the whole phrase is definite. Compare the two sentences below: the gender of the adjective shows which noun it belongs to.

examples.translation: ghurfa al-mudīr al-jadīda — the director’s new room (the room is new)
ghurfa al-mudīr al-jadīd — the room of the new director (the director is new)
miftāḥ al-bayt ʿalā aṭ-ṭāwila. — The house key is on the table.
mudīr al-madrasa jadīd. — The principal of the school is new.

exercises.prompt: Which means “the door of the room”?
exercises.explanation: First noun without ال, second with ال.

exercises.prompt: Which means “the principal of the school”?

exercises.explanation: A chain of three nouns; ال only on the last.
أَبِي already makes the phrase definite.

exercises.prompt: Which noun in an iḍāfa never takes ال?
exercises.explanation: بَيْت الْمُدَرِّس: ال is on the second only.

exercises.prompt: Which means “the director’s new room” (the room is new)?
exercises.explanation: الْجَدِيدَة is feminine like غُرْفَة, with ال.
The first noun has no ال.
exercises.promptTranslation: The house key is on the table.

exercises.explanation: The room is new: feminine, with ال.
exercises.promptTranslation: the director’s new room

explanations.title: One, two, three or more
explanations.body: Each unit of time follows the same pattern as everything you have just learned. Notice the gender: يَوْم, أُسْبُوع and شَهْر are masculine; سَنَة, سَاعَة and دَقِيقَة are feminine.

explanations.title: Words for “for”, “since”, “after”, “before”
explanations.body: لِمُدَّة means “for a period of”, مُنْذُ means “since” or “for (up to now)”, and بَعْد and قَبْل mean “after” and “before”. After مُنْذُ, بَعْد and قَبْل a dual noun ends in ـَيْن.

examples.translation: ʾaskun hunā mundhu sanatayn. — I have lived here for two years.

examples.text: سَأَذْهَب إِلَى الْقَاهِرَة لِمُدَّة ثَلَاثَة أَيَّام.
examples.translation: saʾadhhab ʾilā al-qāhira limudda thalātha ʾayyām. — I will go to Cairo for three days.
ar-riḥla sāʿatān. — The trip is two hours.
baʿd ʾusbūʿ saʾadhhab ʾilā ʿammān. — In a week I will go to Amman.
ad-dars qabl al-ʿashāʾ. — The lesson is before dinner.

exercises.prompt: Which means “I have lived here for two years”?

exercises.promptTranslation: I will go to Amman for three days.
The lesson is before dinner.

lessons.title: 77. First, second, third: floors and ordinals
lessons.subtitle: الطَّابِق الْأَوَّل · الْغُرْفَة الثَّانِيَة

explanations.title: Ordinal numbers
explanations.body: “First”, “second” and so on are adjectives. They follow the noun, take ال if the noun does, and agree in gender. The first is irregular; the others add ة for the feminine as usual.

explanations.title: Floors
explanations.body: Floors are masculine (الطَّابِق). The ground floor is الطَّابِق الْأَرْضِيّ; أَرْضِيّ is an adjective made from أَرْض, “ground”.

examples.translation: ʾaskun fī aṭ-ṭābiq ath-thālith. — I live on the third floor.
al-maṭbakh fī aṭ-ṭābiq al-ʾarḍiyy. — The kitchen is on the ground floor.
ghurfa an-nawm fī aṭ-ṭābiq al-ʾawwal. — The bedroom is on the first floor (one floor above the ground floor).
al-ghurfa ath-thāniya kabīra. — The second room is big.

examples.text: الدَّرْس الْأَوَّل سَهْل وَالدَّرْس الثَّانِي صَعْب.
examples.translation: ad-dars al-ʾawwal sahl wad-dars ath-thānī ṣaʿb. — The first lesson is easy and the second lesson is hard.

exercises.explanation: The feminine of الْأَوَّل is irregular.

exercises.promptTranslation: I live on the third floor.
The second room is big.

explanations.title: Words used in ads
explanations.body: Property ads are short and use much of the vocabulary of this unit.

explanations.title: Two ads
explanations.body: Read each line. The word قَرِيب or قَرِيبَة (“near”) agrees with the thing advertised: شَقَّة is feminine and بَيْت is masculine.

examples.translation: shaqqa lil-ʾījār fī aṭ-ṭābiq ath-thālith. — Apartment for rent on the third floor.
thalāth ghuraf wamaṭbakh waḥammāmān. — Three rooms, a kitchen and two bathrooms.
qarība mina al-jāmiʿa. — Near the university.
bayt lil-bayʿ. — House for sale.
ʾarbaʿ ghuraf waḥadīqa kabīra. — Four rooms and a big garden.
qarīb mina as-sūq wal-masjid. — Near the market and the mosque.

exercises.prompt: «شَقَّة لِلْإِيجَار فِي الطَّابِق الثَّالِث.» What is advertised?
options: An apartment to rent on the third floor
A room to rent on the first floor
An apartment for sale on the third floor

exercises.prompt: «ثَلَاث غُرَف وَمَطْبَخ وَحَمَّامَان.» How many rooms are there?
«ثَلَاث غُرَف وَمَطْبَخ وَحَمَّامَان.» How many bathrooms?
«بَيْت لِلْبَيْع. أَرْبَع غُرَف وَحَدِيقَة كَبِيرَة.» What does the house have?
options: Four rooms and a big garden
Three rooms and a small garden

exercises.prompt: The ad says «قَرِيبَة مِنَ الْجَامِعَة». What is being advertised?
options: A feminine thing, such as an apartment

exercises.promptTranslation: Apartment for rent on the second floor.
A house for sale near the market.

lessons.title: 79. Review: a visit to a new home
lessons.subtitle: Welcome, rooms, numbers

explanations.title: Khalid welcomes Sara
explanations.body: Khalid has invited Sara to see his home. Read the conversation, then answer the questions.

examples.text: تَفَضَّلِي يَا سَارَة. أَهْلًا بِكِ فِي بَيْتِي.
examples.translation: tafaḍḍalī yā sāra. ʾahlan biki fī baytī. — Khalid: Please come in, Sara. Welcome to my home.
shukran ʿalā ad-daʿwa. al-bayt jamīl! — Sara: Thank you for the invitation. The house is beautiful!

examples.text: هَذَا هُوَ الصَّالُون. فِي الصَّالُون أَرِيكَة وَطَاوِلَتَان وَتِلْفَاز.
examples.translation: hādhā huwa aṣ-ṣālūn. fī aṣ-ṣālūn ʾarīka waṭāwilatān watilfāz. — Khalid: This is the living room. In the living room there is a sofa, two tables and a television.
kam ghurfa fī al-bayt? — Sara: How many rooms are there in the house?

examples.text: فِي الْبَيْت أَرْبَع غُرَف وَحَمَّامَان وَمَطْبَخ وَاحِد.
examples.translation: fī al-bayt ʾarbaʿ ghuraf waḥammāmān wamaṭbakh wāḥid. — Khalid: There are four rooms, two bathrooms and one kitchen.
waʾayna ghurfa an-nawm? — Sara: And where is the bedroom?

examples.text: فِي الطَّابِق الثَّانِي. أَسْكُن هُنَا مُنْذُ سَنَتَيْن.
examples.translation: fī aṭ-ṭābiq ath-thānī. ʾaskun hunā mundhu sanatayn. — Khalid: On the second floor. I have lived here for two years.

exercises.prompt: Khalid says تَفَضَّلِي to Sara. What does it mean?
What is in the living room?
options: A sofa, two tables and a television

exercises.prompt: How many rooms are in the house?
How long has Khalid lived there?

exercises.explanation: The dual of a feminine noun.

exercises.promptTranslation: How many rooms are there in the house?

units.title: الأوامر والواجبات: commands, endings and obligations

explanations.title: From the present to the command
explanations.body: To tell one man to do something, start with the present form for “you (man)” and take off the تَـ. What is left starts with two consonants, so Arabic adds a helping alif in front. The alif gets ُ if the verb’s present vowel is ُ, and ِ if it is anything else. The end of the verb has a sukūn.

explanations.title: Commands in use
explanations.body: A command is one word. تَفَضَّل was an invitation; these are plain requests, so add مِنْ فَضْلِكَ (“please”) when you speak to someone you do not know.

examples.translation: ijlis hunā. — Sit here. (to a man)
udkhul min hunā. — Come in this way. (to a man)
uktub hunāk. — Write there. (to a man)
idhhab ʾilā al-madrasa. — Go to school. (to a man)
min faḍlika, udrusi al-yawm. — Please study today. (to a man)

exercises.prompt: Which is the command “Sit!” to a man?
exercises.explanation: Drop the تَـ and add اِ because the present vowel is ِ.

exercises.prompt: Which is the command “Write!” to a man?
exercises.explanation: The present vowel of تَكْتُب is ُ, so the helping alif has ُ.

exercises.prompt: Which is the command “Open!” to a man?
exercises.explanation: تَفْتَح has the vowel َ, so the helping alif has ِ.

exercises.prompt: Which is the command “Enter!” to a man?
What goes on the last letter of a command to a man?

exercises.explanation: اِذْهَبْ is the command; إِلَى = to.

exercises.prompt: Which is polite when you ask a stranger to sit?

exercises.promptTranslation: Sit here. (to a man)

exercises.explanation: Come in this way = from here.
exercises.promptTranslation: Come in this way. (to a man)

lessons.title: 81. Commands to a woman and to groups
lessons.subtitle: اُكْتُبِي · اُكْتُبَا · اُكْتُبُوا · اُكْتُبْنَ

explanations.title: One command, five addressees
explanations.body: Arabic has a command for a man, a woman, two people, a group of men and a group of women. The endings are those of the present without the final ن: تَكْتُبِين becomes اُكْتُبِي and تَكْتُبُون becomes اُكْتُبُوا, while ـْنَ stays. In the men’s group form the ending ـُوا has a silent alif after the و.

explanations.title: Choosing the right one
explanations.body: A mixed group of men and women takes the masculine group form. Teachers use the group forms all day.

examples.translation: ijlisī hunā yā sāra. — Sit here, Sara. (to a woman)
ijlisā min faḍlikumā. — Please sit. (to two people)
udkhulū yā ṭullāb. — Come in, students. (to a group)
uktubna ʾasmāʾakunna. — Write your names. (to a group of women)
udrusī al-yawm yā laylā. — Study today, Layla. (to a woman)

exercises.prompt: Which is “Write!” to a group of men?
Which is “Sit!” to a group of women?
A teacher talks to a class of men and women. Which does she use?
exercises.explanation: A mixed group takes the masculine plural.

exercises.promptTranslation: Sit, Sara.
Come in, students.

explanations.title: More verbs, same pattern
explanations.body: The same rule works for these verbs. For قَرَأَ the last root letter is a hamza, which sits on an alif with a sukūn: اِقْرَأْ. Before the ـِي of the feminine it sits on a ي seat: اِقْرَئِي.

explanations.title: A class and a home
explanations.body: Before ال the final sukūn of a command takes a short kasra, so the two words run together smoothly: اِفْتَحِ الْبَاب, اِقْرَأِ الْكِتَاب. This is only a matter of pronunciation.

examples.translation: ismaʿ yā ʾaḥmad. — Listen, Ahmad. (to a man)
unẓur ʾilā al-jabal. — Look at the mountain. (to a man)
iqraʾi al-kitāb. — Read the book. (to a man)
iftaḥi al-bāb min faḍlika. — Open the door, please. (to a man)
iḥmilī al-ḥaqība yā laylā. — Carry the bag, Layla. (to a woman)

exercises.explanation: The present vowel is َ, so the alif has ِ.

exercises.prompt: What happens to the final sukūn of a command before ال?

exercises.promptTranslation: Read the book.
Look at the mountain.

explanations.title: لَا + تَـ
explanations.body: A negative command is not built from the positive one. Use لَا and the present form for “you”, but with a sukūn at the end instead of the usual ḍamma. The endings for a woman, two people and a group are the same as in the positive command.

explanations.title: Rules and warnings
explanations.body: Compare: اُدْخُلْ is “Enter!” and لَا تَدْخُلْ is “Do not enter!”

examples.translation: lā taftaḥi al-bāb. — Do not open the door. (to a man)
lā tadkhul hunā. — Do not come in here. (to a man)
lā tajlisī hunāk. — Do not sit over there. (to a woman)
lā tadhhabū ʾilā al-jabal al-yawm. — Do not go to the mountain today. (to a group)
lā taktub hunā, uktub hunāk. — Do not write here; write there. (to a man)

exercises.prompt: Which is “Do not enter!” to a man?
Which is “Do not sit!” to a woman?
Which is “Do not sit!” to a group of men?
Which is “Do not go!” to a man?
Which word is in front of a negative command?
Which means “Do not open the door”?
Which is the negative command of اُدْخُلْ؟

exercises.promptTranslation: Do not come in here.
Do not sit over there.

lessons.title: 84. To me, to you: لِـ with endings
lessons.subtitle: لِي · لَكَ · لَهُ · لَهَا · لَنَا

explanations.title: The preposition لِـ
explanations.body: لِـ means “to” or “for”. When a pronoun follows it, the pronoun is not a separate word. It is a short ending joined to the preposition. Arabic uses لِـ plus an ending to say “I have”: لِي أَخ, literally “to me a brother”.

explanations.title: Having and giving
explanations.body: To say “I do not have”, put لَيْسَ in front: لَيْسَ لِي أَخ. The thing you have comes after, with no ال.

examples.translation: lī ʾakh wāḥid. — I have one brother.
lahā ʾukht fī al-madīna. — She has a sister in the city.
lanā bayt kabīr. — We have a big house.

examples.text: هَذَا الْمِفْتَاح لِي، وَهَذَا الْمِفْتَاح لَكَ.
examples.translation: hādhā al-miftāḥ lī, wahādhā al-miftāḥ laka. — This key is for me, and this key is for you.
laysa lī ʾakh. — I do not have a brother.

exercises.prompt: Which means “She has a sister in the city”?
Which means “We have a big house”?
Which means “I do not have a brother”?

exercises.promptTranslation: I have one brother.
This key is for you.

explanations.title: عِنْدَ and مَعَ with endings
explanations.body: عِنْدَ means “at”, and with an ending it is the usual way to say “have”: عِنْدِي سَيَّارَة. مَعَ means “with”, and with an ending it says that you have something on you right now: مَعِي هَاتِف. The endings are the same as in the last lesson. عِنْدَ and مَعَ keep their final fatḥa (عِنْدَكَ, مَعَهُ), except before ـِي, “me”: عِنْدِي, مَعِي.

explanations.title: Questions and answers
explanations.body: To answer no, use لَيْسَ: لَيْسَ عِنْدِي وَقْت.

examples.translation: hal ʿindaka sayyāra? — Do you have a car? (to a man)
naʿam, ʿindī sayyāra. — Yes, I have a car.
lā, laysa ʿindī sayyāra. — No, I do not have a car.
hal maʿaki hātif? — Do you have a phone with you? (to a woman)
laysa ʿindī waqt al-yawm. — I do not have time today.
huwa maʿahā fī al-bayt. — He is with her in the house.

exercises.prompt: Which means “Do you (man) have a car?”
Which means “Do you (woman) have a phone with you?”
Which says that you have no time?
Which is best when your phone is in your pocket right now?
Which means “He is with her in the house”?

exercises.promptTranslation: Do you have a phone with you? (to a woman)
No, I do not have a car.

explanations.title: بِـ, فِي and مِنْ
explanations.body: The same endings attach to every preposition. Three things change: after ِ or ـيْ the pronoun ـهُ becomes ـهِ (and ـهُم becomes ـهِم), “me” after فِي is فِيَّ, and “me” after مِنْ is مِنِّي, with a doubled ن.

explanations.title: إِلَى and عَلَى
explanations.body: The final ى of these two becomes ـَيْ in front of an ending, and “me” is ـَيَّ.

explanations.title: In sentences
explanations.body: The ending refers back to a noun that has already been named.

examples.translation: hādhā bayt. ʾanā ʾaskun fīhi. — This is a house. I live in it.
hādhihi madrasa. ʾanā ʾadrus fīhā. — This is a school. I study in it.
hādhihi hiya aṭ-ṭāwila. al-kitāb ʿalayhā. — This is the table. The book is on it.
hādhā ṣadīqī. ʾanā ʾaktub ʾilayhi. — This is my friend. I write to him.
hādhihi risāla minhā. — This is a letter from her.
as-salām ʿalaykum. — Peace be upon you. (to a group)

exercises.explanation: مِنَّا also has a doubled ن.

exercises.prompt: Which means “This is the table. The book is on it.”?

exercises.promptTranslation: This is a house. I live in it.
This is a letter from her.

lessons.title: 87. In front of me, behind you
lessons.subtitle: أَمَامِي · خَلْفَكَ · بِجَانِبِهَا

explanations.title: Position words with endings
explanations.body: The position words you know take the endings too. Because they are nouns in disguise, they keep their vowels in front of an ending: أَمَامَ becomes أَمَامِي, أَمَامَكَ, أَمَامَهُ. The ending “me” is ـِي, which forces a kasra on the letter before it, so أَمَامَ turns into أَمَامِي.

explanations.title: Where is it?
explanations.body: بَيْنَ means “between”. It needs two things: بَيْنِي وَبَيْنَكَ, “between me and you”.

examples.translation: al-mudarris ʾamāmanā wal-bāb khalfanā. — The teacher is in front of us and the door is behind us.
al-kitāb fawqa aṭ-ṭāwila, wal-ḥaqība taḥtahā. — The book is on top of the table, and the bag is under it.
baytī bijānibi al-madrasa. — My house is next to the school.
jalasa ʾaḥmad bijānibī. — Ahmad sat next to me.
baynī wabaynaka jabal. — Between me and you is a mountain.

exercises.explanation: With pronouns, بَيْنَ is repeated before each.

exercises.prompt: Which means “The teacher is in front of us”?
Which means “The bag is under it”, speaking of the table?

exercises.promptTranslation: The door is behind us.
Ahmad sat next to me.

explanations.title: A short conversation
explanations.body: Layla cannot find her key. Notice each ending and what it points to.

examples.translation: laylā: ʾayna miftāḥī? — Layla: Where is my key?
ʾaḥmad: huwa ʿalā aṭ-ṭāwila. — Ahmad: It is on the table.
laylā: laysa ʿalayhā. — Layla: It is not on it.
ʾaḥmad: hal huwa maʿaki? — Ahmad: Do you have it with you?
laylā: lā, laysa maʿī. — Layla: No, I do not have it.
ʾaḥmad: unẓurī fī al-ḥaqība. — Ahmad: Look in the bag.

examples.text: لَيْلَى: نَعَمْ! هُوَ فِيهَا. شُكْرًا لَكَ.
examples.translation: laylā: naʿam! huwa fīhā. shukran laka. — Layla: Yes! It is in it. Thank you.

exercises.prompt: Layla says «أَيْنَ مِفْتَاحِي؟». What is she looking for?
Ahmad says «هُوَ عَلَى الطَّاوِلَة». Where is the key, he thinks?
«لَيْسَ عَلَيْهَا». What does عَلَيْهَا stand for?
«هَلْ هُوَ مَعَكِ؟». Who is Ahmad speaking to?

options: I do not have it with me

exercises.prompt: «اُنْظُرِي فِي الْحَقِيبَة». What does Ahmad ask her to do?
exercises.explanation: اُنْظُرِي is a command to a woman.

exercises.prompt: «هُوَ فِيهَا». What does فِيهَا stand for?

exercises.promptTranslation: Look in the bag.
Thank you. (to a man)

lessons.title: 89. I must: يَجِب أَنْ
lessons.subtitle: يَجِب أَنْ أَدْرُس · يَجِب أَنْ نَذْهَب

explanations.title: يَجِب + أَنْ + verb
explanations.body: يَجِب means “it is necessary”. It never changes. Put أَنْ after it (“that”), and then the present verb with the person you mean. The verb carries the person, so the same sentence works for I, you, he and she.

explanations.title: Must and must not
explanations.body: To say “must not”, join أَنْ and لَا into أَلَّا: يَجِب أَلَّا تَدْخُل. Here يَجِب is followed by أَنْ and a verb, so the sentence has this three-part shape.

examples.translation: yajib ʾan ʾadrus al-yawm. — I must study today.
yajib ʾan tadhhab ʾilā al-madrasa. — You must go to school. (to a man)
yajib ʾan naktub al-wājib. — We must write the homework.

examples.text: يَجِب أَنْ تَرْجِع لَيْلَى إِلَى الْبَيْت.
examples.translation: yajib ʾan tarjiʿ laylā ʾilā al-bayt. — Layla must go back home.
yajib ʾallā tadkhul hunā. — You must not come in here. (to a man)

exercises.explanation: تَـ = she. يَجِب does not change.

exercises.prompt: Which means “You (man) must not come in”?
Which part of the sentence changes with the person?
Which means “We must go to school”?

exercises.promptTranslation: I must study today.
We must write the homework.

lessons.title: 90. After أَنْ: the ن falls away
lessons.subtitle: أَنْ تَكْتُبِي · أَنْ يَكْتُبُوا

explanations.title: Dropping the final ن
explanations.body: After أَنْ the verb loses a final ن. Endings that finish in ن (ـِينَ, ـَانِ, ـُونَ) lose that ن. The ـُوا ending gets a silent alif after the و. The feminine plural ـْنَ keeps its ن. The forms with no ending look the same in our spelling (in full vowelling they end in fatḥa: أَنْ أَكْتُبَ).

explanations.title: Other verbs that take أَنْ
explanations.body: The same rule applies after أُرِيد أَنْ (“I want to”) and after any other word that is followed by أَنْ.

examples.text: يَجِب أَنْ تَكْتُبِي الْوَاجِب يَا لَيْلَى.
examples.translation: yajib ʾan taktubī al-wājib yā laylā. — You must write the homework, Layla.
yajib ʾan tadrusū yā ṭullāb. — You must study, students.
yajib ʾan yadkhulā al-ʾān. — The two of them must come in now.
yajib ʾan yadhhabū ʾilā al-madrasa. — They must go to school.
ʾurīd ʾan ʾajlis hunā. — I want to sit here.
yajib ʾan yajlisna hunā. — They (women) must sit here.

exercises.prompt: Which is correct after أَنْ for “you (woman) write”?
exercises.explanation: The ن of ـِين is dropped.

exercises.prompt: Which is correct after أَنْ for “they (men) go”?
Which is correct after أَنْ for “the two of them enter”?
Which keeps its ن after أَنْ?
exercises.explanation: The feminine plural does not change.

exercises.prompt: Which means “I want to sit here”?
In تَكْتُبُوا, why is there an alif after the و?
options: it is only a spelling mark and is not pronounced
it is pronounced as a long vowel
exercises.explanation: The silent alif is written after the plural و.

exercises.promptTranslation: You must write the homework, Layla.
You must study, students.

lessons.title: 91. I have to: عَلَيَّ أَنْ
lessons.subtitle: عَلَيَّ أَنْ أَغْسِل · لَيْسَ عَلَيْكَ أَنْ تَذْهَب

explanations.title: عَلَى + ending + أَنْ
explanations.body: A second way to say “must” uses عَلَى with an ending, which you met earlier in this unit: عَلَيَّ أَنْ أَدْرُس, literally “upon me, that I study”. The person is the ending on عَلَى, and the verb after أَنْ agrees with it.

explanations.title: Must not versus do not have to
explanations.body: The two ways of saying “not” have different meanings. يَجِب أَلَّا means “must not” (it is forbidden). لَيْسَ عَلَيَّ أَنْ means “I do not have to” (it is not required).

examples.translation: ʿalayya ʾan ʾaghsil aṣ-ṣuḥūn. — I have to wash the dishes.
ʿalayhā ʾan taktub risāla. — She has to write a letter.
ʿalaynā ʾan nadhhab ʾilā as-sūq. — We have to go to the market.
laysa ʿalayka ʾan tadhhab. — You do not have to go. (to a man)
yajib ʾallā tadhhab. — You must not go. (to a man)

exercises.prompt: Which means “I have to wash the dishes”?
Which means “She has to write a letter”?
Which means “We have to go to the market”?
Which means “You do not have to go”?
A friend says «لَيْسَ عَلَيْكَ أَنْ تَدْرُس الْيَوْم». Does he forbid you?

exercises.promptTranslation: I have to wash the dishes.
You do not have to go.

explanations.title: Everyday jobs
explanations.body: Here are some jobs around the house with the present form for “he” and the command to a man. The command of غَسَلَ is اِغْسِلْ, with ِ because the present vowel is ِ.

explanations.title: Who does what
explanations.body: Use the three patterns you now know to ask, order and report.

examples.text: يَجِب أَنْ أَغْسِل الصُّحُون بَعْد الْعَشَاء.
examples.translation: yajib ʾan ʾaghsil aṣ-ṣuḥūn baʿd al-ʿashāʾ. — I must wash the dishes after dinner.
ʿalayhā ʾan taṭbukh al-ʿashāʾ al-yawm. — She has to cook dinner today.
iftaḥi an-nāfidha min faḍlika. — Open the window, please. (to a man)
lā taḥmili al-ḥaqība, hiya kabīra. — Do not carry the bag; it is big. (to a man)

examples.text: هَلْ عَلَيْكَ أَنْ تَذْهَب إِلَى السُّوق؟
examples.translation: hal ʿalayka ʾan tadhhab ʾilā as-sūq? — Do you have to go to the market? (to a man)

exercises.prompt: Which means “She has to cook dinner”?
Which is the command “Wash the dishes!” to a man?
Which is the command “Cook dinner!” to a man?
Which means “Do not carry the bag” (to a man)?
Which means “I must wash the dishes after dinner”?
options: يَجِب أَنْ يَغْسِل الصُّحُون بَعْد الْعَشَاء
يَجِب أَنْ أَغْسِل الصُّحُون بَعْد الْعَشَاء
عَلَيْهِ أَنْ أَغْسِل الصُّحُون بَعْد الْعَشَاء
يَجِب أَنْ أَغْسِل الصُّحُون قَبْل الْعَشَاء

exercises.explanation: What do you wash after dinner?
exercises.promptTranslation: I must wash the dishes after dinner.
She has to cook dinner.

explanations.title: Meals and what we drink
explanations.body: Arabic has three main meals. For the verb “to eat”, the present is يَأْكُل, with a hamza, and “I eat” is the special form آكُل.

explanations.title: Eating and drinking
explanations.body: شَرِبَ has the present يَشْرَب. أَكَلَ has يَأْكُل, نَأْكُل and تَأْكُل. Only “I” is special: آكُل.

examples.translation: ʾākul al-ʾifṭār fī al-bayt. — I eat breakfast at home.
naʾkul al-ghadāʾ fī al-madrasa. — We eat lunch at school.
ʾashrab al-qahwa fī aṣ-ṣabāḥ. — I drink coffee in the morning.

examples.text: هُوَ يَشْرَب الشَّايْ وَهِيَ تَشْرَب الْحَلِيب.
examples.translation: huwa yashrab ash-shāy wahiya tashrab al-ḥalīb. — He drinks tea and she drinks milk.
mādhā taʾkul fī al-ʿashāʾ? — What do you eat for dinner? (to a man)

exercises.prompt: Which means “I eat breakfast at home”?
Which means “We eat lunch at school”?
Which means “I drink coffee in the morning”?
Which means “What do you eat for dinner?”

exercises.promptTranslation: I drink coffee in the morning.
We eat lunch at school.

explanations.title: Main foods
explanations.body: Many food words are mass or collective nouns. They are singular in form and stand for the food in general, so you can say الْخُبْز لَذِيذ, “bread is delicious”.

explanations.title: Likes and dislikes
explanations.body: You already know أُحِبّ (“I like”) and the negative لَا أُحِبّ. Add the food directly, with ال, when you mean it in general.

examples.translation: ʾuḥibb as-samak war-ruzz. — I like fish and rice.
hal taʾkul al-laḥm? — Do you eat meat? (to a man)
lā, ʾanā lā ʾākul al-laḥm. — No, I do not eat meat.

examples.text: فِي الْإِفْطَار نَأْكُل الْبَيْض وَالْجُبْن وَالْخُبْز.
examples.translation: fī al-ʾifṭār naʾkul al-bayḍ wal-jubn wal-khubz. — For breakfast we eat eggs, cheese and bread.
hiya taṭbukh ad-dajāj war-ruzz. — She cooks chicken and rice.

exercises.prompt: Which means “I like fish and rice”?
Which means “I do not eat meat”?
Which means “For breakfast we eat eggs, cheese and bread”?
options: فِي الْإِفْطَار نَأْكُل الْبَيْض وَالْجُبْن وَالْخُبْز
فِي الْعَشَاء نَأْكُل الْبَيْض وَالْجُبْن وَالْخُبْز
فِي الْإِفْطَار آكُل الْبَيْض وَالْجُبْن وَالْخُبْز

exercises.promptTranslation: She cooks chicken and rice.
No, I do not eat meat.

explanations.title: From the market
explanations.body: These words are collective nouns too: تُفَّاح stands for apples in general. فَاكِهَة is the general word for fruit.

explanations.title: At the market and at home
explanations.body: Combine these words with the verbs, the commands and the endings from this unit.

examples.translation: ʾuḥibb al-fākiha, wakhāṣṣatan at-tuffāḥ. — I like fruit, especially apples.

examples.text: اِذْهَبْ إِلَى السُّوق، ثُمَّ اُطْلُبْ بُرْتُقَال.
examples.translation: idhhab ʾilā as-sūq, thumma uṭlub burtuqāl. — Go to the market, then ask for oranges. (to a man)

examples.text: عَلَيْنَا أَنْ نَذْهَب إِلَى السُّوق، لَيْسَ عِنْدَنَا بَطَاطِس.
examples.translation: ʿalaynā ʾan nadhhab ʾilā as-sūq, laysa ʿindanā baṭāṭis. — We have to go to the market; we do not have potatoes.

examples.text: الطَّمَاطِم فِي الْحَقِيبَة، وَالْمَوْز فِيهَا أَيْضًا.
examples.translation: aṭ-ṭamāṭim fī al-ḥaqība, wal-mawz fīhā ʾayḍan. — The tomatoes are in the bag, and the bananas are in it too.
hal ʿindakum tuffāḥ? — Do you have apples? (to a shopkeeper)

exercises.prompt: Which means “We do not have potatoes”?
«الطَّمَاطِم فِي الْحَقِيبَة، وَالْمَوْز فِيهَا أَيْضًا». What does فِيهَا stand for?

exercises.promptTranslation: I like fruit, especially apples.
Go to the market, then ask for oranges.

lessons.title: 96. Cups, plates and spoons
lessons.subtitle: كُوب مِنَ الشَّايْ · طَبَق مِنَ الرُّزّ

explanations.title: A container of something
explanations.body: To say “a cup of tea” put the container first and then مِنْ with the drink: كُوب مِنَ الشَّايْ. The thing inside is definite after مِنْ. Counting works as before: dual for two, the polarity numbers from three to ten followed by a plural noun.

explanations.title: Ordering by the cup
explanations.body: Remember that numbers from 3 to 10 take the form that is opposite in gender to the noun they count.

examples.translation: kūb mina ash-shāy min faḍlika. — A cup of tea, please. (to a man)
finjān mina al-qahwa. — A small cup of coffee.
kūbān mina al-ʿaṣīr. — Two glasses of juice.
thalātha ʾaṭbāq mina ar-ruzz. — Three plates of rice.
thalāth malāʿiq mina as-sukkar. — Three spoonfuls of sugar.

exercises.explanation: طَبَق is masculine, so the number ends in ة.
مِلْعَقَة is feminine, so the number has no ة.

exercises.prompt: What is the plural of طَبَق?

exercises.promptTranslation: A cup of tea.
Three plates of rice.

explanations.title: Describing food
explanations.body: An adjective after a definite noun, with no ال of its own, makes a complete sentence: الشَّايْ سَاخِن. It agrees with the noun in gender. قَهْوَة is feminine and شَايْ is masculine.

explanations.title: Tasting and wanting
explanations.body: To ask for something, say أُرِيد (“I want”) and then the thing.

examples.translation: ash-shāy sākhin wal-qahwa sākhina. — The tea is hot and the coffee is hot.
al-ʿaṣīr bārid jiddan. — The juice is very cold.
al-fākiha ḥulwa waladhīdha. — The fruit is sweet and delicious.
ʾanā jāʾiʿ. ʾurīd khubz wajubn. — I am hungry. I want bread and cheese. (a man speaking)

examples.text: هِيَ جَائِعَة وَتُرِيد طَبَق مِنَ الرُّزّ.
examples.translation: hiya jāʾiʿa waturīd ṭabaq mina ar-ruzz. — She is hungry and wants a plate of rice.

exercises.prompt: Which means “The juice is very cold”?
A woman says she is hungry. Which does she say?
Which means “I want bread and cheese”?
What is the opposite of سَاخِن?

exercises.promptTranslation: The tea is very hot.
The fruit is sweet and delicious.

lessons.title: 98. At the restaurant
lessons.subtitle: قَائِمَة الطَّعَام · أُرِيد · الْحِسَاب لَوْ سَمَحْتَ

explanations.title: Words for eating out
explanations.body: قَائِمَة الطَّعَام is the menu (literally “the list of the food”, an iḍāfa). You ask the waiter for things with أُرِيد, and you ask for the bill with الْحِسَاب.

explanations.title: A short exchange
explanations.body: When you ask هَلْ عِنْدَكُم…؟ you use the plural because you are asking the whole restaurant. The waiter answers you with تَفَضَّل (to a man) or تَفَضَّلِي (to a woman).

examples.translation: ʾurīd qāʾima aṭ-ṭaʿām min faḍlika. — I would like the menu, please. (to a man)
hal ʿindakum samak? — Do you have fish?
naʿam, ʿindanā samak wadajāj. — Yes, we have fish and chicken.

examples.text: أُرِيد طَبَق مِنَ الرُّزّ وَكُوب مِنَ الْعَصِير.
examples.translation: ʾurīd ṭabaq mina ar-ruzz wakūb mina al-ʿaṣīr. — I would like a plate of rice and a glass of juice.

examples.text: الطَّعَام لَذِيذ جِدًّا. الْحِسَاب لَوْ سَمَحْتَ.
examples.translation: aṭ-ṭaʿām ladhīdh jiddan. al-ḥisāb law samaḥta. — The food is very good. The bill, please. (to a man)

exercises.prompt: Which means “I would like a plate of rice and a glass of juice”?
options: أُرِيد طَبَق مِنَ الرُّزّ وَكُوب مِنَ الْعَصِير
أُرِيد طَبَق مِنَ الْعَصِير وَكُوب مِنَ الرُّزّ
أُرِيد طَبَقَان مِنَ الرُّزّ وَكُوب مِنَ الْعَصِير

exercises.promptTranslation: Do you have fish?
The bill, please.

explanations.title: A conversation
explanations.body: Layla and Ahmad are home in the evening. Read it for the commands, the endings and “must”.

examples.text: لَيْلَى: أَنَا جَائِعَة. يَجِب أَنْ أَطْبُخ الْعَشَاء.
examples.translation: laylā: ʾanā jāʾiʿa. yajib ʾan ʾaṭbukh al-ʿashāʾ. — Layla: I am hungry. I must cook dinner.
ʾaḥmad: hal ʿindanā ruzz? — Ahmad: Do we have rice?

examples.text: لَيْلَى: نَعَمْ، عِنْدَنَا رُزّ وَدَجَاج. اُنْظُرْ فِي الْمَطْبَخ.
examples.translation: laylā: naʿam, ʿindanā ruzz wadajāj. unẓur fī al-maṭbakh. — Layla: Yes, we have rice and chicken. Look in the kitchen.

examples.text: أَحْمَد: عَلَيَّ أَنْ أَغْسِل الصُّحُون بَعْد الْعَشَاء.
examples.translation: ʾaḥmad: ʿalayya ʾan ʾaghsil aṣ-ṣuḥūn baʿd al-ʿashāʾ. — Ahmad: I have to wash the dishes after dinner.

examples.text: لَيْلَى: لَا تَفْتَحِ النَّافِذَة، الْجَوّ بَارِد.
examples.translation: laylā: lā taftaḥi an-nāfidha, al-jaww bārid. — Layla: Do not open the window; the weather is cold.

examples.text: أَحْمَد: الْعَشَاء لَذِيذ جِدًّا، شُكْرًا لَكِ!
examples.translation: ʾaḥmad: al-ʿashāʾ ladhīdh jiddan, shukran laki! — Ahmad: Dinner is delicious, thank you!

exercises.prompt: «أَنَا جَائِعَة. يَجِب أَنْ أَطْبُخ الْعَشَاء.» What will Layla do?
«هَلْ عِنْدَنَا رُزّ؟». What does Ahmad ask?
«نَعَمْ، عِنْدَنَا رُزّ وَدَجَاج». What do they have?
«اُنْظُرْ فِي الْمَطْبَخ». Who is she speaking to, and what does she say?
options: a man; look in the kitchen
a man; do not enter the kitchen
a woman; sit in the kitchen
a group; cook in the kitchen
exercises.explanation: اُنْظُرْ is a command to a man.

exercises.prompt: «عَلَيَّ أَنْ أَغْسِل الصُّحُون بَعْد الْعَشَاء». What must Ahmad do?
«لَا تَفْتَحِ النَّافِذَة، الْجَوّ بَارِد». Why not?
«الْعَشَاء لَذِيذ جِدًّا، شُكْرًا لَكِ!». Who is thanked?

exercises.promptTranslation: Do not open the window.
I have to wash the dishes.

lessons.title: 100. Review: commands, endings, obligations and food
lessons.subtitle: اِفْتَحْ · لَا تَدْخُلْ · فِيهِ · يَجِب أَنْ · لَذِيذ

explanations.title: What you can do now
explanations.body: Commands: اِفْتَحْ, اِفْتَحِي, لَا تَفْتَحْ. Endings: لِي, عِنْدِي, مَعِي, فِيهِ, عَلَيْهَا. Obligation: يَجِب أَنْ + verb, عَلَيَّ أَنْ + verb. Food and drink: خُبْز, رُزّ, شَايْ, قَهْوَة, كُوب, طَبَق.

examples.translation: iftaḥī al-bāb yā laylā. — Open the door, Layla.
lā tadkhulū al-maṭbakh. — Do not enter the kitchen. (to a group)
ʿindī kitāb, wahuwa ʿalā aṭ-ṭāwila. — I have a book, and it is on the table.
yajib ʾan tashrabī al-māʾ. — You must drink water. (to a woman)
kūb mina ash-shāy min faḍlika. — A cup of tea, please. (to a man)

exercises.prompt: Which tells a woman to open the door?
Which tells a group not to enter the kitchen?
exercises.explanation: لَا تَدْخُلُوا is for a group.

exercises.prompt: Which means “It is on it” (a book on the table)?
Which means “I do not have to go”?
Which is a correct way to order tea?

exercises.promptTranslation: Open the door, Layla.
This is a kitchen. Dinner is in it.

units.title: المراجعة: review of the whole course

lessons.title: 101. Review: meeting someone
lessons.subtitle: اِسْمِي سَارَة · أَنَا مِنْ مِصْر · هُوَ مُدَرِّس

explanations.title: Two people meet
explanations.body: A first conversation uses almost everything from the first two units: greetings, the pronouns, a noun sentence with no “is”, and مِنْ for where you come from.

examples.translation: as-salām ʿalaykum. — Peace be upon you.
waʿalaykumu as-salām. — And upon you, peace.
ismī sāra. mā ismuka? — My name is Sara. What is your name? (to a man)
ismī ʾaḥmad. ʾanā mudarris. — My name is Ahmad. I am a teacher.
min ʾayna ʾanti yā sāra? — Where are you from, Sara? (to a woman)

examples.text: أَنَا مِنْ مِصْر. هِيَ طَالِبَة وَهُوَ مُدَرِّس.
examples.translation: ʾanā min miṣr. hiya ṭāliba wahuwa mudarris. — I am from Egypt. She is a student and he is a teacher.

exercises.prompt: Which means “What is your name?” to a man?
Which asks a woman where she is from?
What do you answer to «السَّلَام عَلَيْكُم»?

exercises.promptTranslation: What is your name?
I am from Egypt.

lessons.title: 102. Review: asking and saying no
lessons.subtitle: هَلْ · مَنْ · مَاذَا · أَيْنَ · لَا · لَيْسَ

explanations.title: Choosing the right word
explanations.body: Question words go first. هَلْ asks yes or no. لَا negates a present-tense verb, and لَيْسَ negates a noun sentence.

explanations.title: Question and answer
explanations.body: A negative answer picks لَا or لَيْسَ depending on what comes after it.

examples.translation: hal ʾanta ṭālib? — Are you a student? (to a man)

examples.text: لَا، أَنَا لَسْتُ طَالِبًا. أَنَا مُدَرِّس.
examples.translation: lā, ʾanā lastu ṭāliban. ʾanā mudarris. — No, I am not a student. I am a teacher.
mādhā tadrus? — What do you study? (to a man)
ʾadrus al-ʿarabiyya walā ʾadrus al-faransiyya. — I study Arabic and I do not study French.
ʾayna al-madrasa? — Where is the school?
al-madrasa laysat hunā. — The school is not here.

exercises.prompt: Which word starts a yes/no question?
Which question word asks about a person?
Which means “I am not a student”?

exercises.promptTranslation: Are you a student?
I do not study today.

lessons.title: 103. Review: places and weather
lessons.subtitle: فِي الشِّتَاء الْجَوّ بَارِد · أَذْهَب إِلَى السُّوق

explanations.title: Describing a day
explanations.body: Weather sentences are noun sentences, and travel sentences use a present verb with إِلَى.

examples.translation: fī ash-shitāʾ al-jaww bārid. — In winter the weather is cold.
fī aṣ-ṣayf al-jaww ḥārr. — In summer the weather is hot.
ʾuḥibb ar-rabīʿ liʾanna al-jaww jamīl. — I like spring because the weather is nice.
ʾadhhab ʾilā as-sūq kull yawm. — I go to the market every day.
al-madīna kabīra, wal-jabal baʿīd. — The city is big, and the mountain is far.

exercises.prompt: Which means “In winter the weather is cold”?
Which means “In summer the weather is hot”?
Which means “I go to the market every day”?
Why does the adjective in «الْجَوّ بَارِد» have no ة?

exercises.promptTranslation: In summer the weather is hot.
I go to the market.

lessons.title: 104. Review: plurals, agreement and the family
lessons.subtitle: طُلَّاب · طَالِبَات · كِتَاب كَبِير · أَبِي وَأُمِّي

explanations.title: Number and gender
explanations.body: A noun can be singular, dual or plural. An adjective after a noun matches its gender and its definiteness (a plural of things takes a feminine singular adjective). A sound plural adds an ending; a broken plural changes the inside of the word.

explanations.title: Family and agreement
explanations.body: Add ـِي to say “my”: أَبِي, أُمِّي. The adjective follows the noun and matches it.

examples.translation: ʾabī mudarris waʾummī ṭāliba. — My father is a teacher and my mother is a student.
ʿindī kitāb kabīr. — I have a big book.
ʿindahā kutub kabīra. — She has big books.
hādhā huwa al-bayt al-kabīr. — This is the big house.
aṭ-ṭālibān fī al-madrasa. — The two (male) students are at school.

exercises.prompt: What is the plural of كِتَاب?
What is the plural of طَالِبَة?
Which means “I have a big book”?

exercises.explanation: A plural of a thing agrees as feminine singular.

exercises.promptTranslation: My father is a teacher and my mother is a student.
She has big books.

lessons.title: 105. Review: numbers, the iḍāfa and the house
lessons.subtitle: ثَلَاث غُرَف · بَاب الْبَيْت · كَمْ غُرْفَة؟

explanations.title: Counting and joining nouns
explanations.body: Numbers 3 to 10 take the form with the opposite gender from the noun, and the noun after them is plural. Two nouns side by side, the first with no ال, can make an iḍāfa; the second may have ال.

examples.translation: fī al-bayt thalāth ghuraf. — There are three rooms in the house.
ʿindī khamsa kutub. — I have five books.
bāb al-bayt kabīr. — The door of the house is big.
miftāḥ al-ghurfa ʿalā aṭ-ṭāwila. — The key of the room is on the table.
kam ghurfa ʿindakum? — How many rooms do you have?
ʿindanā ghurfatān wamaṭbakh. — We have two rooms and a kitchen.

exercises.explanation: غُرْفَة is feminine, so the number has no ة.
كِتَاب is masculine, so the number ends in ة.

exercises.prompt: Which means “the door of the house”?
exercises.explanation: The first noun has no ال.

exercises.prompt: Which means “The key of the room is on the table”?

exercises.promptTranslation: There are three rooms in the house.
The door of the house is big.

lessons.title: 106. A day with Sara
lessons.subtitle: تَسْكُن سَارَة فِي الْقَاهِرَة · هِيَ طَالِبَة

explanations.title: A short text
explanations.body: Read the whole text first, then answer the questions at the end.

examples.text: اِسْمِي سَارَة. أَنَا طَالِبَة وَأَسْكُن فِي الْقَاهِرَة.
examples.translation: ismī sāra. ʾanā ṭāliba waʾaskun fī al-qāhira. — My name is Sara. I am a student and I live in Cairo.

examples.text: عِنْدِي أَخ وَأُخْت. أَبِي مُدَرِّس وَأُمِّي تَعْمَل فِي مَطْعَم.
examples.translation: ʿindī ʾakh waʾukht. ʾabī mudarris waʾummī taʿmal fī maṭʿam. — I have a brother and a sister. My father is a teacher and my mother works in a restaurant.

examples.text: فِي الصَّبَاح أَشْرَب الشَّايْ وَآكُل الْخُبْز وَالْجُبْن.
examples.translation: fī aṣ-ṣabāḥ ʾashrab ash-shāy waʾākul al-khubz wal-jubn. — In the morning I drink tea and eat bread and cheese.
thumma ʾadhhab ʾilā al-madrasa. — Then I go to school.

examples.text: بَعْد الْمَدْرَسَة يَجِب أَنْ أَكْتُب الْوَاجِب.
examples.translation: baʿd al-madrasa yajib ʾan ʾaktub al-wājib. — After school I must write my homework.

examples.text: فِي الْمَسَاء نَأْكُل الْعَشَاء فِي الْبَيْت، وَأَغْسِل الصُّحُون.
examples.translation: fī al-masāʾ naʾkul al-ʿashāʾ fī al-bayt, waʾaghsil aṣ-ṣuḥūn. — In the evening we eat dinner at home, and I wash the dishes.

exercises.prompt: «أَنَا طَالِبَة وَأَسْكُن فِي الْقَاهِرَة». Where does Sara live?
«أَبِي مُدَرِّس وَأُمِّي تَعْمَل فِي مَطْعَم». What does her mother do?
«أَشْرَب الشَّايْ وَآكُل الْخُبْز وَالْجُبْن». What does she have for breakfast?
«ثُمَّ أَذْهَب إِلَى الْمَدْرَسَة». What does she do next?
«يَجِب أَنْ أَكْتُب الْوَاجِب». What must she do after school?
«نَأْكُل الْعَشَاء فِي الْبَيْت». Who eats dinner?
Which of these does Sara NOT say?
exercises.explanation: She has one brother and one sister.

exercises.promptTranslation: In the morning I drink tea.
After school I must write my homework.

units.title: كَانَ: was, used to, and free time

explanations.title: Free-time activities
explanations.body: Here are seven things people do in their free time, all with the present-tense “I” form. Most of the verbs take the same أَـ prefix as أَكْتُب and أَدْرُس, though the middle vowel can differ: أَلْعَب, أَسْبَح.

explanations.title: I like…
explanations.body: There are two ways to say what you like. After أُحِبّ you can put a noun, or أَنْ and a present verb (the pattern you know from يَجِب أَنْ). The verb after أَنْ shows who does the action; for “I like to…” it is also the “I” form.

examples.translation: ʾuḥibb al-mūsīqā. — I like music.
ʾuḥibb ʾan ʾalʿab kura al-qadam. — I like to play football.
ʾuḥibb ʾan ʾasbaḥ fī aṣ-ṣayf. — I like to swim in summer.
hal tuḥibb as-sīnamā? — Do you like the cinema? (to a man)

examples.text: مَاذَا تُحِبّ أَنْ تَفْعَل فِي وَقْت الْفَرَاغ؟
examples.translation: mādhā tuḥibb ʾan tafʿal fī waqt al-farāgh? — What do you like to do in your free time? (to a man)
ʾuḥibb ʾan ʾaqraʾ waʾasmaʿ al-mūsīqā. — I like to read and listen to music.

exercises.prompt: Which asks a man “Do you like the cinema?”
Which means “What do you like to do in your free time?” (to a man)
options: أَيْنَ تُحِبّ أَنْ تَفْعَل فِي وَقْت الْفَرَاغ؟
مَاذَا تُحِبّ أَنْ تَفْعَل فِي وَقْت الْفَرَاغ؟
مَاذَا أُحِبّ أَنْ أَفْعَل فِي وَقْت الْفَرَاغ؟
مَنْ تُحِبّ أَنْ تَفْعَل فِي وَقْت الْفَرَاغ؟

exercises.promptTranslation: I play football.
I like to swim in the sea.
I like to read a book.

lessons.title: 108. Was: كَانَ
lessons.subtitle: كَانَ الْجَوّ جَمِيلًا · كَانَتِ الْمَدِينَة كَبِيرَةً

explanations.title: The verb كَانَ
explanations.body: Until now every sentence about “now” had no verb for “is”. To say “was”, put كَانَ first and then the subject. كَانَ is a verb, so it agrees with the subject: كَانَ for a masculine subject, كَانَتْ for a feminine one. The description that follows gets the same ending as after لَيْسَ: ـًا, or ـَةً on a feminine word. Before ال, كَانَتْ takes a helping kasra: كَانَتِ الْمَدِينَة.

explanations.title: Yesterday, last week
explanations.body: Words like أَمْس (yesterday) and الْمَاضِي (last, past) place the sentence in the past.

examples.translation: kāna al-jaww jamīlan ʾams. — The weather was nice yesterday.
kānati al-madīna kabīratan wajamīlatan. — The city was big and beautiful.
kāna al-ʾusbūʿ al-māḍī ṭawīlan. — Last week was long.
kāna ash-shitāʾ al-māḍī bāridan. — Last winter was cold.
kānati al-madrasa qarībatan mina al-bayt. — The school was close to the house.

exercises.promptTranslation: The house was old.
The school was near.
The weather was nice yesterday.

lessons.title: 109. I was, you were: كُنْتُ · كُنْتَ · كُنْتِ
lessons.subtitle: كُنْتُ طَالِبًا · كُنْتِ سَعِيدَةً · كُنَّا فِي الْبَيْت

explanations.title: Was: six persons
explanations.body: The past tense changes at the END of the word. With “I”, “you” and “we” the middle ا of كَانَ falls out and a ضَمَّة replaces it: كُنْتُ, كُنَّا. With “he” and “she” the ا stays.

explanations.title: With a description
explanations.body: The description that follows takes ـًا (or ـَةً) and agrees with the person: a man says طَالِبًا, a woman says طَالِبَةً.

examples.translation: kuntu ṭāliban fī al-qāhira. — I was a student in Cairo. (a man speaking)
kuntu ṭālibatan fī jāmiʿa kabīra. — I was a student at a big university. (a woman speaking)
kunta saʿīdan yā ʾaḥmad. — You were happy, Ahmad. (to a man)
kunti mashghūlatan ʾams yā sāra. — You were busy yesterday, Sara. (to a woman)
kāna ʾakhī ṣaghīran. — My brother was little.
kunnā fī al-bayt. — We were at home.

exercises.prompt: A woman says “I was a student”. Which is right?
exercises.explanation: كُنْتُ for “I”, and ـَةً for a woman.

exercises.prompt: What happens to the middle ا of كَانَ in كُنْتُ?

exercises.promptTranslation: We were at home.
My brother was little.

explanations.title: Was: the rest of the persons
explanations.body: A group of men ends in ـُوا (with a silent alif), two people end in ـَا (or ـَتَا for women), and a group of women ends in ـْنَ (كُنْ + نَ → كُنَّ). For “you”, the stem كُنْـ is followed by تُ and the ending of the person: كُنْتُمْ, كُنْتُنَّ.

explanations.title: In sentences
explanations.body: With a plural description a broken plural takes ـًا (طُلَّابًا), a plural with ـَات keeps its ending, and سُعَدَاء (happy, plural) takes no extra ending. A verb that comes before its subject stays singular, as you learned: كَانَ الطُّلَّاب سُعَدَاء.

examples.translation: kuntum suʿadāʾ fī al-madrasa. — You (all) were happy at school.
hum kānū ṭullāban fī al-jāmiʿa. — They were students at the university.
al-bintān kānatā fī al-ḥadīqa. — The two girls were in the garden.
ʾantunna kuntunna fī al-maktaba. — You (women) were in the library.
al-mudarrisāt kunna mashghūlāt. — The (women) teachers were busy.
kāna aṭ-ṭullāb suʿadāʾ. — The students were happy.

exercises.explanation: كُنَّ ends in the feminine plural.

exercises.prompt: Which is right? “The students were happy” with the verb first.
exercises.explanation: A verb before its subject stays singular.

exercises.promptTranslation: The two girls were in the garden.
They were students.

explanations.title: Questions with كَانَ
explanations.body: A question word goes first and كَانَ follows it. The answer begins with كَانَ or كُنْتُ and the place or description comes after.

explanations.title: A short conversation
explanations.body: Two friends talk about yesterday.

examples.translation: ʾayna kunta ʾams yā ʾaḥmad? — Where were you yesterday, Ahmad? (to a man)
kuntu fī al-maktaba maʿa ṣadīqī. — I was in the library with my friend.
wakayfa kānati al-maktaba? — And how was the library?
kānat kabīratan wajamīlatan. — It was big and beautiful.
waman kāna maʿaka? — And who was with you? (to a man)
kānat maʿī sāra. — Sara was with me.

exercises.prompt: Which asks a man “Where were you?”
Which asks a woman “Where were you?”
Which asks a man “Who was with you?”

exercises.promptTranslation: Where were you yesterday?
How was the weather?

explanations.title: كَانَ + present verb
explanations.body: Put كَانَ in front of a present verb and the meaning becomes “used to” (or “was …ing”). Both words show the person: كُنْتُ for “I” and أَلْعَب for “I”. Nothing is dropped from the verb.

explanations.title: Habits in the past
explanations.body: This is the way to describe what you used to do every day, every summer, or when you were young.

examples.text: كُنْتُ أَلْعَب كُرَة الْقَدَم كُلّ يَوْم.
examples.translation: kuntu ʾalʿab kura al-qadam kull yawm. — I used to play football every day.
kāna ʾakhī yasbaḥ fī al-baḥr. — My brother used to swim in the sea.
kānat ʾummī taṭbukh al-ʿashāʾ. — My mother used to cook dinner.
hal kunta taqraʾ kathīran? — Did you use to read a lot? (to a man)
kunti tadhhabīn ʾilā al-madrasa. — You used to go to school. (to a woman)
kunnā naskun fī bayt ṣaghīr. — We used to live in a small house.

exercises.prompt: Which asks a man “Did you use to read?”
A woman says “I used to go to school”. Which is right?
exercises.explanation: “I” is the same for men and women.

exercises.promptTranslation: I used to play football.
My mother used to cook.
We used to live in a small house.

lessons.title: 113. Used to: they, you all, and how often
lessons.subtitle: كَانُوا يَلْعَبُون · دَائِمًا · أَحْيَانًا

explanations.title: Plural “used to”
explanations.body: Both words take the ending of the person. The present verb keeps its full ending (ـُون, ـَان, ـْنَ). The ن is not dropped here, because there is no أَنْ in front of it.

rows: the two of them (men) used to play
the two of them (women) used to play

explanations.title: How often?
explanations.body: These words say how often a habit happened. They usually sit right after كَانَ or at the end of the sentence.

examples.text: كَانُوا يَلْعَبُون فِي الْحَدِيقَة كُلّ يَوْم.
examples.translation: kānū yalʿabūn fī al-ḥadīqa kull yawm. — They used to play in the park every day.

examples.text: كُنَّا نَذْهَب إِلَى الشَّاطِئ كُلّ صَيْف.
examples.translation: kunnā nadhhab ʾilā ash-shāṭiʾ kull ṣayf. — We used to go to the beach every summer.
kuntu dāʾiman ʾasmaʿ al-mūsīqā. — I always used to listen to music.
kānat ʾukhtī ʾaḥyānan talʿab maʿanā. — My sister sometimes used to play with us.

examples.text: كُنَّ يَدْرُسْنَ فِي الْمَكْتَبَة كُلّ يَوْم.
examples.translation: kunna yadrusna fī al-maktaba kull yawm. — They (women) used to study in the library every day.

exercises.explanation: ـُوا and ـُون for a group of men.

exercises.prompt: Which means “the two girls used to play”?
exercises.explanation: A dual feminine: كَانَتَا and تَلْعَبَان.

exercises.prompt: Which means “We used to go to the beach every summer”?
options: كُنْتُ أَذْهَب إِلَى الشَّاطِئ كُلّ صَيْف
كُنَّا نَذْهَب مِنَ الشَّاطِئ كُلّ صَيْف
كُنَّا نَذْهَب إِلَى الشَّاطِئ كُلّ صَيْف
كَانُوا يَذْهَبُون إِلَى الشَّاطِئ كُلّ صَيْف

exercises.promptTranslation: They (women) used to study in the library.
They used to play every day.

explanations.title: Time words for the past
explanations.body: Use عِنْدَمَا (“when”) with a past clause, and بَعْد and قَبْل for “after” and “before”. To say “… ago”, put قَبْل in front of the length of time.

explanations.title: A childhood
explanations.body: A few sentences are enough to tell a story: put the time first, then the habit.

examples.text: عِنْدَمَا كُنْتُ صَغِيرًا، كُنْتُ أَسْكُن فِي قَرْيَة.
examples.translation: ʿindamā kuntu ṣaghīran, kuntu ʾaskun fī qarya. — When I was little, I used to live in a village.

examples.text: كُنْتُ أَلْعَب مَعَ أَصْدِقَائِي فِي الشَّارِع.
examples.translation: kuntu ʾalʿab maʿa ʾaṣdiqāʾī fī ash-shāriʿ. — I used to play with my friends in the street.

examples.text: كَانَتْ جَدَّتِي تَطْبُخ لَنَا كُلّ يَوْم.
examples.translation: kānat jaddatī taṭbukh lanā kull yawm. — My grandmother used to cook for us every day.

examples.text: بَعْد الْمَدْرَسَة كُنَّا نَذْهَب إِلَى النَّهْر.
examples.translation: baʿd al-madrasa kunnā nadhhab ʾilā an-nahr. — After school we used to go to the river.
fī ṭufūlatī kuntu ʾuḥibb as-sibāḥa. — In my childhood I used to like swimming.

exercises.explanation: قَبْل + a length of time = ago.

exercises.prompt: Which means “my grandmother used to cook for us”?
Which means “In my childhood I used to like swimming”?
___ كُنْتُ صَغِيرًا، كُنْتُ أَلْعَب فِي الْحَدِيقَة.
exercises.promptTranslation: When I was little, I used to play in the garden.
We used to go to the river after school.
I used to live in a small village.

lessons.title: 115. I used to have: كَانَ عِنْدِي
lessons.subtitle: كَانَ عِنْدِي كَلْب · كَانَ هُنَاك مَطْعَم

explanations.title: I had
explanations.body: To say “I had”, put كَانَ in front of عِنْدِي (or مَعِي). كَانَ agrees with the thing that was had, because that is the subject: كَانَ for a masculine thing and كَانَتْ for a feminine one.

explanations.title: There was, there were
explanations.body: كَانَ هُنَاك (or كَانَ فِي … ) means “there was”. The thing that existed comes after it.

examples.translation: kāna ʿindī kalb ṣaghīr. — I used to have a small dog.
kānat ʿindanā darrāja qadīma. — We had an old bicycle.
hal kāna ʿindaka kalb? — Did you have a dog? (to a man)
kāna fī madīnatī masraḥ kabīr. — There was a big theatre in my city.

examples.text: كَانَ هُنَاك مَطْعَم قَدِيم قَرِيب مِنَ الْبَيْت.
examples.translation: kāna hunāk maṭʿam qadīm qarīb mina al-bayt. — There was an old restaurant close to the house.
kānat hunāk ḥadīqa jamīla. — There was a beautiful garden.

exercises.prompt: Which means “I used to have a dog”?
Which means “I had an old bicycle”?
Which asks a man “Did you have a dog?”
Which means “There was a big theatre in my city”?
Which means “I had a phone with me”?

exercises.promptTranslation: I used to have a small dog.

exercises.prompt: كَانَ ___ كَلْب. (We used to have a dog.)
exercises.promptTranslation: We used to have a dog.
There was an old restaurant.

lessons.title: 116. I used to work at…
lessons.subtitle: كُنْتُ أَعْمَل فِي شَرِكَة · كَانَ أَبِي مُدِيرًا

explanations.title: More jobs
explanations.body: These are all regular words: add ة for a woman. You have met others in the first units.

explanations.title: What I used to do
explanations.body: Use كَانَ + عَمِلَ in the present form for “used to work”, with فِي for the place and لِمُدَّة for how long. Or use كَانَ with the job itself: كَانَ أَبِي مُدِيرًا.

examples.translation: kuntu ʾaʿmal fī sharika kabīra. — I used to work at a big company.

examples.text: كُنْتُ أَعْمَل مُهَنْدِسًا لِمُدَّة ثَلَاث سَنَوَات.
examples.translation: kuntu ʾaʿmal muhandisan limudda thalāth sanawāt. — I worked as an engineer for three years.
kānat ʾukhtī mumarriḍatan fī mustashfā. — My sister was a nurse in a hospital.
kāna ʾabī mudīran. — My father was a manager.
ʾayna kunta taʿmal? — Where did you use to work? (to a man)

examples.text: كُنْتُ أَعْمَل فِي مَكْتَب قَرِيب مِنَ الْبَيْت.
examples.translation: kuntu ʾaʿmal fī maktab qarīb mina al-bayt. — I used to work in an office near home.

exercises.prompt: Which means “I used to work at a company”?
Which means “My sister was a nurse”?
exercises.explanation: كَانَتْ and ـَةً for a woman.

exercises.prompt: Which means “My father was a manager”?
exercises.explanation: كَانَ and ـًا for a man.

exercises.prompt: Which asks a man “Where did you use to work?”

exercises.promptTranslation: I used to work at a big company.
My father was a manager.
My sister was a nurse.

explanations.title: Words in a job ad
explanations.body: Job ads are short. مَطْلُوب means “wanted”, and the ad lists what the job needs.

explanations.title: An ad and a reply
explanations.body: Read the ad first. Then see how a person who used to work somewhere answers it.

examples.translation: maṭlūb muwaẓẓaf fī sharika kabīra. — Wanted: an employee at a big company.

examples.text: يَجِب أَنْ تَكُون عِنْدَهُ خِبْرَة سَنَتَيْن.
examples.translation: yajib ʾan takūn ʿindahu khibra sanatayn. — He must have two years of experience.
ar-rātib jayyid. — The salary is good.
uktub ʾilaynā bil-barīd al-ʾiliktrūniyy. — Write to us by email. (to a man)
ʾanā ʾabḥath ʿan ʿamal. — I am looking for a job.

examples.text: كُنْتُ أَعْمَل فِي شَرِكَة لِمُدَّة سَنَتَيْن.
examples.translation: kuntu ʾaʿmal fī sharika limudda sanatayn. — I worked at a company for two years.
ʿindī khibra jayyida. — I have good experience.

Which means “I am looking for a job”?
Which means “Write to us by email” (to a man)?
Which means “He must have two years of experience”?

يَجِب أَنْ تَكُون عِنْدَهُ خِبْرَة سَنَتَيْن
exercises.explanation: تَكُون agrees with خِبْرَة (feminine): يَجِب أَنْ تَكُون عِنْدَهُ خِبْرَة.

exercises.promptTranslation: Wanted: an employee at a big company.
I am looking for a job.
I have good experience.

explanations.title: Everything about كَانَ
explanations.body: Three patterns: كَانَ + a description (was), كَانَ + a present verb (used to), and كَانَ + عِنْدِي (had). The verb shows the person in all three.

explanations.title: A short story
explanations.body: Read the story of a woman who used to live in a village.

examples.text: عِنْدَمَا كُنْتُ صَغِيرَةً، كُنَّا نَسْكُن فِي قَرْيَة.
examples.translation: ʿindamā kuntu ṣaghīratan, kunnā naskun fī qarya. — When I was little, we used to live in a village.

examples.text: كَانَ عِنْدَنَا بَيْت قَدِيم وَحَدِيقَة كَبِيرَة.
examples.translation: kāna ʿindanā bayt qadīm waḥadīqa kabīra. — We had an old house and a big garden.

examples.text: كَانَ أَبِي يَعْمَل فِي مَكْتَب فِي الْمَدِينَة.
examples.translation: kāna ʾabī yaʿmal fī maktab fī al-madīna. — My father used to work in an office in the city.

examples.text: وَكُنْتُ أَلْعَب مَعَ أُخْتِي فِي الْحَدِيقَة كُلّ يَوْم.
examples.translation: wakuntu ʾalʿab maʿa ʾukhtī fī al-ḥadīqa kull yawm. — And I used to play with my sister in the garden every day.
kānati al-ḥayāh basīṭatan wajamīlatan. — Life was simple and beautiful.

exercises.prompt: Which means “I used to have a dog”?
Which means “Where were you?” (to a woman)
Which means “My father used to work in an office”?
A woman says “I was little”. Which is right?
