My sister used to play in the garden.
We had an old house.

units.title: الْمَاضِي وَالدِّرَاسَة: the past tense, school and work

lessons.title: 119. Women in the plural: هُنَّ · أَنْتُنَّ
lessons.subtitle: هُنَّ يَدْرُسْنَ · بَيْتُهُنَّ

explanations.title: A plural for women
explanations.body: You met هُنَّ and أَنْتُنَّ with كَانَ (كُنَّ, كُنْتُنَّ). Ordinary verbs have the same separate plural for “you” and “they” when every person is a woman: أَنْتُنَّ and هُنَّ. (A group with even one man in it uses the masculine plural.) The present verb ends in ـْنَ for both. Most words for women, and adjectives describing them, that end in ة take ـَات.

explanations.title: In sentences
explanations.body: The plural pronoun can be dropped, since the verb already shows who is meant.

examples.translation: hunna mudarrisāt fī madrasa kabīra. — They (women) are teachers at a big school.
ʾantunna ṭālibāt fī al-jāmiʿa. — You (women) are students at the university.
hunna yadrusna al-ʿarabiyya. — They (women) study Arabic.
ʾantunna taʿmalna fī al-maktab. — You (women) work in the office.
al-banāt yalʿabna fī al-ḥadīqa. — The girls are playing in the garden.
hal ʾantunna mashghūlāt? — Are you (women) busy?

explanations.title: Their, your: ـهُنَّ and ـكُنَّ
explanations.body: The matching endings attach to nouns and to prepositions, just as ـهُم and ـكُم do for men.

rows: for them · with them · they have
for you · with you · you have

exercises.prompt: Which is the plural of طَالِبَة (women only)?
exercises.explanation: ـَات is the plural of women.

exercises.promptTranslation: They (women) work in the office.
You (women) are students at the university.

lessons.title: 120. Yesterday: the past tense, he and she
lessons.subtitle: كَتَبَ · كَتَبَتْ · ذَهَبَ · ذَهَبَتْ

explanations.title: The past tense: he and she
explanations.body: The simplest form of an Arabic verb is the past tense for “he”: usually three consonants with a fatḥa on each: كَتَبَ (he wrote). For “she” add ـَتْ: كَتَبَتْ. There is no prefix. Compare the present يَكْتُب (he writes) with the past كَتَبَ (he wrote). Dictionaries list a verb under this “he” form.

explanations.title: The verb comes first
explanations.body: As in the present, the verb usually comes first and agrees with its subject in gender. Before ال the ـَتْ ending takes a helping kasra: جَلَسَتِ الطَّالِبَة.

examples.translation: kataba ʾaḥmad risāla. — Ahmad wrote a letter.
dhahabat sāra ʾilā as-sūq. — Sara went to the market.
dakhala al-mudarris al-ghurfa. — The teacher entered the room.
kharajat laylā mina al-bayt. — Layla left the house.
fataḥa al-mudīr an-nāfidha. — The manager opened the window.
jalasati aṭ-ṭāliba hunā. — The student sat here.

exercises.prompt: Which of these is a past tense verb?
Which means “Sara went to the market”?

exercises.promptTranslation: Ahmad wrote a letter.
Sara went to the market.

exercises.explanation: A feminine verb needs a feminine subject.
exercises.promptTranslation: The student sat here.

lessons.title: 121. I, you, we in the past
lessons.subtitle: كَتَبْتُ · كَتَبْتَ · كَتَبْتِ · كَتَبْنَا

explanations.title: Endings for I, you, we
explanations.body: For these persons the last letter of the stem gets a sukūn and an ending is added: ـْتُ (I), ـْتَ (you, man), ـْتِ (you, woman), ـْنَا (we). They are the same endings you saw in كُنْتُ, كُنْتَ, كُنْتِ, كُنَّا.

explanations.title: In sentences
explanations.body: Now the verb carries the person, so the pronoun is not needed.

examples.translation: katabtu risāla ʾilā ṣadīqī. — I wrote a letter to my friend.
dhahabta ʾilā al-madrasa ʾams. — You went to school yesterday. (to a man)
dakhalti al-maktab yā sāra. — You entered the office, Sara. (to a woman)
kharajnā mina al-bayt. — We left the house.
fataḥtu al-bāb. — I opened the door.
jalasnā fī al-ḥadīqa. — We sat in the garden.

exercises.prompt: Which ending means “I” on a past verb?

exercises.promptTranslation: I went to school yesterday.
We sat in the garden.
You entered the office, Sara.

lessons.title: 122. They, you all, the two in the past
lessons.subtitle: كَتَبُوا · كَتَبْنَ · كَتَبَا · كَتَبْتُمْ

explanations.title: The rest of the past tense
explanations.body: Here is the whole past tense of كَتَبَ. A group of men ends in ـُوا (with a silent alif), a group of women in ـْنَ, and two people in ـَا (men) or ـَتَا (women). For “you” the ـْتـ stays and the ending follows: ـْتُمَا, ـْتُمْ, ـْتُنَّ.

explanations.title: In sentences
explanations.body: Remember that a verb which comes before a plural subject stays singular: دَخَلَ الطُّلَّاب. When the subject comes first, or is only a pronoun, the verb takes the plural ending. Before ال, a final ـْتُمْ takes a helping ḍamma.

examples.translation: dakhala aṭ-ṭullāb aṣ-ṣaff. — The students entered the classroom.
aṭ-ṭullāb dakhalū aṣ-ṣaff. — The students entered the classroom.
al-banāt dhahabna ʾilā al-maktaba. — The girls went to the library.
al-waladān jalasā hunā. — The two boys sat here.
hal katabtumu al-wājib? — Did you (men) write the homework?
hunna kharajna mina al-madrasa. — They (women) left the school.

exercises.explanation: ـُوا for a group of men.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence puts the verb first? “The students entered the classroom”
exercises.explanation: A verb before its subject stays singular.

exercises.promptTranslation: The girls went to the library.
Did you (men) write the homework?

lessons.title: 123. Past verbs with a kasra: شَرِبَ · فَهِمَ
lessons.subtitle: شَرِبْتُ الشَّايْ · فَهِمْتُ الدَّرْس

explanations.title: Another past vowel
explanations.body: In most past verbs the middle letter has a fatḥa (كَتَبَ). A group of common verbs have a kasra instead: شَرِبَ (drank), فَهِمَ (understood), سَمِعَ (heard), عَمِلَ (worked, did), لَعِبَ (played), رَكِبَ (rode). The endings are exactly the same as before. Learn the middle vowel with each verb; the dictionary shows it.

explanations.title: In sentences
explanations.body: Sentences about what happened yesterday.

examples.translation: sharibtu ash-shāy. — I drank the tea.
fahimtu ad-dars. — I understood the lesson.
samiʿat sāra al-mūsīqā. — Sara heard the music.
laʿiba al-ʾawlād kura al-qadam. — The boys played football.
ʿamilnā fī al-ḥadīqa. — We worked in the garden.
rakibtu ad-darrāja. — I rode the bicycle.

exercises.prompt: Which verb has a kasra on the middle letter in the past?

exercises.promptTranslation: I understood the lesson.

exercises.explanation: A masculine verb needs masculine boys.
exercises.promptTranslation: The boys played football.

exercises.explanation: A feminine verb needs a woman.
exercises.promptTranslation: Sara heard the music.

lessons.title: 124. Questions about yesterday
lessons.subtitle: هَلْ ذَهَبْتَ؟ · مَاذَا فَعَلْتَ؟ · أَيْنَ ذَهَبْتِ؟

explanations.title: Asking in the past
explanations.body: Question words work with the past tense exactly as with the present: they go first and the past verb follows. The person asked decides the ending (ـْتَ to a man, ـْتِ to a woman).

explanations.title: A conversation
explanations.body: A yes–no question can be answered with نَعَمْ followed by the verb; when you are asked “did you…?”, the verb is in the “I” form.

examples.translation: mādhā faʿalti ʾams yā sāra? — What did you do yesterday, Sara? (to a woman)

examples.text: دَرَسْتُ فِي الْمَكْتَبَة، ثُمَّ ذَهَبْتُ إِلَى السُّوق.
examples.translation: darastu fī al-maktaba, thumma dhahabtu ʾilā as-sūq. — I studied in the library, then I went to the market.
hal sharibti al-qahwa hunāk? — Did you drink coffee there? (to a woman)
naʿam, sharibtu al-qahwa wash-shāy. — Yes, I drank coffee and tea.
wamatā rajaʿti ʾilā al-bayt? — And when did you go back home? (to a woman)
rajaʿtu fī al-masāʾ. — I went back in the evening.

exercises.prompt: Which asks a man “Did you go to school?”
Which asks a woman “What did you do yesterday?”
Which asks a woman “Where did you go?”
Which answers «هَلْ شَرِبْتِ الْقَهْوَة؟» with yes?

exercises.promptTranslation: What did you do yesterday?
Did you go to the market? (to a man)

lessons.title: 125. Verbs with an object, verbs with a preposition
lessons.subtitle: كَتَبْتُهَا · فَتَحَهُ · ذَهَبَ إِلَى · بَحَثَ عَنْ

explanations.title: Direct object, or a preposition?
explanations.body: Some verbs act directly on something: كَتَبَ الرِّسَالَة (wrote the letter). These are transitive and take their object with no preposition (the last column is empty; دَخَلَ is like this, though دَخَلَ إِلَى is also used). Other verbs need a preposition before the next word: ذَهَبَ إِلَى الْمَدْرَسَة (went to school). The preposition is part of what you learn with the verb.

explanations.title: Replacing the object: ـهُ ـهَا ـكَ ـنِي
explanations.body: To avoid repeating a noun, attach a pronoun to the verb. It is the same set you know on nouns, except that “me” is ـنِي: ـنِي (me), ـكَ (you, man), ـهُ (him, it), ـهَا (her, it), ـنَا (us).

examples.translation: katabtu ar-risāla. katabtuhā ʾams. — I wrote the letter. I wrote it yesterday.
ghasala al-mudīr al-kūb, thumma ḥamalahu. — The manager washed the cup, then carried it.
shakartuka ʾams. — I thanked you yesterday. (to a man)
shakaratnī sāra. — Sara thanked me.

examples.text: بَحَثْتُ عَنْ عَمَل وَحَصَلْتُ عَلَى وَظِيفَة.
examples.translation: baḥathtu ʿan ʿamal waḥaṣaltu ʿalā waẓīfa. — I looked for work and got a job.

exercises.prompt: Which means “I wrote it” (the letter, الرِّسَالَة)?
Which means “He opened it” (the door, الْبَاب)?

exercises.explanation: ـنِي = me; the verb is feminine.

exercises.prompt: Which means “I looked for a job”?

exercises.promptTranslation: I got a certificate.
I looked for a job.
We went to the market.

explanations.title: لَمْ + the “short” present
explanations.body: To say that something did NOT happen, put لَمْ in front of a present verb. The verb looks like the present but loses its final vowel: it ends in a sukūn (and the ن of ـِين falls away), as in لَا تَدْخُلْ. The meaning is past even though the verb looks present. Before ال, the sukūn becomes a helping kasra: لَمْ أَكْتُبِ الْوَاجِب.

explanations.title: In sentences
explanations.body: Use لَمْ for what did not happen yesterday, last week or last year.

examples.translation: lam ʾadhhab ʾilā al-madrasa ʾams. — I did not go to school yesterday.
lam ʾaktubi al-wājib. — I did not write the homework.
lam tadrus sāra ʾams. — Sara did not study yesterday.
lam yaftaḥi al-mudīr al-bāb. — The manager did not open the door.
lam nasmaʿi al-mūsīqā. — We did not hear the music.
limādhā lam tadhhab? — Why didn’t you go? (to a man)

exercises.explanation: The ن of ـِين falls away.

exercises.prompt: What time does a sentence with لَمْ describe?

exercises.promptTranslation: I did not go to school yesterday.
Sara did not study yesterday.
Why didn’t you go? (to a man)

lessons.title: 127. لَمْ with plurals, and لَمْ يَكُنْ
lessons.subtitle: لَمْ يَكْتُبُوا · لَمْ يَكْتُبْنَ · لَمْ أَكُنْ

explanations.title: Plurals after لَمْ
explanations.body: The same rule you know from أَنْ applies: endings that finish in ن lose it. The “short” present of the plurals is therefore the same as the form after أَنْ. The feminine plural ـْنَ keeps its ن.

explanations.title: Saying “was not”
explanations.body: To say that something was not so, use لَمْ with the present of كَانَ. The middle letter of يَكُون is dropped: لَمْ يَكُنْ, لَمْ أَكُنْ, لَمْ تَكُنْ, لَمْ نَكُنْ. Before ال the sukūn becomes a kasra. You may also meet مَا + the past tense (مَا ذَهَبْتُ) with the same meaning, but it is less common in modern writing.

examples.translation: lam yakun ʾakhī fī al-bayt. — My brother was not at home.
lam ʾakun mashghūlan ʾams. — I was not busy yesterday. (a man speaking)
lam yakuni al-jaww jamīlan. — The weather was not nice.
aṭ-ṭullāb lam yadkhulū aṣ-ṣaff. — The students did not enter the classroom.
hunna lam yakhrujna mina al-bayt. — They (women) did not leave the house.
ʾalam tadhhabā ʾilā al-ḥafla? — Didn’t you two go to the party?

exercises.prompt: Which means “the two (men) did not write”?
Which means “I was not busy” (a man speaking)?
Which means “My brother was not at home”?
What happens to the middle letter of يَكُون after لَمْ?

exercises.promptTranslation: The students did not enter the classroom.
They (women) did not leave the house.
The weather was not nice.

explanations.title: Stages of education
explanations.body: The names and the number of years differ from country to country, but these words are widely understood. A school adjective follows the noun and agrees with it (feminine, with ال).

explanations.title: Where do you study?
explanations.body: Grades and years use the ordinal numbers: الْأَوَّل, الثَّانِي, الثَّالِث … الْعَاشِر. With a feminine noun the ordinal is feminine (السَّنَة الثَّانِيَة).

examples.translation: ʾanā fī aṣ-ṣaff al-khāmis. — I am in the fifth grade.
ʾukhtī tilmīdha fī al-madrasa al-ibtidāʾiyya. — My sister is a pupil at primary school.
ʾakhī ṭālib fī al-madrasa ath-thānawiyya. — My brother is a student at secondary school.
ʾadrus fī kulliyya al-handasa. — I study at the engineering college.

examples.text: هِيَ فِي السَّنَة الثَّانِيَة فِي الْجَامِعَة.
examples.translation: hiya fī as-sana ath-thāniya fī al-jāmiʿa. — She is in her second year at the university.
darasa ʾabī fī kulliyya aṭ-ṭibb. — My father studied at the medical college.

exercises.prompt: What does الصَّفّ mean at school?
Which means “I am in the fifth grade”?
Which means “She is in her second year”?
Which means “My father studied at the medical college”?

exercises.promptTranslation: I am in the fifth grade.
My brother is a student at secondary school.
She is in her second year at the university.

explanations.title: Subjects
explanations.body: Ten subjects you may study. They all take ال when you talk about them.

explanations.title: Talking about subjects
explanations.body: You know أَدْرُس (I study) and أُحِبّ (I like). Add a subject after them, and use صَعْب and سَهْل to describe it.

examples.translation: ʾuḥibb at-tārīkh wal-jughrāfiyā. — I like history and geography.
ʾadrus ar-riyāḍiyyāt wal-fīziyāʾ. — I study mathematics and physics.
al-kīmiyāʾ ṣaʿba wal-jughrāfiyā sahla. — Chemistry is difficult and geography is easy.
mādhā tadrus fī al-jāmiʿa? — What do you study at the university? (to a man)
ʾadrus al-ʾadab al-ʿarabiyy. — I study Arabic literature.
ʿindī imtiḥān fī ar-riyāḍiyyāt. — I have an exam in mathematics.

exercises.prompt: Which asks a man “What do you study at the university?”

exercises.promptTranslation: I study Arabic literature.
I have an exam in mathematics.

explanations.title: Seven days
explanations.body: The names of Sunday to Thursday come from the numbers one to five (one, two, three …). Friday is الْجُمْعَة, and in many Arab countries Friday and Saturday are the weekend. After يَوْم, the name of the day gives “on …”.

explanations.title: Today, tomorrow, yesterday
explanations.body: الْيَوْم is “today”, غَدًا “tomorrow” and أَمْس “yesterday”. To talk about yesterday’s day, use كَانَ.

examples.translation: al-yawm yawm ath-thulāthāʾ. — Today is Tuesday.
ghadan yawm al-ʾarbiʿāʾ. — Tomorrow is Wednesday.
ʾams kāna yawm al-ithnayn. — Yesterday was Monday.

examples.text: أَذْهَب إِلَى الْمَدْرَسَة مِنَ الْأَحَد إِلَى الْخَمِيس.
examples.translation: ʾadhhab ʾilā al-madrasa mina al-ʾaḥad ʾilā al-khamīs. — I go to school from Sunday to Thursday.

examples.text: لَا أَذْهَب إِلَى الْمَدْرَسَة يَوْم الْجُمْعَة وَيَوْم السَّبْت.
examples.translation: lā ʾadhhab ʾilā al-madrasa yawm al-jumʿa wayawm as-sabt. — I do not go to school on Friday and Saturday.
mādhā tafʿal yawm as-sabt? — What do you do on Saturday? (to a man)

exercises.prompt: Which day name comes from the number five?

exercises.promptTranslation: Today is Tuesday.
Tomorrow is Wednesday.

explanations.title: A week of lessons
explanations.body: Here is a timetable. A lesson is دَرْس (plural دُرُوس). The ordinals give the order: الدَّرْس الْأَوَّل (the first lesson), الدَّرْس الثَّانِي (the second).

explanations.title: Talking about the week
explanations.body: Use عِنْدِي (I have) with a lesson or an exam, and عَلَيَّ أَنْ (I have to) for work you must do.

examples.translation: hādhā huwa jadwal ad-durūs. — This is the timetable.
ʿindī dars at-tārīkh yawm al-ithnayn. — I have the history lesson on Monday.
ad-dars al-ʾawwal huwa ar-riyāḍiyyāt. — The first lesson is mathematics.
hal ʿindaka imtiḥān yawm al-khamīs? — Do you have an exam on Thursday? (to a man)
naʿam, waʿalayya ʾan ʾadrus al-yawm. — Yes, and I have to study today.
lam ʾaktubi al-wājib ʾams. — I did not write the homework yesterday.

exercises.prompt: What does الْوَاجِب mean at school?
Which means “I have the history lesson on Monday”?
Which asks a man “Do you have an exam on Thursday?”
Which means “I did not write the homework”?

exercises.promptTranslation: I have an exam on Thursday.
The first lesson is mathematics.
I have to study today.

explanations.title: The twelve months
explanations.body: Most Arab countries use these names, which sound like the English ones. A month is شَهْر (plural شُهُور). “In the month of March” is فِي شَهْر مَارِس.

explanations.title: Other names and another calendar
explanations.body: In Syria, Lebanon, Jordan, Palestine and Iraq the months have different names, for example آذَار (March), أَيَّار (May), حَزِيرَان (June), تَمُّوز (July) and أَيْلُول (September). Many Arab countries also use the Islamic calendar, which follows the moon, so its year is about eleven days shorter. Its months include مُحَرَّم, رَمَضَان and شَوَّال.

examples.text: فِي شَهْر مَارِس يَكُون الْجَوّ جَمِيلًا.
examples.translation: fī shahr māris yakūn al-jaww jamīlan. — In the month of March the weather is nice.
nadhhab ʾilā al-jāmiʿa fī sibtambir. — We go to university in September.
ash-shitāʾ fī dīsambir wayanāyir wafibrāyir. — Winter is in December, January and February.
ʾayyār huwa shahr māyū. — Ayyar is the month of May.
ʾādhār huwa shahr māris. — Adhar is the month of March.
ramaḍān shahr fī at-taqwīm al-ʾislāmiyy. — Ramadan is a month in the Islamic calendar.

exercises.prompt: Which means “in the month of May”?
In Syria, Lebanon and Jordan, which name is used for March?
What does the Islamic calendar follow?
exercises.explanation: Its year is about eleven days shorter.

exercises.promptTranslation: In the month of March the weather is nice.

explanations.title: More professions
explanations.body: Add ة for a woman, as before. The ـيّ ending takes a feminine ـِيَّة.

explanations.title: Who works where?
explanations.body: A person’s job is a noun sentence (أَبِي طَيَّار). To say where, add يَعْمَل فِي. To say “I want to be …”, use أُرِيد أَنْ أَكُون, and the job takes the ـًا ending.

examples.translation: ʾakhī mubarmij fī sharika kabīra. — My brother is a programmer at a big company.

examples.text: أُخْتِي صَيْدَلِيَّة. تَعْمَل فِي صَيْدَلِيَّة قَرِيبَة مِنَ الْبَيْت.
examples.translation: ʾukhtī ṣaydaliyya. taʿmal fī ṣaydaliyya qarība mina al-bayt. — My sister is a pharmacist. She works at a pharmacy near home.
al-khabbāz yaʿmal fī al-makhbiz. — The baker works at the bakery.
aṭ-ṭabbākh yaʿmal fī al-maṭʿam. — The cook works in the restaurant.
ʾabī ṭayyār wahuwa mashghūl dāʾiman. — My father is a pilot and he is always busy.
ʾurīd ʾan ʾakūn mubarmijan. — I want to be a programmer. (a man speaking)

exercises.prompt: Which means “My sister is a pharmacist”?
Which means “I want to be a programmer” (a man speaking)?

exercises.explanation: A baker works at a bakery.
exercises.promptTranslation: The baker works at the bakery.
My father is a pilot and he is busy.

lessons.title: 134. What do you do?
lessons.subtitle: مَاذَا تَعْمَل؟ · أَيْنَ تَعْمَل؟ · كَمْ سَنَةً عَمِلْتَ؟

explanations.title: Asking about work
explanations.body: Questions about what you do now use the present, and questions about the past use the past or كَانَ. Remember that «تَعْمَل» is for a man and «تَعْمَلِين» for a woman.

explanations.title: At a party
explanations.body: Two people meet at a party, and one asks about the other’s work.

examples.translation: mādhā taʿmalīn yā hind? — What do you do, Hind? (to a woman)

examples.text: أَنَا مُصَمِّمَة. أَعْمَل فِي شَرِكَة صَغِيرَة.
examples.translation: ʾanā muṣammima. ʾaʿmal fī sharika ṣaghīra. — I am a designer. I work at a small company.
waʾayna kunti taʿmalīn qabl sanatayn? — And where were you working two years ago? (to a woman)

examples.text: عَمِلْتُ فِي مَكْتَب لِمُدَّة ثَلَاث سَنَوَات.
examples.translation: ʿamiltu fī maktab limudda thalāth sanawāt. — I worked in an office for three years.
hal tuḥibbīn ʿamalaki? — Do you like your job? (to a woman)
naʿam, ʾuḥibb ʿamalī kathīran. — Yes, I like my job a lot.

exercises.prompt: Which asks a man “What do you do?”
Which asks a woman “What do you do?”
Which asks a man “Where do you work?”
Which asks a man “How many years did you work there?”
Which means “I worked for three years”?
Which means “I like my job a lot”?
A woman asks a woman: “Do you like your job?”

exercises.explanation: To a woman, in the past.
exercises.promptTranslation: Where were you working two years ago?
I worked in an office for two years.

explanations.title: Telling your story
explanations.body: A short biography is a list of past verbs with “I”. Join the steps with ثُمَّ (“then”) and use لِمُدَّة and بَعْد for how long and when. The verbs تَخَرَّجَ (“graduated”) and تَعَلَّمَ (“learned”) are a new kind of verb, with تَـ in front and a doubled middle letter; their past endings are the same.

explanations.title: A short biography
explanations.body: One person tells where she studied and worked.

examples.translation: darastu al-handasa fī jāmiʿa kabīra. — I studied engineering at a big university.
takharrajtu baʿd khams sanawāt. — I graduated after five years.
ḥaṣaltu ʿalā shahāda fī al-handasa. — I got a degree in engineering.
baḥathtu ʿan ʿamal limudda shahrayn. — I looked for a job for two months.

examples.text: ثُمَّ عَمِلْتُ فِي شَرِكَة لِمُدَّة سَنَتَيْن.
examples.translation: thumma ʿamiltu fī sharika limudda sanatayn. — Then I worked at a company for two years.
taʿallamtu al-ʿarabiyya fī al-jāmiʿa. — I learned Arabic at the university.

exercises.prompt: Which means “I looked for a job for two months”?
Which means “Then I worked at a company”?

exercises.promptTranslation: I graduated after five years.
I got a degree in engineering.
Then I worked at a company.

lessons.title: 136. Making an appointment
lessons.subtitle: هَلْ أَنْتَ مُتَفَرِّغ يَوْم الثُّلَاثَاء؟ · الْمَوْعِد مُنَاسِب

explanations.title: Words for an appointment
explanations.body: A meeting needs a day and a time of day. Here are the key words and the parts of the day.

explanations.title: Fixing a time
explanations.body: Ask when the other person is free, say when you are busy, and agree on a day.

examples.translation: ʾurīd mawʿid maʿa al-mudīr. — I would like an appointment with the manager.
hal ʾanta mutafarrigh yawm ath-thulāthāʾ? — Are you free on Tuesday? (to a man)
lā, ʾanā mashghūl fī aṣ-ṣabāḥ. — No, I am busy in the morning.
wabaʿd aẓ-ẓuhr? — And in the afternoon?
naʿam, hādhā al-mawʿid munāsib. — Yes, this appointment is suitable.

examples.text: حَسَنًا، الْمَوْعِد يَوْم الثُّلَاثَاء بَعْد الظُّهْر.
examples.translation: ḥasanan, al-mawʿid yawm ath-thulāthāʾ baʿd aẓ-ẓuhr. — Good, the appointment is on Tuesday afternoon.

exercises.prompt: Which asks a man “Are you free on Tuesday?”
Which means “I am busy in the morning”?
Which means “I would like an appointment with the manager”?

exercises.promptTranslation: Are you free on Tuesday?
This appointment is suitable.

explanations.title: The past tense on one page
explanations.body: The past tense of ذَهَبَ: the stem ذَهَبـ with an ending. Negative: لَمْ + the short present: لَمْ يَذْهَبْ.

explanations.title: My day yesterday
explanations.body: A woman tells what she did, and what she did not do.

examples.text: أَمْس خَرَجْتُ مِنَ الْبَيْت فِي الصَّبَاح.
examples.translation: ʾams kharajtu mina al-bayt fī aṣ-ṣabāḥ. — Yesterday I left the house in the morning.

examples.text: ذَهَبْتُ إِلَى الْجَامِعَة وَدَرَسْتُ فِي الْمَكْتَبَة.
examples.translation: dhahabtu ʾilā al-jāmiʿa wadarastu fī al-maktaba. — I went to the university and studied in the library.
samiʿtu al-mūsīqā maʿa ṣadīqatī. — I heard music with my friend (a woman).

examples.text: لَمْ أَكْتُبِ الْوَاجِب لِأَنِّي كُنْتُ مَشْغُولَةً.
examples.translation: lam ʾaktubi al-wājib liʾannī kuntu mashghūlatan. — I did not write the homework because I was busy.
rajaʿtu ʾilā al-bayt fī al-masāʾ. — I went back home in the evening.

exercises.prompt: Which means “I went to the university and studied”?
Which means “I was busy (a woman speaking) and did not write”?

exercises.promptTranslation: Yesterday I went to the library.
I did not write the homework yesterday.

lessons.title: 138. Review: school and work
lessons.subtitle: طَالِب · مُدَرِّس · مَوْعِد · عَمِلْتُ فِي شَرِكَة

explanations.title: A conversation at the university
explanations.body: Two students meet and talk about school, subjects, work and the days of the week.

examples.text: مَرْحَبًا يَا سَامِي. مَاذَا تَدْرُس فِي الْجَامِعَة؟
examples.translation: marḥaban yā sāmī. mādhā tadrus fī al-jāmiʿa? — Hello, Sami. What do you study at the university? (to a man)

examples.text: أَدْرُس الْحَاسُوب. عِنْدِي دَرْس يَوْم الْأَحَد وَيَوْم الثُّلَاثَاء.
examples.translation: ʾadrus al-ḥāsūb. ʿindī dars yawm al-ʾaḥad wayawm ath-thulāthāʾ. — I study computing. I have lessons on Sunday and Tuesday.
hal ʿamilta qabl al-jāmiʿa? — Did you work before university? (to a man)

examples.text: نَعَمْ، عَمِلْتُ فِي مَطْعَم لِمُدَّة سَنَة.
examples.translation: naʿam, ʿamiltu fī maṭʿam limudda sana. — Yes, I worked at a restaurant for a year.

examples.text: وَالْآن؟ هَلْ أَنْتَ مَشْغُول يَوْم الْخَمِيس؟
examples.translation: wal-ʾān? hal ʾanta mashghūl yawm al-khamīs? — And now? Are you busy on Thursday? (to a man)

examples.text: لَا، أَنَا مُتَفَرِّغ. لَيْسَ عِنْدِي اِمْتِحَان.
examples.translation: lā, ʾanā mutafarrigh. laysa ʿindī imtiḥān. — No, I am free. I do not have an exam.

examples.text: لَمْ يَكُنْ عِنْدِي اِمْتِحَان يَوْم الْأَحَد الْمَاضِي.
examples.translation: lam yakun ʿindī imtiḥān yawm al-ʾaḥad al-māḍī. — I did not have an exam last Sunday.

exercises.prompt: Which means “I have a lesson on Sunday”?
Which asks a man “Did you work?”
Which means “I worked at a restaurant for a year”?
Which means “I did not have an exam”?
Which means “Are you busy on Thursday?” (to a man)
Which is the correct word order for “the second year”?

exercises.promptTranslation: What do you study at the university?

exercises.explanation: A man says he is free.
exercises.promptTranslation: No, I am free.

units.title: الْيَوْم وَالْغَد: my day, numbers and the future

lessons.title: 139. Eleven to nineteen
lessons.subtitle: أَحَدَ عَشَرَ كِتَابًا · خَمْسَ عَشْرَةَ طَاوِلَةً

explanations.title: The teens
explanations.body: From 11 to 19 the number is two words: a unit and “ten” (عَشَرَ or عَشْرَةَ). For 11 and 12 the unit agrees with the noun. For 13 to 19 the unit takes the opposite gender, as in 3–10, but the word for “ten” agrees with the noun. Apart from 12, both parts keep their ending whatever their job in the sentence is.

explanations.title: What comes after the number
explanations.body: The thing you count is SINGULAR and takes the ending ـًا (ـَةً for a feminine word): أَحَدَ عَشَرَ كِتَابًا (eleven books, literally “eleven a book”). The number 12 shows ـَا in the nominative, as اِثْنَا عَشَرَ; after a preposition or as an object it shows ـَيْ instead.

examples.translation: fī aṣ-ṣaff ʾaḥada ʿashara ṭāliban. — There are eleven students in the class.
fī al-maktaba khamsa ʿashrata ṭāwilatan. — There are fifteen tables in the library.
ʿindī thalāthata ʿashara kitāban. — I have thirteen books.
fī as-sana ithnā ʿashara shahran. — There are twelve months in the year.
kam ʿumruka? — How old are you? (to a man)
ʿumrī tisʿa ʿashrata sanatan. — I am nineteen years old.

exercises.prompt: Which is “eleven” with a masculine noun?
Which is “fifteen” with a feminine noun?
exercises.explanation: The unit has no ة and “ten” is عَشْرَةَ.

exercises.prompt: Which means “She is nineteen years old”?

exercises.promptTranslation: There are eleven students in the class.
I have thirteen books.
There are twelve months in the year.

explanations.title: The tens
explanations.body: The tens end in ـُون (the sound masculine plural). They are the same for men and women. After a preposition or as an object ـُون becomes ـِين, just as in the plural of men.

explanations.title: Units and tens: 21 to 99
explanations.body: Say the unit first, then وَ (“and”), then the ten: خَمْسَة وَعِشْرُون (“five and twenty”). The unit follows the rules you know: 1 and 2 agree with the noun, and 3–9 take the opposite gender. The thing you count is singular and takes ـًا, as after 11–19.

examples.translation: fī aṣ-ṣaff khamsa waʿishrūn ṭāliban. — There are twenty-five students in the class.
fī al-kulliyya thalāthūn mudarrisatan. — There are thirty (women) teachers in the college.
ʿumru ʾabī sitt wakhamsūn sanatan. — My father is fifty-six years old.
maʿī ʾarbaʿūn dīnāran. — I have forty dinars with me.
fī al-kitāb tisʿūn ṣafḥatan. — There are ninety pages in the book.

exercises.explanation: Unit, وَ, ten; the noun is singular.
Opposite gender for the unit: خَمْس.

exercises.prompt: Which means “My father is fifty-six years old”?
exercises.explanation: سَنَة is feminine, so the unit is سِتّ.
A singular noun after the tens.
exercises.promptTranslation: There are ninety pages in the book.
Twenty-five students.

lessons.title: 141. A hundred, a thousand, and prices
lessons.subtitle: مِئَة دِينَار · أَلْف دُولَار · كَمْ ثَمَنُهُ؟

explanations.title: 100 and 1000
explanations.body: After مِئَة (100) and أَلْف (1000) the thing counted is a singular noun with no ـًا: it is the second part of an iḍāfa, like بَاب الْبَيْت. So you say مِئَة دِينَار and أَلْف دُولَار. For 3–10 you still use the plural: ثَلَاثَة دُولَارَات.

explanations.title: How much is it?
explanations.body: كَمْ ثَمَنُهُ؟ and كَمْ سِعْرُهُ؟ both mean “how much is it?”. The prices go in a noun sentence. رَخِيص is “cheap” and غَالِي is “expensive”.

examples.translation: kam thaman hādhā al-kitāb? — How much is this book?
thamanuhu ʿishrūn dūlāran. — It costs twenty dollars.
hādhā ghālī. siʿruhu miʾa dūlār. — This is expensive. Its price is a hundred dollars.
al-qahwa rakhīṣa hunā. — The coffee is cheap here.
siʿr ash-shaqqa miʾa ʾalf dūlār. — The price of the flat is a hundred thousand dollars.
bikam hādhihi al-ḥaqība? — How much is this bag?

exercises.promptTranslation: How much is this book?
It costs a hundred dollars.

explanations.title: The hours
explanations.body: Ask كَمِ السَّاعَة؟ (“how much is the hour?”). The answer is السَّاعَة and a feminine ordinal: السَّاعَة الثَّالِثَة (the third hour = three o’clock). One o’clock is السَّاعَة الْوَاحِدَة. After 10 the hours use الْحَادِيَةَ عَشْرَةَ and الثَّانِيَةَ عَشْرَةَ.

explanations.title: In the morning, in the evening
explanations.body: To say “at three”, use فِي السَّاعَة الثَّالِثَة. Add صَبَاحًا (in the morning), ظُهْرًا (around midday), مَسَاءً (in the afternoon or evening) or لَيْلًا (at night).

examples.translation: kami as-sāʿa al-ʾān? — What time is it now?
as-sāʿa ath-thālitha. — It is three o’clock.
as-sāʿa ath-thāmina ṣabāḥan. — It is eight in the morning.
ʾastayqiẓ fī as-sāʿa as-sādisa. — I wake up at six o’clock.
ad-dars fī as-sāʿa at-tāsiʿa. — The lesson is at nine o’clock.
nataghaddā fī as-sāʿa al-wāḥida ẓuhran. — We have lunch at one o’clock in the afternoon.

exercises.prompt: Which means “I wake up at six”?

exercises.promptTranslation: What time is it now?
We have lunch at one in the afternoon.

lessons.title: 143. Half past, quarter to, ten minutes
lessons.subtitle: وَالنِّصْف · وَالرُّبْع · إِلَّا رُبْعًا

explanations.title: Parts of the hour
explanations.body: Add the part after the hour with وَ: وَالنِّصْف (and the half), وَالرُّبْع (and the quarter), وَالثُّلُث (and the third = twenty minutes). To say “to”, use إِلَّا (“except”): إِلَّا رُبْعًا (a quarter to), إِلَّا ثُلُثًا (twenty to). Minutes follow the hour with وَ and a number: وَعَشْر دَقَائِق (and ten minutes).

explanations.title: In sentences
explanations.body: A time can end a sentence or follow فِي السَّاعَة.

examples.translation: as-sāʿa ath-thālitha wan-niṣf. — It is half past three.
ad-dars fī as-sāʿa al-ʿāshira war-rubʿ. — The lesson is at a quarter past ten.

examples.text: وَصَلَ الْقِطَار فِي السَّاعَة الْخَامِسَة إِلَّا رُبْعًا.
examples.translation: waṣala al-qiṭār fī as-sāʿa al-khāmisa ʾillā rubʿan. — The train arrived at a quarter to five.
as-sāʿa ath-thāmina waʿashr daqāʾiq. — It is ten past eight.
nataghaddā fī as-sāʿa ath-thāniya wan-niṣf. — We have lunch at half past two.

examples.text: أَنَام فِي السَّاعَة الْحَادِيَةَ عَشْرَةَ مَسَاءً.
examples.translation: ʾanām fī as-sāʿa al-ḥādiyata ʿashrata masāʾan. — I go to bed at eleven in the evening.

exercises.prompt: What is وَالثُّلُث after the hour?
exercises.explanation: ثُلُث = a third of an hour.

exercises.prompt: Which means “We have lunch at half past two”?

exercises.promptTranslation: It is a quarter to eight.
It is half past three.
I go to bed at eleven in the evening.

explanations.title: Getting ready
explanations.body: These verbs describe a morning. أَسْتَيْقِظ (I wake up) and أَسْتَحِمّ (I take a shower) are built on a pattern with an initial سْتـ; for now, learn them as whole words.

explanations.title: A morning in order
explanations.body: Use فِي السَّاعَة for the time, ثُمَّ for “then” and وَ for “and”.

examples.translation: ʾastayqiẓ fī as-sāʿa as-sādisa ṣabāḥan. — I wake up at six in the morning.
ʾaghsil wajhī waʾastaḥimm. — I wash my face and take a shower.
thumma ʾalbas thiyābī. — Then I put on my clothes.
ʾatanāwal al-ʾifṭār maʿa ʾukhtī. — I have breakfast with my sister.

examples.text: أَخْرُج مِنَ الْبَيْت فِي السَّاعَة السَّابِعَة وَالنِّصْف.
examples.translation: ʾakhruj mina al-bayt fī as-sāʿa as-sābiʿa wan-niṣf. — I leave the house at half past seven.
ʾadhhab ʾilā al-madrasa bid-darrāja. — I go to school by bicycle.

exercises.prompt: Which means “I put on my clothes”?
Which means “I go to school by bicycle”?

exercises.promptTranslation: I wash my face and take a shower.
Then I put on my clothes.
I leave the house at seven o’clock.

explanations.title: After school
explanations.body: Here is the second half of a day. أَرْجِع (I come back), أَدْرُس (I study) and أَلْعَب (I play) are ordinary verbs you know how to conjugate. أَتَغَدَّى (I have lunch) and أَتَعَشَّى (I have dinner) belong to a verb pattern that gets its own lesson soon; for now learn them as whole words.

explanations.title: To sleep
explanations.body: نَامَ (to sleep) has a long vowel ā in the middle of the present. The long vowel stays in the singular and the plural with ـُون, so the verb looks like this:

examples.text: أَرْجِع إِلَى الْبَيْت فِي السَّاعَة الرَّابِعَة مَسَاءً.
examples.translation: ʾarjiʿ ʾilā al-bayt fī as-sāʿa ar-rābiʿa masāʾan. — I come back home at four in the afternoon.
baʿda al-ghadāʾ ʾadrus durūsī. — After lunch I study my lessons.
qabla al-ʿashāʾ ʾalʿab maʿa ʾakhī. — Before dinner I play with my brother.
nataʿashshā fī as-sāʿa as-sābiʿa. — We have dinner at seven o’clock.
hal tanāmīn fī as-sāʿa al-ʿāshira? — Do you go to bed at ten o’clock? (to a woman)

examples.text: أَخِي يَنَام فِي السَّاعَة الْحَادِيَةَ عَشْرَةَ.
examples.translation: ʾakhī yanām fī as-sāʿa al-ḥādiyata ʿashrata. — My brother goes to bed at eleven o’clock.

exercises.prompt: Which means “After lunch I study my lessons”?
Which means “Before dinner I play with my brother”?

exercises.explanation: The ـِين ending is for “you” (to a woman).
بَعْدَ is followed by a noun.
exercises.promptTranslation: After lunch I study my lessons.
I come back home at four o’clock.

exercises.prompt: هَلْ ___ فِي السَّاعَة الْعَاشِرَة؟ (to a woman)
exercises.promptTranslation: Do you go to bed at ten o’clock?

lessons.title: 146. Measure II: the doubled middle letter
lessons.subtitle: دَرَسَ ← دَرَّسَ · يُدَرِّس

explanations.title: Doubling the middle
explanations.body: Arabic builds many verbs from one root by changing the pattern. If you double the middle letter of a root you get Measure II, written فَعَّلَ. It often means “to cause someone to do it”: دَرَسَ (he studied) becomes دَرَّسَ (he taught).

explanations.title: The present tense
explanations.body: In the present tense every Measure II verb has a prefix with ḍamma (أُ نُ تُ يُ) and a kasra before the last letter: يُدَرِّس, أُدَرِّس. The endings are the ones you already know. The teacher is مُدَرِّس, “the one who teaches”.

examples.translation: ʾummī tudarris al-ʿarabiyya fī al-madrasa. — My mother teaches Arabic at school.
ʿallamatnī mudarrisatī al-kitāba. — My teacher taught me writing.
ḥaḍḍarat ʾummī al-ʿashāʾ. — My mother prepared dinner.
naẓẓaftu al-ghurfa ʾams. — I cleaned the room yesterday.
ʾurattib ghurfatī kull yawm. — I tidy my room every day.
hum yunaẓẓifūn al-madrasa baʿda ad-dars. — They clean the school after the lesson.

exercises.explanation: Doubling the middle: “cause to study” = teach.
Measure II of the root ن-ظ-ف.
The prefix أُ and a kasra before the last letter.

exercises.prompt: Which means “I cleaned the room yesterday”?

exercises.promptTranslation: My mother teaches Arabic at school.
My mother prepared dinner.

explanations.title: Adding تَـ to Measure II
explanations.body: Put تَـ in front of a Measure II verb and you get Measure V, written تَفَعَّلَ. It often means doing the action to yourself, or the result of the Measure II action: عَلَّمَ (he taught) gives تَعَلَّمَ (he learned). In the present, the usual person prefix goes in front of the تَـ: أَتَعَلَّم, تَتَعَلَّم, يَتَعَلَّم.

explanations.title: In sentences
explanations.body: The past tense is easy to spot: the verb begins with تَـ and has a doubled middle letter, as in تَكَلَّمْتُ (I spoke). The verbs for lunch and dinner you met before belong here: تَغَدَّى and تَعَشَّى.

examples.translation: ʾataʿallam al-ʿarabiyya mundhu sana. — I have been learning Arabic for a year.
hal tatakallam al-ʿarabiyya? — Do you speak Arabic? (to a man)
takallamtu maʿa mudarrisī ʾams. — I spoke with my teacher yesterday.
nataḥaddath ʿani al-ʿamal. — We talk about work.

examples.text: تَعَلَّمَ أَخِي الْقِرَاءَة فِي الصَّفّ الْأَوَّل.
examples.translation: taʿallama ʾakhī al-qirāʾa fī aṣ-ṣaff al-ʾawwal. — My brother learned to read in the first grade.
taghaddaynā maʿa al-ʾusra. — We had lunch with the family.

exercises.explanation: Measure V of the root ع-ل-م.
Prefix أَ + تَـ + the doubled letter.

exercises.prompt: Which means “I spoke with my teacher yesterday”?

exercises.explanation: “You” (to a man): تَـ + a plain ending.
exercises.promptTranslation: Do you speak Arabic?
My brother learned to read in the first grade.

lessons.title: 148. Next week and in three days
lessons.subtitle: غَدًا · الْأُسْبُوع الْقَادِم · بَعْدَ ثَلَاثَة أَيَّام

explanations.title: Time words for the future
explanations.body: You already know سَـ and سَوْفَ. Now add words for when. بَعْدَ before a time means “in”: بَعْدَ أُسْبُوع is “in a week”. الْقَادِم (“coming”) follows the noun and agrees with it: الْأُسْبُوع الْقَادِم, السَّنَة الْقَادِمَة.

explanations.title: Plans
explanations.body: The time word can come first or last. Look at how سَـ is joined to the verb.

examples.translation: ghadan saʾadhhab ʾilā al-maktaba. — Tomorrow I will go to the library.

examples.text: سَنَرْجِع إِلَى الْبَيْت بَعْدَ ثَلَاثَة أَيَّام.
examples.translation: sanarjiʿ ʾilā al-bayt baʿda thalātha ʾayyām. — We will go back home in three days.

examples.text: فِي الْأُسْبُوع الْقَادِم سَأَعْمَل فِي الْمَكْتَب.
examples.translation: fī al-ʾusbūʿ al-qādim saʾaʿmal fī al-maktab. — Next week I will work in the office.

examples.text: فِي الشَّهْر الْقَادِم سَتَدْرُس أُخْتِي فِي الْجَامِعَة.
examples.translation: fī ash-shahr al-qādim satadrus ʾukhtī fī al-jāmiʿa. — Next month my sister will study at the university.
saʾaktub ʾilayka baʿda ʾusbūʿ. — I will write to you in a week. (to a man)

examples.text: فِي السَّنَة الْقَادِمَة سَيَفْتَح أَخِي مَطْعَم.
examples.translation: fī as-sana al-qādima sayaftaḥ ʾakhī maṭʿam. — Next year my brother will open a restaurant.

exercises.prompt: Which means “Next month my sister will study at the university”?
options: فِي الشَّهْر الْمَاضِي سَتَدْرُس أُخْتِي فِي الْجَامِعَة
فِي الْأُسْبُوع الْقَادِم سَتَدْرُس أُخْتِي فِي الْجَامِعَة
فِي الشَّهْر الْقَادِم سَتَدْرُس أُخْتِي فِي الْجَامِعَة
فِي الشَّهْر الْقَادِم سَيَدْرُس أَخِي فِي الْجَامِعَة

exercises.promptTranslation: Tomorrow I will go to the library.
We will go back home in three days.

exercises.explanation: سَنَة is feminine and the year is still to come.
exercises.promptTranslation: Next year my brother will open a restaurant.

explanations.title: لَنْ + verb
explanations.body: لَنْ means “will not”. Put it in front of the present verb, with no سَـ. After لَنْ the verb takes the same shortened form as after أَنْ: the final ن of ـِينَ, ـَانِ and ـُونَ falls away, and ـُوا gets a silent alif. The women’s plural ـْنَ keeps its ن.

explanations.title: Past, present, future
explanations.body: You now have three ways to say no, one for each time. لَمْ is for the past, لَا for the present and لَنْ for the future.

examples.translation: lan ʾadhhab ʾilā al-madrasa ghadan. — I will not go to school tomorrow.

examples.text: لَنْ نَرْجِع إِلَى الْبَيْت قَبْلَ الْعَشَاء.
examples.translation: lan narjiʿ ʾilā al-bayt qabla al-ʿashāʾ. — We will not go back home before dinner.
ʾukhtī lan tadrus ghadan. — My sister will not study tomorrow.
lan yaktubū al-wājib al-yawm. — They will not do the homework today.
lan tajlisī hunā. — You will not sit here. (to a woman)

examples.text: لَمْ أَذْهَب أَمْس وَلَنْ أَذْهَب غَدًا.
examples.translation: lam ʾadhhab ʾams walan ʾadhhab ghadan. — I did not go yesterday and I will not go tomorrow.

exercises.explanation: After لَنْ the final ن falls away.

exercises.prompt: Which means “you (to a woman) will not go”?
exercises.explanation: ـِين loses its ن after لَنْ.

exercises.prompt: Which means “My sister will not study tomorrow”?
Which means “We will not go back before dinner”?

exercises.promptTranslation: I will not go to school tomorrow.
They will not do the homework today.
We will not go back home before dinner.

lessons.title: 150. Could you repeat?
lessons.subtitle: كَرِّرْ مِنْ فَضْلِكَ · هَلْ يُمْكِنُكَ أَنْ تُكَرِّر؟

explanations.title: Asking for help in class
explanations.body: A command for Measure II is the present stem without its prefix: تُكَرِّر (you repeat) gives كَرِّرْ (repeat!). A command for Measure V drops one تَـ: تَتَكَلَّم gives تَكَلَّمْ. The endings for a woman and a group are the same as for any command: ـِي and ـُوا.

rows: How do I say “three” in English?

explanations.title: Can you…? May I…?
explanations.body: يُمْكِن means “it is possible”. Add an ending to say who: يُمْكِنُنِي (it is possible for me), يُمْكِنُكَ (for you, to a man), يُمْكِنُكِ (for you, to a woman). Then use أَنْ and a verb, as after يَجِب.

examples.translation: hal yumkinuka ʾan tukarrir? — Can you repeat? (to a man)
hal yumkinuki ʾan tatakallamī bibuṭʾ? — Can you speak slowly? (to a woman)
hal yumkinunī ʾan ʾajlis hunā? — May I sit here?
lam ʾafham hādhihi al-kalima. — I did not understand this word.
mā maʿnā hādhihi al-kalima? — What does this word mean?
karrirū min faḍlikum. — Please repeat. (to a group)

exercises.explanation: ـِي is added for a woman.

exercises.prompt: What does مَا مَعْنَى هَذِه الْكَلِمَة؟ ask?
options: How do you spell this word?

exercises.prompt: Which asks a man “Can you repeat?”
___ مِنْ فَضْلِكَ. (Please repeat, to a man)
exercises.promptTranslation: Please repeat.

exercises.prompt: هَلْ يُمْكِنُكِ أَنْ ___ بِبُطْء؟ (to a woman)
exercises.explanation: After أَنْ the ـِين loses its ن.
exercises.promptTranslation: Can you speak slowly?

explanations.title: Ordinals for the days of the month
explanations.body: The days of the month are numbered with masculine ordinals, because يَوْم is masculine. You know 1–5. Here are the next ones and some larger days. For 11–19 the ordinal is followed by عَشَرَ. From 21 the ordinal is joined with وَ to the ten, and the ten takes the ال: الْخَامِس وَالْعِشْرُون.

explanations.title: Saying the date
explanations.body: Ask مَا تَارِيخ الْيَوْم؟ (“what is today’s date?”). The answer is الْيَوْم هُوَ and the day, then مِنْ and the month. To say “on the 10th”, put فِي in front of the ordinal. After فِي the ending ـُون changes to ـِين.

examples.translation: mā tārīkh al-yawm? — What is today’s date?
al-yawm huwa al-khāmis min māris. — Today is the fifth of March.

examples.text: الْيَوْم هُوَ الْحَادِيَ عَشَرَ مِنْ دِيسَمْبِر.
examples.translation: al-yawm huwa al-ḥādiya ʿashara min dīsambir. — Today is the eleventh of December.

examples.text: عِيد مِيلَادِي فِي الْعَاشِر مِنْ أُكْتُوبَر.
examples.translation: ʿīd mīlādī fī al-ʿāshir min ʾuktūbar. — My birthday is on the tenth of October.

examples.text: سَنَذْهَب إِلَى الْمَكْتَبَة فِي الْعِشْرِين مِنْ نُوفِمْبِر.
examples.translation: sanadhhab ʾilā al-maktaba fī al-ʿishrīn min nūfimbir. — We will go to the library on the twentieth of November.

examples.text: اِمْتِحَانِي فِي الثَّالِث وَالْعِشْرِين مِنْ يَنَايِر.
examples.translation: imtiḥānī fī ath-thālith wal-ʿishrīn min yanāyir. — My exam is on the twenty-third of January.

exercises.explanation: A day of the month is masculine.

exercises.prompt: Which means “Today is the fifth of March”?
Which means “My birthday is on the tenth of October”?
options: عِيد مِيلَادِي فِي الْعَاشِر مِنْ أُكْتُوبَر
عِيد مِيلَادِي فِي التَّاسِع مِنْ أُكْتُوبَر
عِيد مِيلَادِي فِي الْعَاشِر مِنْ نُوفِمْبِر
عِيد مِيلَادِي فِي الْعَاشِرَة مِنْ أُكْتُوبَر

exercises.promptTranslation: Today is the eleventh of December.

exercises.prompt: سَنَذْهَب إِلَى الْمَكْتَبَة فِي ___ مِنْ نُوفِمْبِر.
exercises.explanation: After فِي the ending is ـِين.
exercises.promptTranslation: We will go to the library on the twentieth of November.

lessons.title: 152. Holidays and good wishes
lessons.subtitle: عِيد سَعِيد · كُلّ عَام وَأَنْتَ بِخَيْر · مَبْرُوك

explanations.title: Words for holidays
explanations.body: عِيد is a feast or a holiday that comes back every year, such as a national day or a religious festival. عُطْلَة is time off work or school. A birthday is عِيد مِيلَاد, literally “a feast of birth”.

explanations.title: What to say
explanations.body: On a feast or a birthday people say عِيد سَعِيد (“a happy feast”) or كُلّ عَام وَأَنْتَ بِخَيْر (“every year and you are well”). The answer is وَأَنْتَ بِخَيْر, “and you too”. For a woman the words change to وَأَنْتِ and for a group to وَأَنْتُمْ. For good news, say مَبْرُوك, “congratulations”. Many Arab countries have the feasts of the Islamic calendar, and Christian communities also celebrate عِيد الْمِيلَاد (Christmas).

examples.translation: ʿīd saʿīd! — Happy holiday!
kull ʿām waʾanta bikhayr. — Many happy returns. (to a man)
waʾanti bikhayr. — And you too. (to a woman)
ghadan ʿīd mīlād ʾukhtī. — Tomorrow is my sister’s birthday.
ʿindanā ʿuṭla ṭawīla fī al-ʿīd. — We have a long holiday for the Eid.
ʾayna satakūn fī al-ʿuṭla? — Where will you be during the holiday? (to a man)

exercises.prompt: A man says كُلّ عَام وَأَنْتَ بِخَيْر. What do you answer?
How do you answer a woman who says كُلّ عَام وَأَنْتِ بِخَيْر?
Which means “We have a long holiday”?

exercises.promptTranslation: Tomorrow is my sister’s birthday.
Happy holiday!

explanations.title: Asking about plans
explanations.body: Use مَاذَا سَتَفْعَل؟ (“what will you do?”) and answer with سَـ for what you will do and لَنْ for what you will not do. A friend can invite you with هَلْ تُرِيد أَنْ تَذْهَب مَعِي؟

explanations.title: A holiday plan
explanations.body: Here is a short text. Read it, then answer the questions.

examples.text: فِي الْأُسْبُوع الْقَادِم عِنْدَنَا عُطْلَة طَوِيلَة.
examples.translation: fī al-ʾusbūʿ al-qādim ʿindanā ʿuṭla ṭawīla. — Next week we have a long holiday.

examples.text: سَنَسْتَيْقِظ فِي السَّاعَة التَّاسِعَة وَلَنْ نَذْهَب إِلَى الْمَدْرَسَة.

examples.translation: fī as-sāʿa ath-thāniya sanataghaddā maʿa al-ʾusra. — At two o’clock we will have lunch with the family.

examples.translation: yajib ʾan ʾaktub al-wājib qabla al-ʿashāʾ. — I must do my homework before dinner.

lessons.title: 154. Buying things

explanations.title: In the shop
explanations.body: Use the numbers you know. أَدْفَع (I pay) is a regular verb. أُرِيد أَنْ أَشْتَرِي (“I want to buy”) is a phrase to learn as it is for now.

explanations.title: Prices
explanations.body: Ask كَمْ ثَمَن…؟ or بِكَمْ…؟ and answer with the number and the money.

examples.translation: kam thaman hādhā al-qamīṣ? — How much is this shirt?
thamanuhu khamsa waʿishrūn dīnāran. — It costs twenty-five dinars.

examples.text: هَذِه الْحَقِيبَة غَالِيَة. ثَمَنُهَا مِئَة دُولَار.

ʾurīd ʾan ʾashtarī ḥidhāʾ. — I want to buy shoes.
ʾadfaʿ thalāthīn dīnāran. — I pay thirty dinars.

lessons.title: 155. Review: time and numbers
lessons.subtitle: كَمِ السَّاعَة؟ · خَمْسَة وَعِشْرُون · مِئَة دِينَار

explanations.title: Questions with كَمْ
explanations.body: Five short exchanges use the time, a count, an age and a price.

examples.text: كَمِ السَّاعَة الْآن؟ السَّاعَة الثَّالِثَة وَالرُّبْع.
examples.translation: kami as-sāʿa al-ʾān? as-sāʿa ath-thālitha war-rubʿ. — What time is it now? It is a quarter past three.

examples.text: مَتَى الدَّرْس؟ الدَّرْس فِي السَّاعَة الْخَامِسَة إِلَّا رُبْعًا.
examples.translation: matā ad-dars? ad-dars fī as-sāʿa al-khāmisa ʾillā rubʿan. — When is the lesson? The lesson is at a quarter to five.

examples.text: كَمْ طَالِبًا فِي الصَّفّ؟ فِي الصَّفّ ثَمَانِيَةَ عَشَرَ طَالِبًا.
examples.translation: kam ṭāliban fī aṣ-ṣaff? fī aṣ-ṣaff thamāniyata ʿashara ṭāliban. — How many students are in the class? There are eighteen students in the class.

examples.text: كَمْ عُمْرُكِ؟ عُمْرِي خَمْس وَعِشْرُون سَنَةً.
examples.translation: kam ʿumruki? ʿumrī khams waʿishrūn sanatan. — How old are you? (to a woman) I am twenty-five years old.

examples.text: كَمْ ثَمَن هَذَا الْكِتَاب؟ ثَمَنُهُ مِئَة دِينَار.

nataghaddā fī as-sāʿa ath-thāniya wan-niṣf. — We have lunch at half past two.

lessons.title: 156. Review: my day and my plans
lessons.subtitle: أَسْتَيْقِظ · أُنَظِّف · أَتَكَلَّم · لَنْ أَنَام

explanations.title: My day, my plans
explanations.body: A student describes today and next week, with times, new verb patterns and لَنْ.

examples.text: أَسْتَيْقِظ فِي السَّاعَة السَّادِسَة وَأَتَنَاوَل الْإِفْطَار مَعَ أُسْرَتِي.
examples.translation: ʾastayqiẓ fī as-sāʿa as-sādisa waʾatanāwal al-ʾifṭār maʿa ʾusratī. — I wake up at six and have breakfast with my family.

examples.text: أَتَكَلَّم مَعَ مُدَرِّسِي بَعْدَ الدَّرْس وَأَتَعَلَّم كَلِمَات جَدِيدَة.
examples.translation: ʾatakallam maʿa mudarrisī baʿda ad-dars waʾataʿallam kalimāt jadīda. — I talk with my teacher after the lesson and learn new words.

examples.text: أَتَغَدَّى فِي السَّاعَة الْوَاحِدَة ثُمَّ أُنَظِّف غُرْفَتِي.
examples.translation: ʾataghaddā fī as-sāʿa al-wāḥida thumma ʾunaẓẓif ghurfatī. — I have lunch at one and then I clean my room.
ʾanām fī as-sāʿa al-ʿāshira wan-niṣf. — I go to bed at half past ten.

examples.text: فِي الْأُسْبُوع الْقَادِم عِنْدِي عُطْلَة، وَلَنْ أَسْتَيْقِظ فِي السَّاعَة السَّادِسَة.
examples.translation: fī al-ʾusbūʿ al-qādim ʿindī ʿuṭla, walan ʾastayqiẓ fī as-sāʿa as-sādisa. — Next week I have a holiday, and I will not wake up at six.

examples.translation: baʿda thalātha ʾayyām saʾadhhab maʿa ʾaṣdiqāʾī ʾilā al-madīna. — In three days I will go to the city with my friends.

units.title: وَقْت الْفَرَاغ: hobbies, preferences, Measures III and VI, and eating out

lessons.title: 157. Free time
lessons.subtitle: مَاذَا تَفْعَل فِي وَقْت الْفَرَاغ؟ · أُحِبّ الْقِرَاءَة

explanations.title: Hobbies
explanations.body: وَقْت الْفَرَاغ is “free time”. Many hobbies are verbal nouns, and they take ال. You can ask a man مَاذَا تَفْعَل فِي وَقْت الْفَرَاغ؟ and answer with أُحِبّ and a hobby.

explanations.title: I like…
explanations.body: After أُحِبّ you can put a noun, or أَنْ and a verb. You can say it about other people too: تُحِبّ (she or you, to a man), نُحِبّ (we), يُحِبّ (he).

examples.translation: mādhā tafʿal fī waqt al-farāgh? — What do you do in your free time? (to a man)
ʾuḥibb al-qirāʾa wal-mūsīqā. — I like reading and music.
ʾuḥibb ʾan ʾarsum fī al-ḥadīqa. — I like to draw in the park.
ʾukhtī tuḥibb as-sibāḥa fī al-baḥr. — My sister likes swimming in the sea.

examples.text: لَا أُحِبّ الطَّبْخ، لَكِنْ أُحِبّ الْمَشْيْ.
examples.translation: lā ʾuḥibb aṭ-ṭabkh, lākin ʾuḥibb al-mashy. — I do not like cooking, but I like walking.

examples.text: نُحِبّ أَنْ نَذْهَب فِي رِحْلَة كُلّ شَهْر.
examples.translation: nuḥibb ʾan nadhhab fī riḥla kull shahr. — We like to go on a trip every month.

exercises.prompt: Which means “I do not like cooking”?
Which means “We like to go on a trip”?
مَاذَا تَفْعَل فِي وَقْت ___؟ (to a man)
exercises.promptTranslation: What do you do in your free time?
I like to draw in the park.

lessons.title: 158. I prefer… : أُفَضِّل
lessons.subtitle: أُفَضِّل الشَّايْ عَلَى الْقَهْوَة · أَفْضَل رِيَاضَة

explanations.title: Preferring one thing to another
explanations.body: فَضَّلَ (to prefer) is a Measure II verb, like دَرَّسَ. Its present is أُفَضِّل. You prefer one thing to another with عَلَى: أُفَضِّل الشَّايْ عَلَى الْقَهْوَة. To ask a choice, use هَلْ and أَمْ (“or”; formal writing often uses أَ instead of هَلْ): هَلْ تُفَضِّل السِّينَمَا أَمِ الْمَسْرَح؟

explanations.title: Better and best
explanations.body: أَفْضَل means “better” (with مِنْ for “than”) or “best”. For “the best + noun”, put أَفْضَل in front of a singular noun without ال: أَفْضَل رِيَاضَة.

examples.translation: ʾufaḍḍil ash-shāy ʿalā al-qahwa. — I prefer tea to coffee.
hal tufaḍḍil as-sīnamā ʾami al-masraḥ? — Do you prefer the cinema or the theatre? (to a man)
limādhā tufaḍḍilīn al-mūsīqā? — Why do you prefer music? (to a woman)
ʾufaḍḍil al-mashy ʿalā as-sibāḥa. — I prefer walking to swimming.

examples.text: هَذَا الْفِيلْم أَفْضَل مِنَ الْفِيلْم الْآخَر.
examples.translation: hādhā al-fīlm ʾafḍal mina al-fīlm al-ʾākhar. — This film is better than the other film.
ʾafḍal riyāḍa ʿindī hiya as-sibāḥa. — My favourite sport is swimming.

exercises.prompt: Which means “I prefer tea to coffee”?
Which means “Do you prefer the cinema or the theatre?” (to a man)
Which means “Why do you prefer music?” (to a woman)
Which means “This film is better than the other film”?
options: هَذَا الْفِيلْم أَفْضَل عَلَى الْفِيلْم الْآخَر
هَذَا الْفِيلْم أَفْضَل مِنَ الْفِيلْم الْآخَر

exercises.promptTranslation: I prefer walking to swimming.
This film is better than the other film.

lessons.title: 159. Sports and the places for them
lessons.subtitle: أَلْعَب كُرَة الْقَدَم · النَّادِي · الْمَلْعَب

explanations.title: Playing sports
explanations.body: You play a ball sport with لَعِبَ: أَلْعَب كُرَة الْقَدَم (“I play football”, literally “the ball of the foot”). Swimming uses سَبَحَ: أَسْبَح. A sport takes place at a club (نَادِي), a stadium or field (مَلْعَب) or a swimming pool (مَسْبَح).

explanations.title: In sentences
explanations.body: Sport sentences use the verbs you know, with times and places.

examples.translation: ʾalʿab kura al-qadam fī an-nādī. — I play football at the club.
nalʿab kura as-salla yawm al-jumʿa. — We play basketball on Friday.
al-mubārāh fī as-sāʿa as-sābiʿa masāʾan. — The match is at seven in the evening.
farīqī yalʿab fī al-malʿab al-kabīr. — My team plays in the big stadium.
ʾasbaḥ fī al-masbaḥ kull ṣabāḥ. — I swim in the pool every morning.

examples.text: هَلْ تَلْعَب كُرَة الْقَدَم يَا أَحْمَد؟
examples.translation: hal talʿab kura al-qadam yā ʾaḥmad? — Do you play football, Ahmad?

exercises.prompt: Which means “I play football at the club”?
Which means “We play basketball on Friday”?
Which means “I swim in the pool every morning”?
Which means “The match is at seven in the evening”?

exercises.promptTranslation: I play football at the club.
My team plays in the big stadium.

explanations.title: A long ā after the first letter
explanations.body: Measure III has a long ā after the first root letter. The past is فَاعَلَ (سَاعَدَ, “he helped”) and the present is يُفَاعِل (يُسَاعِد). The present prefix has ḍamma, like Measure II, but the long ā comes before the second letter and there is a kasra before the last letter. Many Measure III verbs mean doing something with someone else.

explanations.title: In sentences
explanations.body: The endings are the ones you know. Compare the present of Measure III with Measure II: يُدَرِّس has a doubled letter, يُسَاعِد has a long ā.

examples.translation: ʾusāʿid ʾummī fī al-bayt. — I help my mother at home.
nushāhid fīlm jamīl fī as-sīnamā. — We watch a nice film at the cinema.
sāfara ʾabī ʾilā al-ʾurdunn ʾams. — My father travelled to Jordan yesterday.
qābaltu mudarrisī fī al-maktaba. — I met my teacher in the library.
hal turāfiq ʾakhī ʾilā an-nādī? — Are you going with my brother to the club? (to a man)
ʾukhtī tushārik fī al-mubārāh. — My sister takes part in the match.

exercises.explanation: أُ + a long ā + a kasra.

exercises.prompt: Which means “I met my teacher in the library”?

exercises.promptTranslation: My father travelled to Jordan yesterday.
My sister takes part in the match.

explanations.title: The past of شَاهَدَ
explanations.body: The past endings are the ones you know from كَتَبَ and دَرَسَ. The long ā stays in every form. In the future, put سَـ in front of the present: سَأُشَاهِد.

examples.translation: shāhadtu mubārāh kura al-qadam ʾams. — I watched the football match yesterday.
hal shāhadta hādhā al-fīlm? — Did you watch this film? (to a man)
shāhadat ʾukhtī fīlm jamīl. — My sister watched a nice film.
sanushāhid al-mubārāh fī an-nādī ghadan. — We will watch the match at the club tomorrow.
lan ʾushāhid at-tilfāz al-layla. — I will not watch television tonight.
sāʿadanī ʾakhī fī al-wājib. — My brother helped me with the homework.

exercises.prompt: Which means “We will watch the match tomorrow”?
Which means “I will not watch television tonight”?
Which means “My brother helped me with the homework”?
___ هَذَا الْفِيلْم؟ (Did you watch, to a man)
exercises.explanation: A past verb: you (to a man).
exercises.promptTranslation: Did you watch this film?
We will watch the match at the club tomorrow.

lessons.title: 162. Trying, taking part, agreeing
lessons.subtitle: حَاوَلَ أَنْ · شَارَكَ فِي · وَافَقَ عَلَى

explanations.title: Measure III verbs and what follows them
explanations.body: Many verbs need a particular word after them. حَاوَلَ is followed by أَنْ and a verb, شَارَكَ by فِي, وَافَقَ by عَلَى. Learn the verb together with its word.

explanations.title: In sentences
explanations.body: After أَنْ the present verb has the shortened endings you know.

examples.text: أُحَاوِل أَنْ أَتَكَلَّم الْعَرَبِيَّة كُلّ يَوْم.
examples.translation: ʾuḥāwil ʾan ʾatakallam al-ʿarabiyya kull yawm. — I try to speak Arabic every day.
ḥāwala ʾakhī ʾan yaftaḥ al-bāb. — My brother tried to open the door.
shāraktu fī ar-riḥla. — I took part in the trip.
ʾuwāfiq ʿalā hādhihi al-fikra. — I agree with this idea.
lā ʾuwāfiq ʿalā hādhā al-mawʿid. — I do not agree to this time.
sāʿadatnī ʾukhtī fī al-wājib. — My sister helped me with the homework.

exercises.prompt: Which means “I try to speak Arabic every day”?
options: أُحَاوِل أَنْ أَتَكَلَّم الْعَرَبِيَّة كُلّ يَوْم
أُحَاوِل أَنْ تَتَكَلَّم الْعَرَبِيَّة كُلّ يَوْم
حَاوَلْتُ أَنْ أَتَكَلَّم الْعَرَبِيَّة كُلّ يَوْم

exercises.prompt: Which means “I took part in the trip”?
Which means “I do not agree to this time”?
Which means “My brother tried to open the door”?

exercises.promptTranslation: I agree with this idea.
I took part in the trip.

explanations.title: Doing it to each other
explanations.body: Put تَـ in front of a Measure III verb and you get Measure VI, written تَفَاعَلَ. It usually means two or more people do the action to each other: قَابَلَ (to meet someone) gives تَقَابَلَ (to meet each other). This repeats what happened between Measures II and V: Measure V is II with تَـ, Measure VI is III with تَـ. The present is يَتَفَاعَل.

explanations.title: In sentences
explanations.body: Because the action goes between people, the subject is often “we” or “they”.

examples.translation: nataqābal fī an-nādī yawm al-jumʿa. — We meet at the club on Friday.
taqābalnā ʾams fī al-ḥadīqa. — We met yesterday in the park.
nataḥādath kull masāʾ. — We talk to each other every evening.
natabādal al-kutub. — We exchange books.
yataʿāwan aṭ-ṭullāb fī al-wājib. — The students cooperate on the homework.
sanataqābal baʿda ad-dars. — We will meet after the lesson.

exercises.prompt: Which is “we talk to each other”?
Which means “We met yesterday in the park”?
Which means “We will meet after the lesson”?

exercises.promptTranslation: We meet at the club on Friday.
The students cooperate on the homework.

lessons.title: 164. Let’s meet!
lessons.subtitle: هَلْ تُرِيد أَنْ تُرَافِقَنِي؟ · أَيْنَ نَتَقَابَل؟

explanations.title: An invitation
explanations.body: To invite someone use هَلْ تُرِيد أَنْ … and a verb. With an ending for “me” the verb gets a ن first: تُرَافِقَنِي (you accompany me). Then fix the time and the place with مَتَى and أَيْنَ.

rows: هَلْ تُرِيد أَنْ تُرَافِقَنِي إِلَى السِّينَمَا؟
hal turīd ʾan turāfiqanī ʾilā as-sīnamā?

explanations.title: Saying yes and no
explanations.body: Agree with فِكْرَة جَيِّدَة (“good idea”) or حَسَنًا (“fine”). To refuse politely, say آسِف and give a reason.

examples.text: هَلْ تُرِيدِين أَنْ تُرَافِقِينِي إِلَى الْمُبَارَاة؟
examples.translation: hal turīdīn ʾan turāfiqīnī ʾilā al-mubārāh? — Do you want to come with me to the match? (to a woman)
naʿam, fikra jayyida. matā nataqābal? — Yes, good idea. When shall we meet?

examples.text: نَتَقَابَل فِي السَّاعَة الرَّابِعَة وَالنِّصْف أَمَامَ النَّادِي.
examples.translation: nataqābal fī as-sāʿa ar-rābiʿa wan-niṣf ʾamāma an-nādī. — We meet at half past four in front of the club.
ʾāsif, ʿindī mawʿid ghadan. — Sorry, I have an appointment tomorrow. (a man speaking)
lā ʾuwāfiq ʿalā hādhā al-makān. — This place does not suit me.
ḥasanan, ʾilā al-liqāʾ ghadan. — Fine, see you tomorrow.

exercises.prompt: Which invites someone to the cinema?
options: هَلْ تُرِيد أَنْ تُرَافِقَنِي إِلَى السِّينَمَا؟

explanations.title: Dishes you can find in many places
explanations.body: Falafel is made from chickpeas or beans, shawarma is meat cut from a spit, tabbouleh is a fresh salad of parsley and wheat, hummus is a chickpea dip and baklava is a very sweet pastry. They are eaten in many Arab countries, with small differences from place to place.

explanations.title: Talking about food
explanations.body: Use the words you already know for taste and for likes.

examples.translation: al-falāfil ladhīdha warakhīṣa. — Falafel is delicious and cheap.
ʾuḥibb al-ḥummuṣ maʿa al-khubz. — I like hummus with bread.
hal jarrabta at-tabbūla? — Have you tried tabbouleh? (to a man)
al-baqlāwa ḥulwa jiddan. — Baklava is very sweet.
nashrab ash-shāy bin-naʿnāʿ baʿda al-ghadāʾ. — We drink tea with mint after lunch.
ʾufaḍḍil ash-shāwirmā ʿalā al-falāfil. — I prefer shawarma to falafel.

lessons.title: 166. Booking a table and paying
lessons.subtitle: أُرِيد أَنْ أَحْجِز طَاوِلَة · الْحِسَاب مِنْ فَضْلِكَ

explanations.title: At the restaurant, step by step
explanations.body: Phone the restaurant to book a table. For the number of people use the numbers 3–10 with the plural أَشْخَاص, and remember that شَخْص is masculine, so the number ends in ـَة (أَرْبَعَة). Then ask for the menu and, at the end, for the bill.

rows: I want to book a table

explanations.title: In sentences
explanations.body: Notice how the numbers you learned earlier are used for the people and the bill.

examples.text: أُرِيد أَنْ أَحْجِز طَاوِلَة لِسِتَّة أَشْخَاص.
examples.translation: ʾurīd ʾan ʾaḥjiz ṭāwila lisitta ʾashkhāṣ. — I want to book a table for six people.

examples.text: فِي أَيّ سَاعَة؟ فِي السَّاعَة الثَّامِنَة مَسَاءً.
examples.translation: fī ʾayy sāʿa? fī as-sāʿa ath-thāmina masāʾan. — At what time? At eight in the evening.
min faḍlika, al-qāʾima. — The menu, please. (to a man)
hal tufaḍḍilīn ad-dajāj ʾami as-samak? — Do you prefer chicken or fish? (to a woman)
al-ḥisāb min faḍlika. kami al-ḥisāb? — The bill, please. How much is the bill? (to a man)
al-ḥisāb khamsa wasabʿūn dīnāran. — The bill is seventy-five dinars.

exercises.prompt: Which means “I want to book a table for six people”?
options: أُرِيد أَنْ أَحْجِز طَاوِلَة لِسِتَّة شَخْص
أُرِيد أَنْ أَحْجِز طَاوِلَة لِسِتَّة أَشْخَاص
أُرِيد أَنْ أَحْجِز طَاوِلَة لِسِتّ أَشْخَاص

exercises.prompt: Which means “The bill is seventy-five dinars”?
exercises.explanation: Unit, وَ, ten; masculine noun: خَمْسَة.
I want to + a present verb.
exercises.promptTranslation: I want to book a table.

exercises.explanation: At the end of the meal.
exercises.promptTranslation: The bill, please.

explanations.title: Two friends talk about free time
explanations.body: Rana and Sami compare what they like to do.

examples.text: مَاذَا تَفْعَل فِي وَقْت الْفَرَاغ يَا سَامِي؟
examples.translation: mādhā tafʿal fī waqt al-farāgh yā sāmī? — What do you do in your free time, Sami?

examples.text: أَلْعَب كُرَة الْقَدَم فِي النَّادِي، وَأُحِبّ أَنْ أَسْبَح أَيْضًا.
examples.translation: ʾalʿab kura al-qadam fī an-nādī, waʾuḥibb ʾan ʾasbaḥ ʾayḍan. — I play football at the club, and I also like to swim.

examples.text: وَأَنَا أُفَضِّل الْقِرَاءَة وَالرَّسْم عَلَى الرِّيَاضَة.
examples.translation: waʾanā ʾufaḍḍil al-qirāʾa war-rasm ʿalā ar-riyāḍa. — And I prefer reading and drawing to sport.
hal tushāhidīn al-ʾaflām? — Do you watch films? (to a woman)
naʿam, shāhadtu fīlm jamīl ʾams. — Yes, I watched a nice film yesterday.

examples.translation: lan ʾalʿab ghadan liʾanna ʿindī mawʿid. — I will not play tomorrow because I have an appointment.

lessons.title: 168. Review: Measures III and VI, and a meal out
lessons.subtitle: شَاهَدْنَا · تَقَابَلْنَا · أَحْجِز · الْحِسَاب

explanations.title: A Saturday outing
explanations.body: Laila tells her friend about an outing with her family.

examples.text: تَقَابَلْنَا أَمَامَ الْمَطْعَم فِي السَّاعَة الثَّامِنَة مَسَاءً.
examples.translation: taqābalnā ʾamāma al-maṭʿam fī as-sāʿa ath-thāmina masāʾan. — We met in front of the restaurant at eight in the evening.
ḥajaza ʾabī ṭāwila likhamsa ʾashkhāṣ. — My father booked a table for five people.
sāʿadtu ʾummī fī al-maṭʿam. — I helped my mother at the restaurant.

examples.text: نَظَرْنَا فِي الْقَائِمَة وَجَرَّبْنَا الْفَلَافِل وَالتَّبُّولَة.
examples.translation: naẓarnā fī al-qāʾima wajarrabnā al-falāfil wat-tabbūla. — We looked at the menu and tried the falafel and the tabbouleh.

examples.text: كَانَ الطَّعَام لَذِيذًا، لَكِنَّ الْبَقْلَاوَة كَانَتْ حُلْوَةً جِدًّا.
examples.translation: kāna aṭ-ṭaʿām ladhīdhan, lākinna al-baqlāwa kānat ḥulwatan jiddan. — The food was delicious, but the baklava was very sweet.

examples.text: دَفَعَ أَبِي الْحِسَاب، ثُمَّ رَجَعْنَا إِلَى الْبَيْت.
examples.translation: dafaʿa ʾabī al-ḥisāb, thumma rajaʿnā ʾilā al-bayt. — My father paid the bill, then we went home.

units.title: نِهَايَة الْأُسْبُوع: weekends, trips, weather plans and suggestions

lessons.title: 169. A map of the verb patterns
lessons.subtitle: كَتَبَ · دَرَّسَ · سَاعَدَ · تَعَلَّمَ · تَقَابَلَ

explanations.title: Five patterns side by side
explanations.body: You now know five verb patterns, called Measures. Each one has a clue you can see in the verb. If you see a verb you do not know, look at the clue first and you already know part of what it will do.

rows: a long ā after the first letter
تَـ at the start and the middle letter doubled
تَـ at the start and a long ā

explanations.title: Reading a verb
explanations.body: Measure II often means “cause” (دَرَّسَ, to teach) and Measure V often means “do it to yourself” (تَعَلَّمَ, to learn). Measure III and VI are about other people: with someone, or to each other.

examples.translation: yaktub ʾakhī risāla. — My brother writes a letter.
tudarris ʾukhtī al-ʿarabiyya. — My sister teaches Arabic.
yusāʿid ʾabī ʾummī fī al-maṭbakh. — My father helps my mother in the kitchen.
yataʿallam ʾakhī al-ʿarabiyya. — My brother learns Arabic.
yataqābal aṭ-ṭullāb fī al-maktaba. — The students meet each other in the library.
takallamat mudarrisatī maʿa ʾummī. — My teacher spoke with my mother.

exercises.prompt: Which verb has a long ā after the first letter?
Which verb has a doubled middle letter and no تَـ?

options: people did it to each other

exercises.promptTranslation: The students meet each other in the library.
My brother learns Arabic.

explanations.title: Telling the story in order
explanations.body: Use the past tense for what happened and small words to put the events in order. The weekend is نِهَايَة الْأُسْبُوع (“the end of the week”).

explanations.title: A story in the past
explanations.body: The verbs about what we did are in the past tense with ـنَا (“we”).

examples.text: فِي نِهَايَة الْأُسْبُوع الْمَاضِي ذَهَبْنَا إِلَى الْبَحْر.
examples.translation: fī nihāya al-ʾusbūʿ al-māḍī dhahabnā ʾilā al-baḥr. — Last weekend we went to the sea.
ʾawwalan rakibnā al-ḥāfila ʾilā ash-shāṭiʾ. — First we took the bus to the beach.
thumma sabaḥnā walaʿibnā kura al-qadam. — Then we swam and played football.
baʿdahā taghaddaynā fī maṭʿam ṣaghīr. — After that we had lunch in a small restaurant.

examples.text: أَخِيرًا رَجَعْنَا إِلَى الْبَيْت فِي السَّاعَة التَّاسِعَة.
examples.translation: ʾakhīran rajaʿnā ʾilā al-bayt fī as-sāʿa at-tāsiʿa. — Finally we went home at nine o’clock.
kāna al-jaww jamīlan yawm as-sabt. — The weather was nice on Saturday.

exercises.prompt: Which word means “first” in a story?
Which means “First we took the bus to the beach”?
Which means “Finally we went home at nine”?
options: أَخِيرًا رَجَعْنَا إِلَى الْبَيْت فِي السَّاعَة الثَّامِنَة
أَخِيرًا رَجَعْنَا إِلَى الْبَيْت فِي السَّاعَة التَّاسِعَة
أَخِيرًا سَنَرْجِع إِلَى الْبَيْت فِي السَّاعَة التَّاسِعَة
أَوَّلًا رَجَعْنَا إِلَى الْبَيْت فِي السَّاعَة التَّاسِعَة

exercises.explanation: The first step of the story.
exercises.promptTranslation: First we took the bus to the beach.
Then we swam and played football.

explanations.title: Visit
explanations.body: The verb زَارَ (“to visit”) has a long ā in the middle. In the past, when an ending like ـتُ or ـنَا is added, the long vowel becomes short: زُرْتُ, زُرْنَا. In the present it has a long ū: أَزُور. The place comes straight after the verb, with no preposition.

explanations.title: In sentences
explanations.body: Use زَارَ for places and for people.

examples.translation: zurnā al-mutḥaf yawm as-sabt. — We visited the museum on Saturday.
zurtu al-qalʿa maʿa ʾusratī. — I visited the castle with my family.
hal zurta al-madīna al-qadīma? — Have you visited the old city? (to a man)
nazūr as-sūq kull ʾusbūʿ. — We visit the market every week.
saʾazūr jaddī ghadan. — I will visit my grandfather tomorrow.
zārat ʾukhtī al-mīnāʾ ʾams. — My sister visited the port yesterday.

exercises.explanation: The long vowel shortens before ـتُ.

exercises.prompt: Which means “We visited the museum on Saturday”?
Which means “I will visit my grandfather tomorrow”?
Does زَارَ need a preposition before the place?

exercises.promptTranslation: I visited the castle with my family.
Have you visited the old city?

explanations.title: Vehicles and places
explanations.body: To say “by train”, use بِـ: بِالْقِطَار. A taxi is سَيَّارَة أُجْرَة, literally “a hired car”. The verbs رَكِبَ (to ride, to board), نَزَلَ (to get off), وَصَلَ إِلَى (to arrive at) and سَافَرَ (to travel) go with them.

explanations.title: Travelling
explanations.body: Notice the prepositions: بِـ for the vehicle, إِلَى for the destination, مِنْ for where you left.

examples.translation: sāfarnā biṭ-ṭāʾira ʾilā al-ʾurdunn. — We travelled by plane to Jordan.
ʾadhhab ʾilā al-madrasa bil-ḥāfila. — I go to school by bus.
rakibtu al-qiṭār fī al-maḥaṭṭa. — I took the train at the station.

examples.text: وَصَلْنَا إِلَى الْمَطَار فِي السَّاعَة الْخَامِسَة.
examples.translation: waṣalnā ʾilā al-maṭār fī as-sāʿa al-khāmisa. — We arrived at the airport at five o’clock.
nazalnā mina al-ḥāfila ʾamāma al-mutḥaf. — We got off the bus in front of the museum.
hal tadhhab bis-sayyāra ʾam bil-qiṭār? — Are you going by car or by train? (to a man)

exercises.prompt: Which means “We arrived at the airport”?
Which means “We got off the bus”?
Which means “I took the train at the station”?

exercises.promptTranslation: I go to school by bus.

lessons.title: 173. If the weather is nice: إِذَا
lessons.subtitle: إِذَا كَانَ الْجَوّ جَمِيلًا فَسَنَذْهَب

explanations.title: إِذَا + كَانَ
explanations.body: إِذَا means “if” (or “when”) for something that may well happen. After إِذَا the verb is usually in the PAST tense, even though the sentence is about the future (for “if … not”, use إِذَا لَمْ يَكُنِ …). The second part of the sentence often starts with فَـ (“then”) and has سَـ or the present: فَسَنَذْهَب. Remember that the predicate of كَانَ takes ـًا.

examples.text: إِذَا كَانَ الْجَوّ جَمِيلًا غَدًا فَسَنَذْهَب إِلَى الشَّاطِئ.
examples.translation: ʾidhā kāna al-jaww jamīlan ghadan fasanadhhab ʾilā ash-shāṭiʾ. — If the weather is nice tomorrow, we will go to the beach.

examples.text: إِذَا كَانَ الْجَوّ حَارًّا فَسَأَسْبَح فِي الْمَسْبَح.
examples.translation: ʾidhā kāna al-jaww ḥārran fasaʾasbaḥ fī al-masbaḥ. — If the weather is hot, I will swim in the pool.

examples.text: إِذَا كَانَ الْجَوّ مُمْطِرًا فَسَنُشَاهِد فِيلْم فِي الْبَيْت.
examples.translation: ʾidhā kāna al-jaww mumṭiran fasanushāhid fīlm fī al-bayt. — If the weather is rainy, we will watch a film at home.

examples.text: إِذَا كَانَ عِنْدِي وَقْت فَسَأُرَافِقُكَ إِلَى السُّوق.
examples.translation: ʾidhā kāna ʿindī waqt fasaʾurāfiquka ʾilā as-sūq. — If I have time, I will go with you to the market. (to a man)

examples.text: إِذَا لَمْ يَكُنِ الْجَوّ بَارِدًا فَسَنَلْعَب فِي الْحَدِيقَة.
examples.translation: ʾidhā lam yakuni al-jaww bāridan fasanalʿab fī al-ḥadīqa. — If the weather is not cold, we will play in the park.
kayfa sayakūn al-jaww ghadan? — What will the weather be like tomorrow?

إِذَا كَانَ الْجَوّ بَارِدًا غَدًا فَسَنَذْهَب إِلَى الشَّاطِئ

إِذَا كَانَ الْجَوّ مُمْطِرًا فَسَيُشَاهِدُون فِيلْم فِي الْبَيْت
إِذَا كَانَ الْجَوّ مُشْمِسًا فَسَنُشَاهِد فِيلْم فِي الْبَيْت
إِذَا كَانَ الْجَوّ مُمْطِرًا فَسَنُشَاهِد فِيلْم فِي الْبَيْت

exercises.prompt: Which means “If the weather is not cold”?

explanations.body: To suggest something to a friend, use هَيَّا (“come on”) and a verb with نَـ (“we”), or ask لِمَاذَا لَا نَـ… (“why don’t we…?”), or say أَقْتَرِح أَنْ (“I suggest that”). Ask for an opinion with مَا رَأْيُكَ؟ (to a man) or مَا رَأْيُكِ؟ (to a woman).

units.title: الصَّفّ وَالْمَرَافِق: the classroom, comparing, school places and the genitive

explanations.title: Furniture and equipment
explanations.body: Most of these words are feminine because they end in ـَة (السَّبُّورَة, الطَّاوِلَة, الطَّابِعَة), but الْكُرْسِيّ, الْحَاسُوب, الْبَاب and الْحَائِط are masculine. Two words have more than one name: a wall is الْحَائِط (the outside or standing wall) or الْجِدَار, and a window is النَّافِذَة or الشُّبَّاك.

explanations.title: Plural: more than one
explanations.body: Several of these nouns have a broken plural: one chair is كُرْسِيّ, but chairs are كَرَاسِيّ; the plural of جِدَار (wall) is جُدْرَان. With the numbers 3 to 10 the counted noun is plural, and the number takes the opposite gender (you met this rule in Unit 5).

examples.translation: fī aṣ-ṣaff sabbūra kabīra. — There is a big board in the classroom.
ʿalā al-ḥāʾiṭ kharīṭa lil-ʿālam. — On the wall there is a map of the world.
al-ḥāsūb waṭ-ṭābiʿa ʿalā aṭ-ṭāwila. — The computer and the printer are on the table.
hunāk ʿashara karāsiyy fī aṣ-ṣaff. — There are ten chairs in the classroom.
lawn al-judrān ʾabyaḍ. — The colour of the walls is white.
ʾarā ash-shāsha jayyidan min hunā. — I can see the screen well from here.

exercises.explanation: سَبُّورَة = a board you write on.

lessons.title: 182. Describing the room: opposites
lessons.subtitle: جَدِيد ≠ قَدِيم · وَاسِع ≠ ضَيِّق · نَظِيف ≠ وَسِخ

explanations.title: Pairs of opposites
explanations.body: A room, a table or a lamp is described with an adjective that comes AFTER the noun and agrees with it. Learning adjectives in opposite pairs makes them easy to remember. For a feminine noun add ـَة: نَافِذَة وَاسِعَة, غُرْفَة ضَيِّقَة.

explanations.title: In sentences
explanations.body: With a plural noun that is not a person (chairs, walls, windows) the adjective is feminine singular: كَرَاسِيّ جَدِيدَة, نَوَافِذ وَاسِعَة. After كَثِير and قَلِيل the noun is plural.

examples.translation: ṣaffī jadīd wawāsiʿ. — My classroom is new and spacious.
al-ghurfa al-qadīma ḍayyiqa. — The old room is narrow.
karāsiyy aṣ-ṣaff naẓīfa. — The classroom chairs are clean.
al-maktaba qarība wal-maṭʿam baʿīd. — The library is near and the restaurant is far.
fī aṣ-ṣaff kathīr mina al-kutub. — There are a lot of books in the classroom.
fī al-ghurfa nawāfidh qalīla. — There are few windows in the room.

lessons.title: 183. Where is it? Asking for help in class

explanations.title: Where in the room?
explanations.body: Words for place come before a noun and put it in the genitive (the case ending is not pronounced in this course, but you will study it soon). You already know أَمَامَ, خَلْفَ, تَحْتَ, فَوْقَ and بَيْنَ. Add these:

explanations.title: Polite requests
explanations.body: To ask someone in the room for something, use a command (see Unit 6) with مِنْ فَضْلِكَ (to a man) or مِنْ فَضْلِكِ (to a woman). Some useful commands: اِفْتَحْ (open), أَغْلِقْ (close), أَطْفِئِ الضَّوْء (turn off the light), اِرْفَعْ (raise, lift).

examples.translation: aṭ-ṭāwila fī wasaṭ aṣ-ṣaff. — The table is in the middle of the classroom.
al-miknasa fī az-zāwiya. — The broom is in the corner.

examples.text: الْخَرِيطَة عَلَى الْيَمِين وَالسَّبُّورَة عَلَى الْيَسَار.
examples.translation: al-kharīṭa ʿalā al-yamīn was-sabbūra ʿalā al-yasār. — The map is on the right and the board is on the left.
iftaḥi an-nāfidha min faḍlika. — Open the window, please. (to a man)
ʾaghliqī al-bāb min faḍliki. — Close the door, please. (to a woman)

examples.text: هَلْ يُمْكِنُنِي أَنْ أَنْقُل طَاوِلَتِي إِلَى الْأَمَام؟
examples.translation: hal yumkinunī ʾan ʾanqul ṭāwilatī ʾilā al-ʾamām? — May I move my desk to the front?

exercises.prompt: What does فِي وَسَط الصَّفّ mean?
options: in the middle of the classroom

exercises.prompt: Which command means “Close the door” (to a man)?

exercises.explanation: أَطْفِئ is the verb for turning off a light.

exercises.prompt: How do you say “Open the window, please” to a woman?

exercises.promptTranslation: The broom is in the corner.
The map is on the right and the board is on the left.
May I move my desk?

lessons.title: 184. Bigger, smaller, newer: the أَفْعَل pattern
lessons.subtitle: هَذَا الصَّفّ أَكْبَر مِنَ الصَّفّ الْقَدِيم

explanations.title: One pattern for “more”
explanations.body: English has two forms: “big, bigger, biggest”. Arabic makes “bigger” with one pattern, أَفْعَل. Take the three root letters (ك-ب-ر) and put them in the pattern: أَكْبَر.
